title: Rutherford's Atomic Model
notes: This page covers the foundational concepts of an alpha particle and early atomic models (Thomson's and Rutherford's models).
• Mass & Charge: It has a charge of 2 + and a mass of 4 amu.
• Concept: Often called the watermelon model or plum pudding model.
• Structure: The atom is imagined as a sphere of uniform positive charge, with negatively charged electrons embedded inside like seeds in a watermelon.
• Outcome: Discarded quickly because it could not explain later experimental results, specifically large-angle scattering.
• Setup: High-energy alpha particles from a radioactive source (like Radium) were passed through a slit in a lead plate and directed at a very thin gold foil (0.00006 cm thick).
• Detection: A circular, movable zinc sulphide (ZnS) screen flashed tiny spots of light (scintillations) when struck by alpha particles.
• Most particles: Passed straight through the foil without changing direction.
• A few particles: Were slightly deflected from their original path.
• Very few particles: Were heavily deflected or reflected backward.
Millions of shining spots over a large area indicate that the atom is mostly empty space. The tiny region causing heavy deflections represents the small, dense, positively charged nucleus.
• ~99% of particles: Passed straight through the gold foil.
• ~1 in 10,000: Deflected by large angles of 90° or more.
• 1 in 20,000: Bounced directly backward, suffering a 180° deflection.
• Empty Space: Most of the interior of an atom is hollow or empty because nearly all particles passed straight through.
• Positive Core: A heavy, positively charged center exists because like charges repel, causing the positive α-particles to deflect.
• Tiny Volume: The nucleus is exceptionally small compared to the total size of the atom.
• Straight Penetration: Most α-particles (~99%) passed completely straight through the gold foil.
• Small Deflections: Some α-particles were deflected through small angles.
• Large Deflections: Very few particles (about 1 in 10,000) bounced back at angles larger than 90°.
• Reversal: Approximately 1 in 20,000 particles suffered a maximum deflection of 180°.
• Hollow Atom: Most space inside the atom is empty because particles passed straight through.
• Positive Core: A heavy, positively charged body exists at the center to repel positive α-particles.
• Tiny Volume: The central core occupies an extremely small volume relative to the entire atom.
• Massive Nucleus: The central core contains almost all the atom's mass, enabling it to reflect heavy particles.
• The Nucleus: An atom consists of a tiny, positively charged center called the nucleus (radius ≈ 10⁻¹³ cm).
• Electronic Cloud: Electrons surround the nucleus within a much larger radius (atom radius ≈ 10⁻⁸ cm).
• Size Difference: The overall size of an atom is about 10⁵ (100,000) times larger than its nucleus.
• Electrostatic Attraction: Strong Coulombic electrostatic forces hold the negatively charged electrons and the positively charged nucleus together.
• Electrical Neutrality: The total number of protons inside the nucleus equals the number of electrons outside it, making the atom electrically neutral.

• Planetary Motion: Electrons revolve continuously around the nucleus in circular paths (orbits). The electrostatic pull toward the center is balanced by the outward centrifugal force. Because of this similarity to planets orbiting the sun, it is called the planetary atomic model.
• Continuous Energy Loss: Accelerated charged particles (like revolving electrons) must continuously radiate energy.
• Spiral Collapse: The electron should spiral inward as it loses energy and crash into the nucleus, making the atom unstable.
• Expected vs. Real: The model predicts a continuous spectrum due to continuous energy loss.
• Line Spectrum: In reality, atoms produce a line spectrum (discrete wavelengths), which this model cannot explain.
• Arrangement: The model states that electrons revolve around the nucleus, but it remains completely silent about how they are distributed or arranged in their orbits.
• Energy Levels: It does not explain the specific energies associated with these electronic paths.

1) Gases do not have a fixed shape, size, or definite volume. However, they take the shape of the container in which they are stored.
2) Gaseous molecules, or simply gases, expand on increasing temperature and condense on decreasing temperature.
3) Gases show diffusion (फैलाव) — from higher concentration to lower concentration.
4) Gases exert pressure on the wall of the container.

Postulates of the Kinetic Molecular Theory of Gases
1) Gases consist of tiny particles called gas molecules.
2) Gas molecules are identical, having the same shape and size.
3) There is no (negligible) force of attraction between the gas molecules.
4) The volume of one gas molecule is negligible over the total volume occupied by the gas molecules.
5) The kinetic energy (KE) of gas molecules depends on the temperature of the gas.
6) The gas molecules are not stationary; they are not stable at any fixed position.
7) Gas molecules are in random motion, moving in a zig-zag pathway.
8) Collisions between gas molecules, and between gas molecules and the container wall, are perfectly elastic collisions — kinetic energy is preserved (conserved) during collision.

title: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Its Postulates
notes: The kinetic molecular theory of gases explains the physical behaviour of gases (pressure, volume, temperature) in terms of the motion of their molecules. It treats a gas as a large collection of tiny, rapidly moving particles in constant random motion.
Postulates of the Kinetic Theory of Gases
1. A gas consists of a very large number of tiny particles (molecules) which are identical in mass and size for a given gas.
2. The volume of the individual gas molecules is negligible compared to the total volume occupied by the gas. The molecules are point masses.
3. The molecules are in a state of continuous, rapid, random motion in all directions. Between collisions they move in straight lines.
4. The molecules exert no attractive or repulsive forces on one another except during collisions. Between collisions they move freely.
5. Collisions between molecules and with the walls of the container are perfectly elastic — kinetic energy and momentum are conserved, though individual molecular speeds may change.
6. The duration of a collision is negligible compared to the time between collisions.
7. The pressure of a gas is caused by the bombardment of the container walls by the molecules. The force per unit area exerted on the walls is the pressure.

8. The average kinetic energy of the gas molecules is directly proportional to the absolute temperature of the gas: $KE_{avg} = \frac{3}{2}kT$, where $k$ is Boltzmann's constant. At the same temperature, all gases have the same average kinetic energy per molecule.

title: Numerical
notes: Stoichiometry is the math behind chemistry that allows us to calculate the exact quantities of reactants and products in a chemical reaction.
Word Origin: Derived from the Greek words stoicheion (element) and metron (measure).
Definition: It is the quantitative relationship between the substances that change during a chemical reaction.
Core Rule: It relies completely on the Law of Conservation of Mass — no atoms are created or destroyed during a reaction.
To Avoid Waste: It tells scientists exactly how much of each ingredient to mix so nothing is left over.
To Save Money: In chemical factories, using precise amounts avoids wasting expensive raw materials.
To Predict Outputs: It allows us to calculate exactly how much product (like a medicine or plastic) a reaction will yield before we even start.
To Ensure Safety: Knowing the exact amount of gas or heat produced keeps chemical reactions safe from explosions.
Balance Equations: We count and match atoms on both sides of a chemical reaction.
Convert Units: We change grams into moles, and moles into volumes or molecules.
Find Limiters: We identify the limiting reactant that will run out first and stop the reaction.
Calculate Yields: We determine the maximum possible amount of product we can theoretically create.
Stoichiometry is built on five distinct laws:
Core Rule: Total mass of reactants = Total mass of products.
$$w_1 + w_2 = w_3 + w_4 \quad (\text{where } w \text{ is mass in grams})$$
Apparatus: An H-shaped glass tube called Landolt's tube.
Chemicals used: Silver Nitrate ($AgNO_3$) and Sodium Chloride ($NaCl$).
Conclusion: The total weight of the tube remains exactly the same before and after the chemical reaction.
Statement: When gases react, they do so in volumes that bear a simple whole-number ratio to each other and to the gaseous products, provided temperature and pressure remain constant.
Only for Gases: This law applies strictly to reactants and products that are in the gaseous state (g).
Volume as "Moles": Instead of counting molecules or grams, you can directly use volumes (litres, mL, or cc) to relate reactants and products, as long as temperature and pressure do not change.
Simple Ratios: The relationship between these volumes is always in simple integers (like 1:1:2 or 2:1:2).
Illustration — reaction between hydrogen and chlorine gas:
1 volume of $H_2$ + 1 volume of $Cl_2$ → 2 volumes of $HCl$, a ratio of 1:1:2.

title: Introduction to Short Stories
notes: A short story is a brief work of prose fiction that can normally be read in one sitting. It focuses on a single incident, character, or idea, and develops it with economy of language. Unlike a novel, a short story usually has a limited number of characters, one central conflict, and one main effect.

Plot: the sequence of events in the story — exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Character: the people (or animals, or forces) in the story; they can be round (well developed, changing) or flat (simple, unchanging). Setting: the time and place of the action, which influences mood and conflict. Theme: the central idea or message of the story — what the story means beyond its events. Point of view: the perspective from which the story is told — first person (I), second person (you), or third person (he/she/they; limited or omniscient). Conflict: the struggle at the heart of the story — internal (man vs self) or external (man vs man, man vs nature, man vs society).

A good short story starts with a hook that creates curiosity, moves through rising tension to a climax (the turning point), and ends with a resolution — which may be closed (everything is settled) or open (leaving the reader to decide). Writers often use foreshadowing (hints of what will come) and symbolism (objects or actions standing for larger ideas) to deepen meaning.
Short Stories in the NEB English Syllabus

In the NEB (Nepal Education Board) English curriculum, short stories are studied to develop skills of comprehension, analysis and interpretation. Students are expected to identify the elements above, explain the theme in their own words, relate the story to real life, and answer questions about character, setting, plot and moral values.

title: LIMITS — Infinite Limits, Indeterminate Forms & Evaluation of Limits (Step-by-Step)
notes: 📘 TOPIC OUTLINE: Infinite Limits | Indeterminate Forms | Evaluation of Limits (∞/∞ form) | Evaluation of Limits containing Radicals (Rationalization) | Direct Substitution & Simplification Method

♾️ INFINITE LIMIT — CONCEPT: As x approaches a value very close to a point where the denominator approaches 0, the value of the function grows without bound. Note: 1/0 is UNDEFINED, but 1/(a very small positive number) → a very LARGE positive number, and 1/(a very small negative number) → a very LARGE negative number.
RULE 1: lim(x→0⁺) 1/x = +∞  → As x approaches 0 from the RIGHT (positive side), 1/x grows without bound towards +∞.
RULE 2: lim(x→0⁻) 1/x = −∞  → As x approaches 0 from the LEFT (negative side), 1/x decreases without bound towards −∞.
RULE 3: lim(x→∞) 1/x = 0  → As x grows infinitely large, 1/x shrinks towards 0.

❓ INDETERMINATE FORMS — DEFINITION: These are forms which, upon direct substitution, do NOT determine a unique value of the limit — further simplification (factoring, rationalization, or algebraic manipulation) is required to find the true limiting value. Simply plugging in the value gives an undefined/ambiguous result, so we must find an equivalent expression that IS defined at that point.

💡 KEY INSIGHT: Whenever a limit reduces to one of these 7 forms after direct substitution, we CANNOT conclude the limit directly — we must simplify using factorization, rationalization (multiplying by conjugate), or dividing every term by the highest power of x, before substituting again.

📐 METHOD 1 — Direct Substitution: If substituting x = a directly into the function gives a DEFINED (finite) value, that value itself IS the limit. No further work needed.

📐 METHOD 2 — Simplification & Substitution Method: If direct substitution gives an INDETERMINATE form (usually 0/0), factor the numerator and denominator, CANCEL the common factor causing the zero, then substitute again.

Step 6: Since the numerator still grows unboundedly while denominator approaches a finite constant, the overall limit → ∞ (does not converge to a finite value) UNLESS the original numerator power was matched — always double check degree of numerator vs denominator after rationalizing.

💡 TIP: After rationalizing radicals, ALWAYS re-check whether the resulting expression is now in ∞/∞ or a finite-form — this decides whether you divide by the highest power of x again (Section B method) or simply substitute.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE TO AVOID: Do NOT cancel terms inside a square root directly (e.g., you cannot cancel an 'x' that is buried inside √(2x+a) with an 'x' outside the root) — always rationalize FIRST using the conjugate before attempting any cancellation.

🎯 QUICK SUMMARY OF ALL METHODS: (1) If direct substitution gives a defined value → that IS the answer. (2) If it gives 0/0 with polynomials → FACTOR and cancel. (3) If it gives 0/0 with radicals → RATIONALIZE using the conjugate and cancel. (4) If x→∞ and both parts are polynomials (∞/∞ form) → DIVIDE every term by the highest power of x. (5) If x→∞ with a difference of radicals (∞−∞ form) → RATIONALIZE using the conjugate first to convert it into a ∞/∞ or finite form, THEN apply method (4) if needed.

title: Limits
notes: A limit asks: as x gets infinitely close to a number, what value is the function heading toward? Sometimes the function has a 'hole' at that exact spot — plugging the number in directly gives 0/0, called an Indeterminate Form. This does not mean the limit doesn't exist; it means the answer is hidden and needs algebra or calculus to expose it. Think of Direct Substitution as checking the front door: if it's unlocked (gives a real number), you walk right in. If it's locked with a 0/0 sign, you need the right tool to pick the lock.
When to use: always try this first, for smooth continuous functions. Example: lim(x→2) (3x² − 5x + 1) = 3(2)² − 5(2) + 1 = 3.
When to use: if direct substitution gives 0/0 and you see polynomial expressions that share a common factor. Example: lim(x→3) (x² − 9)/(x − 3) = lim(x→3) (x−3)(x+3)/(x−3) = lim(x→3) (x+3) = 6.
When to use: if you get 0/0 and see a square root expression like √A − B. Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (flip the sign): (√A − B)(√A + B) = A − B².
When to use: for sin(x) or tan(x) ratios approaching zero. The key rule: lim(θ→0) sin(θ)/θ = 1.
When to use: if you get 0/0 or ∞/∞ and know derivatives. Differentiate the top and bottom separately (not using the quotient rule), then re-evaluate: lim f(x)/g(x) = lim f'(x)/g'(x).

title: Matrix.0001
notes: • Matrix: A rectangular array or grid of numbers, symbols, or expressions arranged in rows and columns, used to represent linear transformations, systems of linear equations, and physical states.

• Determinant: A scalar value calculated from a square matrix that represents the scaling factor of the transformation, indicating how area or volume changes, and whether a matrix is invertible (non-zero determinant).
The unit matrix acts like the number 1 in scalar algebra. It represents the state of perfect preservation or "doing nothing."
• Zero Transformation (The Identity Operation): In physical space, if you multiply a vector (representing a force, velocity, or position) by a unit matrix, the vector remains completely unchanged.
- Physical meaning: It represents a system at rest, or an operation that performs no rotation, no scaling, and no translation (e.g., looking at an object from the same unchanging perspective).

• The Baseline State in Quantum Mechanics: In quantum physics, systems are often described by operators. The unit matrix represents a measurement where the outcome is certain, or a state where no transformation has occurred.

• Inertia and Stress-Strain Tensors: When analyzing how materials deform under stress, the unit matrix represents uniform pressure from all sides (hydrostatic pressure), where deformation shape does not distort across axes.

• Determinant (Scaling & Compressibility): Geometrically, the determinant measures how much a spatial volume expands, contracts, or flips under a transformation. In fluid dynamics, a determinant of 1 means incompressible flow, while a determinant of 0 indicates space has been squashed into a lower dimension (loss of information / non-invertible).

• Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (Principal Axes & Natural Frequencies): Eigenvectors represent special directions in space that do not change direction during a matrix transformation, only their magnitude. In structural physics, they represent principal stress axes or natural modes of vibration (e.g., how a bridge or building naturally sways under stress).

• Matrix Inverse (Reversibility & Time-Reversal): The inverse of a matrix undoes a linear transformation. In physics, if a process is represented by matrix A, its inverse A⁻¹ represents restoring the system to its initial state, crucial for modeling reversible physical processes.

• Symmetric & Hermitian Matrices (Observable Quantities): In physics and quantum mechanics, physical observables (such as energy, momentum, or spin) are represented by symmetric or Hermitian matrices, guaranteeing that their measurable values (eigenvalues) are real numbers.
• Matrix: A rectangular array or grid of numbers, symbols, or expressions arranged in rows and columns, used to represent linear transformations, systems of linear equations, and mathematical states.

• Determinant: A single numerical value calculated from a square matrix that represents the scaling factor of the transformation, indicating how space or size changes, and whether a matrix is invertible (non-zero determinant).
The unit matrix acts like the number 1 in basic algebra. It represents the state of perfect preservation or "doing nothing."
• Zero Transformation (The Identity Operation): In coordinate space, if you multiply a vector (representing a direction or position) by a unit matrix, the vector remains completely unchanged.
- General meaning: It represents a unchanged system, or an operation that performs no rotation, no scaling, and no shift (e.g., viewing data from the same unchanging perspective).

• The Baseline State in Systems Analysis: In general systems, operations are often described by operators. The unit matrix represents a process where the output equals the input, or a state where no modification has occurred.
• Isotropic Scaling: When analyzing how structures react under equal pressure, the unit matrix represents uniform change from all sides, where shape does not distort across axes.

• Determinant (Scaling & Size Change): Geometrically, the determinant measures how much a spatial region expands, contracts, or flips under a transformation. A determinant of 1 means size-preserving flow, while a determinant of 0 indicates space has been flattened into a lower dimension (loss of information / non-invertible).

• Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (Principal Axes & Characteristic Values): Eigenvectors represent special directions in space that do not change direction during a matrix transformation, only their magnitude. In structural analysis, they represent principal axes or natural modes of response.

• Matrix Inverse (Reversibility & Undoing Operations): The inverse of a matrix undoes a linear transformation. In general operations, if a process is represented by matrix A, its inverse A⁻¹ represents restoring the system to its initial state, crucial for modeling reversible processes.

• Symmetric & Self-Adjoint Matrices (Real Properties): In mathematical modeling, well-balanced systems are represented by symmetric matrices, guaranteeing that their characteristic values (eigenvalues) are real numbers.

नेपालभित्रका विभिन्न भाषाबाट नेपालीमा आएका शब्दहरू।

अङ्ग्रेजी, अरबी, फारसी, पोर्चुगेली, चिनियाँ, जापानी आदि भाषाबाट आएका शब्दहरू।

title: shabda-srot
notes:
शब्द भनेको एक वा एक भन्दा बढी अक्षरहरू मिलेर बनेको निश्चित, अर्थयुक्त भाषिक एकाइ हो। यो अक्षर भन्दा ठुलो र पदावली वा वाक्यांश भन्दा सानो हुन्छ।

शब्दको स्रोत भन्नाले भाषामा शब्दहरू आएको ठाउँलाई बुझिन्छ, अर्थात् यो शब्दको उत्पत्ति स्थान हो। नेपाली भाषा संस्कृत भाषाबाट विकसित भएको हो त्यसैले संस्कृतलाई नेपाली भाषाको मातृ भाषा भनिन्छ। नेपाली भाषामा धेरैजसो शब्दहरू संस्कृतबाट आएका छन् भने कतिपय शब्दहरू नेपालभित्र बोलिने विभिन्न जातजातिको भाषा र विदेशी भाषाबाट आएका छन्।

title: कविता परिचय (Introduction to Poetry)
notes: कविता साहित्यको त्यस्तो विधा हो जसमा भावना, अनुभव र कल्पनालाई लय, ताल, प्रतीक र अलङ्कारका माध्यमबाट कलात्मक रूपमा प्रस्तुत गरिन्छ। कविता भनेको शब्दहरूबाट बनेको चित्र हो जसले पाठकको मनमा भावना जगाउँछ।

भावना (Emotion): कविताको प्राण भावना नै हो — प्रेम, वेदना, देशभक्ति, प्रकृतिप्रतिको आकर्षण आदि। कल्पना (Imagination): कविले कल्पनाको सहाराले वस्तु र घटनालाई नयाँ रूपमा प्रस्तुत गर्छ। लय (Rhythm): शब्दहरूको आवृत्तिबाट सिर्जना हुने संगीतात्मक प्रवाह। प्रतीक (Symbol): वस्तु वा घटनाले अर्को गहिरो अर्थलाई संकेत गर्छ। अलङ्कार (Figure of speech): उपमा, रूपक, उत्प्रेक्षा आदिको प्रयोगले कवितालाई सुन्दर बनाउँछ।

कविता मुख्यतया दुई प्रकारकी हुन्छन्: गद्य कविता (Free verse) जसमा नियमित लय वा तुक नहुन सक्छ, र छन्दोबद्ध कविता (Metrical poetry) जसमा निश्चित छन्द, गति र तुक हुन्छ। विषयवस्तुका आधारमा कवितालाई प्रकृति कविता, देशभक्ति कविता, प्रेम कविता, आधुनिक कविता आदिमा वर्गीकरण गर्न सकिन्छ।

NEB (राष्ट्रिय परीक्षा बोर्ड) को नेपाली पाठ्यक्रममा कविता अध्ययनको उद्देश्य विद्यार्थीहरूमा भावनात्मक संवेदना, भाषिक सौन्दर्यबोध र आलोचनात्मक चेतना विकास गर्नु हो। कविता पढ्दा भाव, भाषा, शिल्प र सन्देश — यी चार पक्षमा ध्यान दिनुपर्छ।

subject: physics
title: HEAT AND TEMPERATURE — Chapter 9, Class 11 Physics (Concepts, All 5 Scales & Step-by-Step Numericals)
notes: 📘 TOPIC OUTLINE: Temperature vs Heat | Effects of Heat | Thermal Equilibrium & Zeroth Law | Thermometry | The 5 Temperature Scales & Fundamental Interval | General Conversion Formula | Numericals (Direct Conversion, Coincidence/Double-Reading Problems, Faulty Thermometer Problems, Arbitrary/Offset Scale Problems, Rate/Error Problems)

🌡️ TEMPERATURE — DEFINITION: Temperature is the average kinetic energy of all molecules present in a body. It tells you the DIRECTION heat will flow (hot → cold). Measured using a thermometer. SI unit: kelvin (K).

🔥 HEAT — DEFINITION: Heat is the SUM (total) of the kinetic energy of all molecules of a substance. It is a form of energy, measured in joules. Heat flows from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature until equilibrium is reached.

💡 KEY CONCEPTUAL DIFFERENCE (exam favorite): Temperature is an AVERAGE (intensive property — doesn't depend on amount of substance). Heat is a TOTAL/SUM (extensive property — depends on mass/amount). This is why a bucket of lukewarm water can contain MORE heat than a cup of boiling tea, even though its temperature is lower — more molecules means a bigger total, even if each molecule individually has less average energy.

⚡ EFFECTS OF HEAT: When heat is applied to a body, it can bring: (i) Change in temperature (ii) Change in volume (iii) Change of state of matter (iv) Electric effect (v) Generation of light energy (vi) Change in resistance.
⚖️ THERMAL EQUILIBRIUM: Two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when NO heat flows from one to the other after being brought into contact — meaning they are at the same temperature.

📐 ZEROTH LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS: If two systems are separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they must also be in thermal equilibrium with each other. (This law is what actually justifies using a thermometer — the thermometer is the 'third system'.)
🧪 THERMODYNAMIC SYSTEM: A system that can be described using thermodynamic parameters — Temperature, Pressure, Volume, and Heat exchange.
🔬 THERMOMETRY: The science of temperature and its measurement. THREE MAIN STEPS: (i) Construction (ii) Calibration (iii) Sensitiveness.
═══════════ SECTION A: THE 5 TEMPERATURE SCALES & FUNDAMENTAL INTERVAL ═══════════

💡 WHAT IS 'FUNDAMENTAL INTERVAL'? It is simply the NUMBER OF DIVISIONS between the Lower Fixed Point (LFP — ice/melting point) and Upper Fixed Point (UFP — steam/boiling point) on a scale. This single number is the KEY to comparing any two scales, because it tells you how 'coarse' or 'fine' each degree-step is. A bigger fundamental interval = smaller, finer degree-steps.

| Scale | Symbol | LFP (Ice Point) | UFP (Steam Point) | Fundamental Interval (UFP−LFP) | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Celsius | °C | 0 | 100 | 100 | Relative (0 = ice point) |
| Fahrenheit | °F | 32 | 212 | 180 | Relative (0 ≠ ice point) |
| Kelvin | K | 273 | 373 | 100 | Absolute (0 = absolute zero) |
| Réaumur | °R (Ré) | 0 | 80 | 80 | Relative (0 = ice point) |
| Rankine | °Ra | 491.67 | 671.67 | 180 | Absolute (0 = absolute zero) |

🔑 FEEL IT, DON'T MEMORIZE: Kelvin is just Celsius SHIFTED so 0 lands on absolute zero (same degree-SIZE as Celsius, fundamental interval 100). Rankine is just Fahrenheit SHIFTED so 0 lands on absolute zero (same degree-SIZE as Fahrenheit, fundamental interval 180). So Celsius↔Kelvin is a pure SHIFT (add 273), and Fahrenheit↔Rankine is also a pure SHIFT (add 459.67). But Celsius↔Fahrenheit needs both a SHIFT and a SCALE change (×9/5) because their degree-sizes differ.

📐 GENERAL CONVERSION FORMULA (works for ANY two scales, including Rankine): (Reading − LFP)/(Fundamental Interval) is the SAME fraction on every scale, because all scales measure the identical physical range between ice point and steam point.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE: Students often try converting Rankine using the Celsius-style formula (Ra−0)/x. WRONG — Rankine's zero is absolute zero, NOT the ice point, so you MUST use (Ra−491.67)/180, matching Fahrenheit's fundamental interval of 180, not Kelvin's 100.
📝 NUMERICAL B1: Convert 30°C into Fahrenheit scale.
📝 NUMERICAL B2: Convert 98.6°F (normal body temperature) into Kelvin and Rankine.
Step 2: Convert to Kelvin: K = C+273 = 37+273 = 310 K
Step 3: Convert to Rankine directly from Fahrenheit: Ra = F+459.67 = 98.6+459.67 = 558.27

💡 TIP: Kelvin was obtained from Celsius by pure ADDITION (+273), Rankine from Fahrenheit by pure ADDITION (+459.67) — no multiplication needed, since each absolute scale shares its degree-size with its 'parent' relative scale.

📐 METHOD: These problems give a RELATIONSHIP between two scale readings (e.g. 'one is double the other' or 'both are equal') instead of a direct value. Assign a variable to the unknown common temperature, express both readings in terms of it using the given relationship, plug into the master equation, and solve.
📝 NUMERICAL C1: At what temperature will the Kelvin reading double the Fahrenheit reading?
✅ ANSWER: At 176.69°F (353.38 K), Kelvin reading is double Fahrenheit reading.
📝 NUMERICAL C2: At what temperature will the Celsius reading double the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let F = x, so C = 2x
✅ ANSWER: At −12.307°F, Celsius reading is double Fahrenheit reading.
📝 NUMERICAL C3: At what point does the Kelvin reading coincide with (equal) the Fahrenheit reading?
✅ ANSWER: At 574.25 K = 574.25°F, the readings coincide.
📝 NUMERICAL C4 (Concept-challenging — physically impossible case): At what temperature would the Rankine reading equal the Celsius reading numerically?
Step 1: Let both = x. Using Ra = 1.8(C+273): x = 1.8(x+273)
Step 3: Check against absolute zero (−273°C): −614.25°C is colder than absolute zero, so it cannot exist.
✅ ANSWER: No physically valid solution — the equality would require a temperature below absolute zero.
💡 TIP: ALWAYS sanity-check your final answer against absolute zero (−273°C / 0 K) when an absolute scale is involved — algebra can give you a number, but physics can reject it.
📝 NUMERICAL C5: At what temperature will the Réaumur reading be numerically equal to the Fahrenheit reading?
═══════════ SECTION D: FAULTY / MISCALIBRATED THERMOMETER NUMERICALS ═══════════

📐 METHOD: A faulty thermometer has WRONG numbers marked at its LFP and UFP, but still divides the space between them proportionally. Use: (Faulty reading − Faulty LFP)/(Faulty UFP − Faulty LFP) = (Correct reading − Correct LFP)/(Correct UFP − Correct LFP)
📝 NUMERICAL D1: A faulty thermometer has fixed points marked at 2 and 98 (instead of 0 and 100). What is the correct Celsius temperature when it reads 20°C?
📝 NUMERICAL D2: A thermometer reads the melting point of ice as −10°C, and reads 60°C in place of the correct 50°C. Find its reading at the actual boiling point of water (100°C).
✅ ANSWER: The faulty thermometer reads 130°C at the true boiling point.
📝 NUMERICAL D3: The distance between LFP and UFP on a thermometer is 80 cm. Find the Celsius temperature when mercury has risen 10.4 cm above the LFP.
💡 TIP: This is the same ratio logic as the faulty-thermometer formula — physical stem length is just another 'scale' being converted into Celsius.
═══════════ SECTION E: ARBITRARY / OFFSET SCALE NUMERICALS (Concept-Challenging) ═══════════
📐 METHOD: These invent a new scale with its own LFP/UFP. Treat it exactly like Celsius vs Fahrenheit — set up the ratio, don't panic just because the scale is unfamiliar.
📝 NUMERICAL E1: In an arbitrary scale, water freezes at 40° and boils at 290°. Find the reading on this scale corresponding to 62°C.
✅ ANSWER: 62°C corresponds to 195° on the arbitrary scale.
📝 NUMERICAL E2: A new scale 'X' has its ice point at −20°X and steam point at 130°X. Find the reading on X when Celsius reads 50°C.
📝 NUMERICAL E3 (two unknown scales, no Celsius needed): Thermometer P has LFP=10, UFP=160. Thermometer Q has LFP=20, UFP=120. When P reads 70, what does Q read?
💡 TIP: Celsius is not mandatory as a 'bridge' — the ratio method works between ANY two linear scales directly.
📝 NUMERICAL E4: Scale 'Y' has the SAME fundamental interval as Celsius (100 divisions) but its ice point is marked at 50°Y. If Y reads 68°Y, find the Celsius equivalent.
Step 1: Equal fundamental intervals → pure shift relationship: C = Y−50

💡 TIP: When two scales share the SAME fundamental interval, conversion is always pure addition/subtraction (like Celsius↔Kelvin) — no multiplication needed. Different fundamental intervals force a scaling step.
═══════════ SECTION F: RATE / ERROR / CHANGE NUMERICALS ═══════════
📝 NUMERICAL F1: A Fahrenheit thermometer reads 99°F when a standard Celsius thermometer reads 37°C. Find the error in the Fahrenheit scale.
Step 1: True Fahrenheit equivalent of 37°C: 37/100 = (F−32)/180 → 6660 = 100F−3200 → F = 98.6
📝 NUMERICAL F2: A lab thermometer reads only in °F. Initial sample temperature is 68.2°F, and it must be increased by 40°C. Find the final temperature in °F.
Step 1: For a CHANGE (not absolute reading), use only the scaling ratio: 100 parts in °C = 180 parts in °F

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE: Never apply the full C-to-F formula (×9/5, +32) to a temperature CHANGE — the '+32' offset applies only to absolute readings. For a change, only the scaling factor (180/100) applies. This is the single most common error in this topic.
📝 NUMERICAL F3: A Celsius scale reads 30°C when a standard Kelvin scale reads 300 K. Find the error in the Celsius reading.
Step 1: True Celsius equivalent of 300 K: C = 300−273 = 27
📝 NUMERICAL F4: What are the temperatures in Celsius and Fahrenheit when 2/3 of the Fahrenheit reading equals 1/2 of the Celsius reading?
📝 NUMERICAL F5 (Rankine, concept-challenging): A gas thermometer shows a temperature change from 500°Ra to 680°Ra. Express this change in Celsius degrees.
Step 2: Since Rankine shares fundamental interval 180 with Fahrenheit, and Fahrenheit-to-Celsius scaling ratio is 100/180: Celsius change = 180×(100/180) = 100
✅ ANSWER: A 180°Ra change equals a 100°C change.

💡 TIP: This confirms the 'feel': Rankine degree-size = Fahrenheit degree-size, so converting a Rankine CHANGE to Celsius always goes through the F→C scaling ratio (100/180), never through the absolute-zero offset (491.67), since offsets cancel out in a difference.

🎯 QUICK SUMMARY OF ALL METHODS: (1) DIRECT CONVERSION between named scales → plug into the master equation (C−0)/100=(F−32)/180=(K−273)/100=(Ré−0)/80=(Ra−491.67)/180. (2) 'DOUBLE' or 'COINCIDE' problems → assign one variable to the unknown temperature, express both readings in terms of it, substitute into the master equation, and sanity-check against absolute zero. (3) FAULTY THERMOMETER problems → use (Faulty−FaultyLFP)/(FaultyUFP−FaultyLFP) = (Correct−CorrectLFP)/(CorrectUFP−CorrectLFP). (4) ARBITRARY/OFFSET SCALES → same ratio method; Celsius is not mandatory as a bridge. (5) CHANGE/DIFFERENCE in temperature → apply ONLY the scaling ratio between fundamental intervals, NEVER the additive offset.

title: Heat and Temperature
notes: This chapter covers: Heat and Temperature · Thermal Expansion · Quantity of Heat · Rate of Heat Flow · Ideal Gas. The notes below focus on the Heat and Temperature section in full depth.

Before the 19th century, scientists believed in the Caloric Theory — heat was thought to be a fine, weightless fluid called 'caloric', hiding in the pores of a substance and flowing like a liquid or gas.
1) According to this theory, an object contains a fixed amount of caloric; adding caloric raised its temperature, and removing it lowered the temperature.
2) Caloric was assumed to be odorless, tasteless, and invisible — it was never actually detected experimentally.

⚠️ The Fatal Flaw: The caloric theory could not explain heat generated by friction. Rubbing two metals together in water can make it boil — an apparently limitless generation of heat, which directly contradicts the idea of a body containing only a 'fixed amount' of caloric fluid.
Davy and Joule later established heat as a form of energy, arising from the mechanical motion of particles — not a fluid substance at all.

The modern concept: Internal energy is the total energy (kinetic + vibrational + rotational) of all the molecules of a body; when this energy flows between bodies due to a temperature difference, it is called heat.
"Order is manifestly maintained in the universe... governed by the sovereign will of God." — James Prescott Joule
9.2 Heat — Transfer of Energy due to Temperature Difference
Definition: Heat is the form of energy which flows from one body to another due to a temperature difference. Symbol: Q.

Example: A hot iron ball dropped in water → the temperature of the water increases, and the temperature of the ball decreases, until both reach the same temperature. The 'something' transferred between them is heat.

⚠️ Common Misconception: We commonly say a body 'contains heat' — this is incorrect. Just as it is wrong to say work is 'in' a body, it is wrong to say heat is 'in' a body. Heat exists only when there is flow due to a temperature difference; once the flow stops, the word 'heat' can no longer be used — only internal energy can.

Analogy: like a bus passenger versus a pedestrian — the same person, but the label depends on the condition (whether they are in transit or not). Similarly, energy is only called 'heat' while it is in transit between bodies.
Since heat is a form of energy, its dimensional formula is the same as that of energy:

SystemUnit of Heat
SIJoule (J)
CGScalorie (cal)
MKSkilocalorie (kcal)
FPSBritish thermal unit (Btu)
Definition: Temperature is the thermal condition that determines the direction of flow of heat from one body to another — i.e., the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.
1) Hot and cold are relative terms (like motion/rest, or left/right).

2) Classic demonstration: a hand from hot water and a hand from cold water are both placed in tepid (lukewarm) water — the tepid water feels cool to the 'hot-water hand' and warm to the 'cold-water hand', even though it is the same temperature for both. This shows that our sense of hot/cold is a subjective sensation, not a reliable measurement.
3) Heat flows spontaneously from a high temperature body to a low temperature body.
4) There is no upper limit of temperature; the lower limit is 0 Kelvin — temperature cannot go below 0 K.

📚 Did You Know? In 1757, Joseph Black discovered latent heat and was the first to clearly distinguish temperature from heat.

A brick at 20°C, broken into two unequal pieces, leaves both pieces at 20°C (temperature does not depend on size) — but the larger piece has more internal energy. This is because temperature is an intensive quantity (independent of the amount of matter), while heat/internal energy is an extensive quantity (depends on the amount of matter).

HeatTemperature

A form of energyJust a number

9.4 Molecular Concept: Thermal Energy, Heat Energy, Temperature
The molecules of matter are in constant motion (translational, rotational, vibrational) → this gives them kinetic energy. Intermolecular forces between them give rise to potential energy.
1) Thermal energy (internal energy) = sum of the kinetic and potential energies of all the molecules of a body.
2) Temperature = the effect or measure of the thermal energy in a body — higher thermal energy corresponds to higher temperature.
3) Heat energy = thermal energy that is transferred from one body to another due to a temperature difference — in short, "heat is thermal energy in transit."
9.5 Thermal Equilibrium and the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
Thermal equilibrium: a number of bodies are said to be in thermal equilibrium if they have the same temperature, so there is no net exchange of heat between them.

⚠️ Common Misconception: Saying there is 'no flow of heat' at thermal equilibrium is wrong. Heat always flows both ways between bodies, even at equilibrium — but the net flow is zero, since equal amounts flow in each direction.
Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics: If two systems (A and B) are separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system (C), then A and B are also in thermal equilibrium with each other.

Two bodies are said to be in thermal equilibrium if there is no net flow of heat between them when placed in contact. If heat flows from body A to body B, then the temperature of A is greater than that of B (heat flows from the hotter to the colder body, from higher to lower temperature).

Three-body case: Consider bodies A, B, and C. If A and C are in thermal equilibrium, and B and C are also in thermal equilibrium, then A and B must also be in thermal equilibrium with each other. This is exactly the Zeroth Law stated above.
Fig. 9.2: A and B are directly linked; A–C and B–C are linked via dashed lines representing separate equilibrium relationships, concluding A ≡ B.

History: Propounded by R. H. Fowler, this law came to light only in 1930 — much later than the 1st and 2nd Laws of Thermodynamics — yet it is fundamental to both, which is why it is placed 'before' them and called the Zeroth Law.
(i) It defines the temperature of a body.
(ii) It establishes temperature as a valid, fundamental concept underlying the 1st and 2nd Laws of Thermodynamics.
(iii) It clarifies that heat always flows both ways between bodies, even at equilibrium — only the net flow is zero.
9.6 Cause and Direction of Heat Flow

Heat flows from a high-temperature region to a low-temperature region because molecules at a higher temperature have more thermal energy. During collisions, energy transfers from high-thermal-energy molecules to low-thermal-energy ones, until equilibrium is reached — at which point no net energy transfer occurs (no force acts through a distance, so no net work is done).

Key definition: Heat is the spontaneous transfer of thermal energy from a higher to a lower temperature body, in order to attain thermal equilibrium. The cause of heat flow is the temperature difference — not the internal energy difference.

Important example: Consider 200 g of water at 30°C placed in contact with 50 kg of water at 25°C. Heat flows from the 30°C water to the 25°C water — even though the 50 kg body (despite being at the lower temperature) has far more total internal energy than the small 200 g body. This shows that the direction of heat flow depends on the temperature of the bodies, not on their total internal energy.
Definition: Thermometry is the study of the measurement of the temperature of a body. Its basic principle: two bodies in thermal equilibrium have the same temperature.
Thermometer: a temperature-measuring device, marked with a scale of temperature.
History: the earliest thermometer was constructed by Galileo (1593); Newton later suggested the necessity of using fixed points on the scale.

1) Liquid type (e.g. mercury thermometer)
2) Gas thermometers (e.g. hydrogen gas thermometer)
3) Resistance thermometers (e.g. platinum resistance thermometer)
4) Thermoelectric thermometer

Working principle: thermal equilibrium is the working principle of a mercury thermometer — heat transfers between the substance and the thermometer until both reach the same temperature (equilibrium); the thermometer's own reading then equals the substance's temperature.

💡 Stop to Think: How does a thermometer measure the temperature of a body if it's a separate object? — The thermometer actually only ever measures its own temperature; after it reaches thermal equilibrium with the body being measured, its own temperature becomes equal to the body's temperature too, so the reading is valid.
Principle: uses the expansion/contraction of mercury with temperature change — the volume of mercury is proportional to temperature.
Construction parts: Stem, Bore, Bulb, Mercury thread.

1) Mercury expands uniformly (linearly) over its usable range.
2) Being a liquid metal, it conducts heat well and quickly reaches the thermometer's own temperature, giving accurate readings.
3) It does not wet glass and can easily be obtained in pure form.
4) It is opaque and shiny — easy to read.
5) It is not very sensitive to small amounts of heat, so it doesn't draw much heat from the body being measured, keeping the reading accurate.
6) It is practically non-volatile, so it is not much affected by its own vapour pressure.

1) Cannot measure temperatures below -39°C (the freezing point of mercury).
2) Not suitable for use in very cold regions.

Clinical Thermometer: a special mercury thermometer used for humans, with a range of 94°F to 108°F. It has a constriction (kink) near the bulb, which prevents the mercury from flowing back automatically — the thermometer must be 'jerked' to reset the reading below the constricted thread.

1) Fineness of the capillary bore (a thinner bore gives more sensitivity — a larger rise in the mercury thread for a small temperature change).
2) Bulb size (a bigger bulb holds more liquid, giving more expansion and hence more sensitivity).
3) Thermal conductivity of the bulb material (a thin, conducting bulb wall gives faster response and more sensitivity).
4) The nature and expansivity of the thermometric liquid used.
💡 Stop to Think: What does the sensitivity of a thermometer depend on? — Bulb size, bore diameter, and the nature of the thermometric substance used (as listed above).
Range of use: used to measure temperatures below -39°C (mercury's freezing point) — good for very cold regions.

1) Alcohol expands about six times more than mercury for the same temperature rise — making it more sensitive.
2) Its freezing point (-130°C) is much lower than that of mercury (-39°C), so it is suitable for very cold climates.

1) Cannot measure above 78°C (its own boiling point).
2) It wets the wall of the glass tube.
3) It is a poor conductor, so it is slow to reach equilibrium, and its expansion is less uniform.
4) It has a narrow usable range of temperature.

Why is the triple point of water chosen as a standard fixed point in modern thermometry? — It is the unique point where the solid, liquid, and vapour phases of water coexist in equilibrium; it is highly reproducible, unlike the melting/boiling points, which depend on pressure and impurities.

Why should a thermometer bulb have a small heat capacity? — So it absorbs less heat from the body being measured, and its own temperature changes quickly to match the object being measured, giving a fast and accurate reading without altering the object's own temperature.
Why is the bore of the capillary tube chosen to be uniform? — So the scale divisions are equal throughout, ensuring the correctness of readings across the whole scale.

A temperature scale is created by identifying two easily reproducible fixed temperatures (usually the freezing and boiling points of water at standard atmospheric pressure), then dividing the interval between them into equal divisions.

Absolute zero: the lowest possible temperature theoretically attainable in the universe = -273.15°C = 0 K = the point where the properties of an ideal gas (theoretically) vanish. It is defined as an absolute property, independent of any thermometric substance — unlike the ice/steam points, which depend on the properties of water.

Recorded extremes: the lowest temperature recorded in a laboratory is about $1.0 \times 10^{-10}\,K$; the Boomerang Nebula in space is around 1 K; on Earth's surface, Vostok Station, Antarctica recorded 183 K ≈ -89°C.

⚠️ Capitalization Rule: On the Kelvin scale, temperature is conventionally written without the degree symbol (°) — write 1 K, not 1°K. The word 'kelvin' (the unit) is not capitalized when written out in full, but the capital letter 'K' is always used as its abbreviation.

💡 Stop to Think: Is there a temperature at which Celsius and Kelvin thermometers agree? — No. Since $K = C + 273.15$ always holds, there is no temperature at which the Celsius and Kelvin readings are numerically equal.
Difference between Degree Centigrade (C°) and Centigrade Degree (°C)
°C denotes an actual temperature (a point on the scale). C° denotes a temperature interval or difference (a change in temperature).
Example: a change in temperature of 25°C equals a temperature interval of 25 C°, which equals a temperature change of 45 F°.
— i.e., a difference on the centigrade scale equals $\frac{5}{9}$ of the corresponding difference on the Fahrenheit scale.
The general relation is that the following ratio is the same for every scale:
$$\frac{C - \text{Lower fixed pt.}}{\text{Upper fixed pt.} - \text{Lower fixed pt.}} \quad \text{(same for all scales)}$$

A faulty thermometer's fixed points are not correctly marked at 0° and 100° (unlike a correct Celsius thermometer). Its scale must be related back to the true Celsius scale using the ratio of intervals:

Result: this gives an upper fixed point equivalent of $\theta_2 = \theta_1 + n = -10 + 140 = 130°C$ on the true scale. (This example is abbreviated from the source material — refer to the full textbook working for the complete step-by-step derivation.)

Answer: $x = 22°C$. (This is the same faulty-thermometer scenario referenced under both "Self Test Opportunity 9.1" and "Stop to Think 9.4" in the source material — the two are consistent with each other.)

To measure low temperature, liquid thermometers work well up to about $-1000°C$ to $1000°C$, alongside resistance thermometers. For very high temperatures (up to 3000°C and beyond), a device called a Pyrometer is used.
Pyrometry is the measurement of very high temperatures (e.g. of the Sun, stars, or a blast furnace) using a Pyrometer, since ordinary thermometers cannot be used at such extreme temperatures.
The Kelvin scale is the preferred and standard scale for all accurate scientific temperature measurements, and is referred to in preference to all other thermometer scales.

subject: physics
title: Quantity of Heat
notes: Heat is the energy transferred between two bodies due to a temperature difference. It flows from a hotter body to a colder body. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules of a body; it decides the direction of heat flow. The SI unit of heat is the joule (J); the practical unit is the calorie (cal), where $1\,cal = 4.186\,J$.
The heat capacity (C) of a body is the quantity of heat required to raise its temperature by 1°C (or 1 K): $C = \frac{Q}{\Delta\theta}$, unit J/K.
The specific heat capacity (s or c) is the heat required to raise the temperature of unit mass of a substance by 1°C:

where $m$ is the mass, $s$ is the specific heat capacity, and $\Delta\theta$ is the rise in temperature. The SI unit is $J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}$. For water, $s = 4200\,J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1} = 1\,cal\,g^{-1}\,°C^{-1}$.

The heat required to raise the temperature of 1 mole of a substance by 1 K: $C = \frac{1}{n}\frac{Q}{\Delta\theta}$. For gases there are two values: $C_p$ (at constant pressure) and $C_v$ (at constant volume), with $C_p - C_v = R$ (Mayer's relation).

The water equivalent of a body is the mass of water that would require the same quantity of heat as the body to raise its temperature by the same amount: $W = m s$ (mass of water), unit gram or kilogram.

During a change of state (melting, boiling), temperature remains constant while heat is absorbed. The latent heat (L) is the heat required to change the state of unit mass of a substance without changing its temperature:

There is a saying among craftsmen, 'Measure thrice, cut once.' This means that you can reduce the risk of making a mistake in the work by checking the measurement a second or third time before you proceed. In fact it is wise to make any measurement at least three times. Making only one measurement could go completely unnoticed.

Error: All the physical quantities are measurable so accurate measurement is an important part of physics. But the measured value of a physical quantity is usually different from its real value. In other words, we can never make measurements with all certainty and claim that measurements are hundred percent accurate because measurements with all certainty involve a certain error (or uncertainty). We can never take into account the neither instrument may be supposed to be perfect nor any experimenter may be perfect. Since you would not get the same value of x that you try to measure it, your result is obviously uncertain.
The numerical result of a complete measurement is then expressed in the form as
The difference between the measured and the real values of a physical quantity is called error. It is also called uncertainty.
Here x̄ is the mean value of different values measured in the experiment.

For example, if the measured area of your book is 200 ± 0.2 cm². The ± 0.2 cm² ('plus or minus 0.2 cm²') denotes the error in the measurement. The real area of your book most likely lies between 200.2 cm² and 199.8 cm² i.e. the measurement is written as 200 ± 0.2 cm². The correct value of a quantity is not sure so we take the mean value as the correct or true value.
Here x̄ is the mean value of different values measured in the experiment.
An error can be expressed by three ways:
Absolute error: The difference between real value and individual measured value of a physical quantity is called absolute error.
The correct value of a quantity is not sure so we take the mean value as the correct or real value.
Generally, errors in the measurement can be broadly classified into two categories:
The errors which are due to unknown causes are called random errors. They are also called accidental errors because they are not due to any definite cause.

Causes of Random Error: Random errors arise from the fluctuations that are most easily observed by making multiple trials of a given measurement. For example, if you were to measure the period of a pendulum with a stop watch, you would find that your measurements were not always the same. The main source of these fluctuations would probably be the difficulty of judging exactly when the pendulum came to a given point in its motion, and in starting and stopping the watch at that time. Since you would not get the same value of the period each time that you try to measure it, your result is obviously uncertain.

Minimization of Random Error: Systematic errors are generally 'simple' to analyze but random errors require a more careful judge. Experiments with very small random errors are said to have a high degree of precision. Random errors can be minimized by making a number of readings and then taking their mean.

The errors which are due to known causes are called systematic errors. The measurement is made under constant condition and hence the error repeats constantly or systematically. So, the error in this category belong to the same sign and always of the same magnitude of the instrument.
Bias of the experimenter: Errors in the calibration of the measuring instruments. For example, one might make an incorrect reading because of parallax error.
Incorrect measuring technique: For example, the experimenter might consistently read an instrument incorrectly.

Systematic errors are errors that are constant and always of the same sign and thus may be reduced by averaging over a lot of data. Examples of systematic errors would be time constantly or systematically. So, the error belong to the same category of errors.

All instrumental errors belong to this category. All instrumental errors belong to the constancy of unit. Systematic errors are due to imperfections in the instrument and the imperfections of the instrument condition and hence the error repeats constantly or systematically. So, the error in this category belong to the same category.

Systematic errors are errors that are constant and always of the same sign, such as calibrated instruments. distance measurements by an inaccurately marked meter stick, faulty graduations of a Vernier Calipers and micrometer screw, the end error in a meter bridge, measuring scale etc.

Errors in the calibration of the measuring instruments. For example, one might make an incorrect scale reading because of an instrument incorrectly. Errors due to known causes are called systematic errors. The known causes are sources of errors. Systematic errors are not due to random causes but do not affect the precision of a measurement.

Accuracy is not the same as accuracy. Both accuracy and precision reflect how close a measurement is to an actual value, but accuracy reflects how close a measurement is to a known or accepted value, while precision reflects how reproducible measurements are, even if they are far from the accepted value.
The term 'Accuracy' denotes closeness of an experimental value to an experimental value of set or standard value.
Smaller the difference between the mean value and the true value, the larger is the accuracy.
For example, a student measured the mean value and he found the mean value 9.20 m/s². The standard value of g is 9.80 m/s²: Thus, accuracy = 9.80 − 9.20 = 0.60 m/s².

The accuracy of an instrument depends on how well its performance compares to a currently accepted standard. Uncertainties in measurement affect the accuracy of a measurement. Precision, however, is not affected because the accuracy depends on how well its performance compares to a currently accepted standard. The accuracy of an instrument is based on the accuracy of a measurement.

The term 'Precision' refers to how closely two or more measurements agree with one another. Precision is determined by the least count of the measuring instrument. The smaller the least count, the greater the precision.

For example, least count of Vernier calipers is often 0.01 cm and least count of a screw gauge is often 0.001 cm. So, measurement of small length using a screw gauge is more precise than a Vernier calipers.
Precision = individual value − mean value − Arithmetic mean value
In other words, precision gives the extent of agreement between the individual values of measurements.
This means that precision the difference between the individual values of repeated measurements, the smaller is the precision.
For example, a student was conducting an experiment to determine the value of g. He has taken many readings and the values are ranging from 9.80 m/s² to 9.802 m/s² with an average of 9.801 m/s².
Precision = least count of the measuring instrument. The smaller the least count, the greater the precision.

subject: physics
title: Physics and Measurement
notes: Physics is the branch of science that deals with natural phenomena at all scales, from subatomic particles to the entire universe. It deals with matter, energy, and the interactions between them.
The word Science originates from the Latin verb Scientia, meaning 'to know', representing systematically organized knowledge built on observations and experiments.

The term Physics is derived from the Greek word Physika, which means 'nature'. In Sanskrit, it is called Bhautika, which refers to the physical world, and an expert in this field is called a physicist.
Mathematics is considered the language of the universe, and physics heavily utilizes it as a powerful tool to describe basic laws of nature.
Mechanics is the branch of physics dealing with bodies either at rest or in motion.

• Statics: The branch of mechanics that deals with a body at rest.
  • Kinetics: The branch of mechanics that deals with a body in motion. It is further sub-divided into:
    • Kinematics: Derived from the Greek word kinema (meaning motion), it describes how objects move without taking into account the causes of that motion.
    • Dynamics: Derived from the Greek word dynamis (meaning power), it deals with why objects move as they do, acting as the general science of motion.

• Particle (Point Object): A mathematical model of a mass point where its size (dimension) is negligible compared to another body or the distance involved (e.g., a football compared to a house).
  • Body: An object that possesses a certain size, mass, and volume.
Physical quantities are measurable quantities in terms of which the laws of physics are expressed. All physical quantities possess both a magnitude and a unit: Physical Quantity = Magnitude * Unit.
The numerical value N depends on the choice of unit U; a larger unit size results in a smaller numerical value, and vice versa. N is always positive.

• Fundamental (Basic) Quantity: Quantities that do not depend on any other quantities. There are seven basic quantities: length, mass, time (Mechanics); illuminating power/luminous intensity (Optics); temperature (Heat); electric current (Electricity); and amount of chemical substance (Nuclear Physics). Sub-fundamental quantities include plane angle and solid angle.
  • Derived Quantity: Quantities obtained from fundamental quantities (e.g., Area, Density, Speed).

Measurement is the process of comparing an unknown quantity with a known constant unit, determining the quantity of something. To measure a physical quantity, two things must be known: Unit and Numerical Value.

Principle of Measurement: The product of magnitude and unit always remains constant regardless of the system of units used (N * U = Constant or N1 * U1 = N2 * U2). Magnitude is inversely proportional to the scale of the unit.
Measurement provides objective observations identical for everyone. As stated by Lord Kelvin, knowledge is truly satisfactory only when expressed in numbers; measurement is the root of science.

A unit is a standard chosen quantity in terms of which a physical quantity is measured. It must be well-defined, convenient, easily reproducible, and independent of time, place, or physical conditions.
Fundamental Unit: A unit used to measure a fundamental quantity (e.g., kilogram, gram, meter).

• Non-Standard Units: Obscure units based on historical standards (e.g., firkin for volume, eon for time).
  • Hybrid Units: Combining units from two different measurement systems for a single physical quantity (e.g., ohm centimeter for resistivity).

• 1 Fermi (femtometer): 10^-15 m (used for nuclear sizes)
  • 1 Angstrom: 10^-10 m
  • 1 Astronomical Unit (AU): 1.5 * 10^11 m
  • 1 Light Year: 9.5 * 10^15 m
  • 1 Parsec: 3.26 light years (3.08 * 10^16 m; largest practical unit of distance used for stars/galaxies)
  • 1 Litre: 10^-3 m^3
The concept was introduced clearly by Joseph Fourier in 1822, though the foundational principle was known to Isaac Newton in 1686.
Definition: The dimensions of a physical quantity are the powers, indices, or exponents to which the base fundamental quantities must be raised to represent that quantity.

title: Error Propagation & Significant Figures Rules
notes: 1. Often the certainty in a measured value is not specified explicitly. In such cases, the uncertainty is generally assumed to be one or two units in the last digit specified. For example, if a length is given as 6.2 cm, the uncertainty is assumed to be about 0.2 cm (or perhaps 0.1 cm). Here we assume that this implies an uncertainty of 0.01 cm, it assumes that it is probably between 6.19 cm and 6.21 cm, when actually we believe it is between 6.1 and 6.3 cm.
2. Error in sum and difference of quantities.
Let x = a + b. Then Δx = ±(Δa + Δb).
Similarly, let x = a − b. Then Δx = ±(Δa + Δb).
Let x = a × b. Then Δx/x = ±(Δa/a + Δb/b)
Example: Calculate uncertainty in percentage for the measurement 3.22

Answer: Generally, error in a measured value is not specified explicitly. In such cases, the error is assumed to be one or two units in the last digit specified. According to question uncertainty in measurement 3.22 so uncertainty is assumed to be 3.22 ± 0.01.

In physics there are limits to the accuracy of measurement and its reliability. The simple way of expressing this reliability is by using Significant figures. In another way, the number of digits (figures) in a given number which we are reasonably sure about which we are reasonably sure are called significant figures. The more insignificant figure specified, the more precision than the next figure is implied.

For example, we suppose that the diameter of a rod is measured and its value is found to be 0.004mm. Here we feel that 4 is a reasonable value but we are not sure of the next figure. So we have indicated only one significant figure.
Rules to Determine the Number of Significant Figures to keep:

(i) All non-zero digits are significant figures. For example, 2365 has four significant figures. All zeros between two non-zero digits are significant figures. For example, 1003 has four significant digits.

(ii) All zeros to the right of last non-zero digits are not significant if they are not followed by a decimal point are not significant if they are not significant, then they are significant. For example, 2365 has four significant figures.
(iii) All zeros to the right of a decimal point but to the left of a non-zero digit are not significant. For example, 0.00356 has three significant digits.
(iv) All zeros to the right of a decimal point and also to the right of a non-zero digit are significant. For example, 0.07600 has four significant figures.
(v) All zeros to the right of the last non-zero digit after the decimal point are significant. For example, 4.00, 4.000, 4.0000 as per the requirement.
(vi) All zeros to the right of the last non-zero digit are significant only if they come from a measurement.

(vii) The exact numbers appearing in the mathematical formula of various physical quantities have infinite number of significant figures. For example, a square is given by 4 × side. Here, 4 is an exact number and has infinite significant figures.

(viii) Addition and subtraction: In adding or subtracting, the least significant figure of the sum or difference occupies the same relative position as the least significant figures of the quantities being added or subtracted. In this case the position that matters. For example, the sum of three masses 103.9 kg, 2.10 kg and 0.319 kg is 106.319 kg. This distance can be expressed as 202000 cm or 2.020×10⁵ cm or 2.020 Km.
(ix) Multiplication and Division: In multiplying or dividing, the final result should retain as many significant figures as are there in the original number with the least significant figures.

title: Vector
notes: A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction and obeys the triangle law of addition. Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum. A scalar quantity has only magnitude. Examples: mass, time, temperature, speed, work.

Equal vectors: same magnitude and same direction. Negative vector: same magnitude, opposite direction. Null vector: zero magnitude (its direction is undefined). Unit vector: a vector of magnitude 1 along a given direction, written as $\hat{a} = \frac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}$. Parallel and antiparallel vectors: vectors along the same line (same or opposite sense). Position vector: vector joining the origin to a point. Collinear vectors: vectors along the same straight line.
Addition of Vectors — Triangle and Parallelogram Law
If two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ act at an angle $\theta$, the magnitude of their resultant $\vec{R} = \vec{a} + \vec{b}$ is:

and its direction is given by $\tan\alpha = \frac{b\sin\theta}{a + b\cos\theta}$, where $\alpha$ is the angle made by the resultant with $\vec{a}$. Special cases: parallel ($\theta = 0°$) gives $R = a + b$; antiparallel ($\theta = 180°$) gives $R = |a - b|$; perpendicular ($\theta = 90°$) gives $R = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
Any vector $\vec{A}$ can be resolved into two perpendicular components:

title: N1
notes: Think of the mirror as the center of a math graph. Left is negative, Right is positive. Up is positive, Down is negative.
Real images are always on the left and upside down → v is negative, m is negative.
Virtual images are always on the right and upright → v is positive, m is positive.
Some textbooks use an alternative, non-Cartesian system called the "Real-is-Positive" (RIP) sign convention.
Distance rule: Distances to real things (real object, real focus, real image) are given a plus (+) sign.
Virtual rule: Distances to virtual things (virtual focus, virtual image) are given a minus (−) sign.
The catch: This rule applies strictly to distances (u, v, f), not to the magnification's orientation meaning. Even under RIP, a real image is still physically upside down.
Rule: In the RIP system, −m means a Virtual, Erect image. +m means a Real, Inverted image.
Real-is-Positive (RIP) System: m = v/u (the minus sign is dropped from the formula)
How the Sign of m is Determined in RIP
Because the formula is m = v/u, the sign of m depends entirely on whether the image is real or virtual:
Real Image: object distance (u) is real (+), image distance (v) is real (+). Therefore, m = +v/+u = Positive (+m).
Virtual Image: object distance (u) is real (+), image distance (v) is virtual (−). Therefore, m = −v/+u = Negative (−m).
The confusion happens because the same physical image is described with completely opposite math signs depending on which system you choose.
Let's look at a Real, Inverted Image formed by a concave mirror: in the real world, the image is physically upside down and in front of the mirror.

Magnification formulam = −v/um = v/u

1. If your school uses the Standard System:

Think of the mirror as the center of a math graph. Left is negative, Right is positive. Up is positive, Down is negative. Real images are always on the left and upside down → v is negative, m is negative. Virtual images are always on the right and upright → v is positive, m is positive.
2. If your school uses the Real-is-Positive System:

Forget about the graph completely. Just ask: "Is this real or virtual?" Real images can be caught on a sheet of paper → v is positive, m is positive. Virtual images only look like they are inside the mirror → v is negative, m is negative.

Problem: The radius of curvature of a convex mirror is 20 cm and it forms the image of an object kept on its principal axis, at a distance of 5 cm from the pole of the mirror. Find the distance of the object from the pole.
Convex mirrors always form virtual images behind the mirror, so image distance (v) = +5 cm
Answer: The object is at a distance of 10 cm from the pole.

title: N2
notes: Every mirror problem falls into one of three main categories.
What it is: The question gives you two variables (like u and f) and asks you to find the third (v), or asks for the final magnification.

Solving Approach: Write down the givens with correct signs. Use the mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u to find the missing distance. Use the magnification formula (m = −v/u or m = v/u) to find the image characteristics.
What it is: The question gives you the focal length (or radius) and says the image is "n times magnified," but does not give you v.

Solving Approach: Express v in terms of u using the magnification formula (e.g., v = 3u or v = −3u). Substitute this expression into the mirror formula so that u is the only unknown variable. Crucial: if the question does not specify if the image is real or virtual, you must solve for both cases separately.
What it is: The object is placed at one position, then moved to a second position.

Solving Approach: Step 1 (First Position) — use the first set of data to find the focal length (f) of the mirror; the mirror doesn't change, so f stays constant. Step 2 (Second Position) — use the newly found f along with the new position data to solve for the final target.
When reading a physics problem, specific words act as hidden codes.
"Shaving mirror" or "Makeup mirror" → It is a Concave mirror used to create an enlarged, virtual image.
"Rear-view mirror" or "Driver's mirror" → It is a Convex mirror used to see a wide view of smaller, virtual images.
"Reflecting surface is curved inwards" → Concave mirror.
"Reflecting surface is curved outwards" → Convex mirror.

title: N3
notes: "The size of the image is half the size of the object"
Meaning: the numerical value of magnification is |m| = 0.5.

How to decide the sign: if the mirror is convex, it must be a virtual image (Cartesian: m = +0.5, RIP: m = −0.5). If the mirror is concave, it must be a real image (Cartesian: m = −0.5, RIP: m = +0.5) because concave mirrors only produce diminished images when the object is beyond the center of curvature, which always results in a real image.
"Magnified" / "Enlarged" → |m| > 1 (can only be produced by a Concave mirror).
"Diminished" / "Smaller" → |m| < 1 (can be produced by both, but if virtual, it must be Convex).
"Same size as the object" → |m| = 1 (object at Center of Curvature C of a Concave mirror; u = 2f).

"A dentist holds a small mirror..." — Meaning: it is a concave mirror. Hidden Hint: dentists use these to see an enlarged, upright view of teeth, meaning the object (tooth) is placed between the focus and pole (u < f), creating a virtual, magnified image.

"Used as a solar furnace / solar cooker mirror" — Meaning: it is a concave mirror. Hidden Hint: sunlight comes from infinity (u = ∞); the mirror converges parallel rays to a point, so the heat/cooker must be placed exactly at the focus (v = f).

"An object is moved closer to the mirror by 10 cm..." — Meaning: implies a two-state problem where u₂ = u₁ − 10. How to solve: find the initial focal length or object distance using the first scenario before mathematically altering the distance for the second scenario.

Convex mirrors have only one behavioral mode for any real object placed anywhere in front of them:
Condition: u can be anywhere from the pole to infinity.
Resulting Image Location: the image must always form behind the mirror, specifically between the Pole and the Focus (v < f).
Resulting Magnification: the image is always virtual, erect, and diminished (|m| < 1).
Rule: if you calculate an image for a convex mirror that is real, inverted, or magnified, your math is incorrect.

The Real Object Condition: in real-world physics problems, the object is always real and placed in front of the mirror. Standard System: u must always be negative. RIP System: u must always be positive.

The Concave Mirror Virtual Exception: a concave mirror can only form a virtual image if the object is placed closer than the focal length (u < |f|). If your problem states the image is virtual and you're using a concave mirror, your calculated u must come out smaller than f.

The Focal Length Consistency: the focal length (f) is a physical property of the glass. It cannot change within the same problem unless the mirror is physically swapped. In two-step problems, calculate f in part 1, and plug that same value into part 2.
Condition for Zero Size: an image has zero size (m = 0) only when the object is infinitely far away (u = ∞).
Condition for Infinite Size: an image becomes infinitely large (m = ∞) only when the object is placed exactly on the focus (u = f).
Condition for Equal Distance: the image distance equals the object distance (|v| = |u|) only when the object is at the Center of Curvature (u = 2f).
Note: in the RIP system, m = v/u yields a positive sign for real/inverted images, which means a negative sign must be applied if relating it to the physical downward height ratio hᵢ/hₒ.
dₒ, p, or s → alternative symbols for Object Distance (u). dᵢ, q, or s' → alternative symbols for Image Distance (v). hₒ or h → Height of the Object. hᵢ or h' → Height of the Image.

"The mirror is partially covered / blacked out" — Meaning: if half of a concave mirror is covered with black paper, the full image is still formed. Hidden Hint: position, size, and nature of the image remain unchanged, but brightness/intensity decreases because less light is reflected.
"Object size is negligible / point object" — Meaning: the object is treated as a single point on the principal axis; only u and v matter, linear magnification heights (hᵢ) are ignored.

"A plane mirror is placed next to the spherical mirror..." — Meaning: a two-surface problem. The plane mirror forms a virtual image exactly as far behind it as the object is in front. Hidden Hint: questions will say "the two images coincide" — find where the plane mirror creates its image, then use that exact spatial location as the target value for the spherical mirror's image distance (v).
The Trick: The question states: "A concave mirror forms an image 3 times the size of the object." It does not say if it is real or virtual.
The Trap: Students only calculate one position.

The Defeat: Concave mirrors can form both a real-magnified image (inverted) and a virtual-magnified image (erect). Solve twice — Case 1: take m as real (e.g. m = −3 in Cartesian). Case 2: take m as virtual (e.g. m = +3 in Cartesian).
The Trick: The question states: "A convex mirror forms an image magnified 2 times..."
The Trap: Students start calculating using m = 2.

The Defeat: This is a conceptual trick question. Convex mirrors can never magnify a real object; they only form smaller (diminished) images. The answer is immediately "Not physically possible" or "No such position exists."
3. The "Distance Between Object and Image" Trick
The Trick: The question says: "The distance between the object and its image is 10 cm."
The Trap: Students write down v − u = 10 or v = 10.

The Defeat: This means the absolute gap |v − u| = 10. Use the mirror type to figure out which is further away: for a convex mirror, the image is always closer to the mirror than the object, so (−u) − v = 10. For a concave mirror forming a real image, if the object is beyond C, the object is further away (u > v), so (−u) − (−v) = 10.
The Trick: "A concave mirror of focal length 20 cm is completely immersed in a tank of water. Find its new focal length."
The Trap: Students use the refractive index of water (μ = 4/3) to change the focal length.
The Defeat: Mirrors do not change focal length in liquids. The focal length depends purely on the radius of curvature (f = R/2); this only applies to lenses. The focal length remains exactly 20 cm.
The Trick: An object is at 30 cm, then it is "shifted by 10 cm towards the mirror."
The Trap: Students miscalculate the new object distance.

The Defeat: Old distance: u₁ = −30 cm. New distance: shifted towards means it is closer, so u₂ = −(30−10) = −20 cm. Tip: always find the focal length (f) from the first scenario first, as it stays constant for the second scenario.
