title: Mirrors and Lenses
notes: 📘 TOPIC OUTLINE: Core Feeling (Converging vs Diverging) | Concave Mirror (6-case table) | Convex Mirror (1-line answer) | Convex Lens (6-case table) | Concave Lens (1-line answer) | Decoder Table for Hidden Exam Words | Sign Convention Reminder

🎯 THE ONE IDEA THAT REPLACES ALL MEMORIZATION: There are only two behaviors in all of optics — CONVERGING (bends light inward, toward the axis) and DIVERGING (bends light outward, away from the axis). Concave mirror and Convex lens are both CONVERGING devices — they behave identically in logic. Convex mirror and Concave lens are both DIVERGING devices — they also behave identically to each other. So really you only need to learn 2 patterns, not 4 devices.

💡 WHY DIVERGING DEVICES ARE 'FREE MARKS': A diverging device takes light that is already spreading apart and spreads it even MORE. Those rays can never physically meet again — so a real image is IMPOSSIBLE with a diverging device, no matter where the object is placed. Your brain traces the spreading rays backward with dotted lines to find where they 'seem' to meet — that imaginary meeting point is a virtual image: always erect, always smaller, always trapped close to the mirror/lens.

📐 THE FEELING: Push the object from very far away toward the mirror. Watch the image do the OPPOSITE — it starts near F and RUNS AWAY from the mirror, growing bigger as it runs. At the exact tipping point (object at F), the image escapes to infinity — the mirror literally cannot bring the rays back together anymore. Push the object even closer than F, and the reflected rays now diverge going forward, so your brain traces them backward BEHIND the mirror. The image suddenly flips to virtual, erect, and magnified.
📝 TABLE A1 — CONCAVE MIRROR: ALL 6 CASES

| Object Position | Image Position | Nature | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| At infinity | At F | Real, Inverted | Highly diminished (point) |
| Beyond C | Between F and C | Real, Inverted | Diminished |
| At C | At C | Real, Inverted | Same size |
| Between C and F | Beyond C | Real, Inverted | Magnified |
| At F | At infinity | Real, Inverted | Highly magnified |
| Between F and Pole | Behind the mirror | Virtual, Erect | Magnified |

🔑 PATTERN TO FEEL, NOT MEMORIZE: Object and image trade places symmetrically around C. As object moves TOWARD the mirror (∞→C→F), image moves AWAY from the mirror (F→C→∞). The moment object crosses F, the whole system 'breaks' and image teleports behind the mirror as virtual.

📐 THE FEELING: No case-by-case tracking needed. Because it diverges everything, the image is ALWAYS squeezed into the tiny region between the Pole and F, behind the mirror — this is your guaranteed one-line answer on any convex mirror question.
📝 TABLE B1 — CONVEX MIRROR: THE ONLY CASE

| Object Position | Image Position | Nature | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anywhere (infinity to pole) | Always between Pole and F, behind mirror | Virtual, Erect | Always diminished |
🔑 REAL-WORLD ANCHOR TO FEEL IT: This is exactly your car's side mirror — 'objects in mirror are closer than they appear' because it's always shrinking and always upright, never flips, never grows.

📐 THE FEELING: Identical rhythm to the concave mirror, except now F and 2F exist on BOTH sides of the lens because light actually passes through it. As the object moves from infinity toward F1, the image runs away toward infinity on the far side, growing. The instant the object crosses inside F1, the lens can no longer converge the rays on the far side — so the image jumps back to the SAME side as the object, virtual, erect, magnified. This is exactly how a magnifying glass works.
📝 TABLE C1 — CONVEX LENS: ALL 6 CASES

| Object Position | Image Position | Nature | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| At infinity | At F2 | Real, Inverted | Highly diminished (point) |
| Beyond 2F1 | Between F2 and 2F2 | Real, Inverted | Diminished |
| At 2F1 | At 2F2 | Real, Inverted | Same size |
| Between F1 and 2F1 | Beyond 2F2 | Real, Inverted | Magnified |
| At F1 | At infinity | Real, Inverted | Highly magnified |
| Between F1 and optical center | Same side as object | Virtual, Erect | Magnified |

🔑 PATTERN TO FEEL: Just relabel the concave mirror's C as 2F1/2F2, and Pole as the optical center. Everything else — the direction of motion, the flip point, the trade-off between object and image — behaves the same.
📐 THE FEELING: Same free-answer logic as the convex mirror. The image is always squeezed between the optical center and F1, on the SAME side as the object — light never crosses to the other side.
📝 TABLE D1 — CONCAVE LENS: THE ONLY CASE

| Object Position | Image Position | Nature | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anywhere (infinity to optical center) | Always between optical center and F1, same side as object | Virtual, Erect | Always diminished |
🔑 REAL-WORLD ANCHOR: Think of a door peephole lens — everything looks small, upright, and stays on your side of the door.

🎯 ONE-LINE EXAM SHORTCUT: If the question says CONVEX MIRROR or CONCAVE LENS, don't even read the object distance — answer 'virtual, erect, diminished' immediately. Only concave mirror and convex lens actually need the 6-case table.

💡 CORE TRUTH TO INTERNALIZE (this single fact generates the entire table below): REAL means light rays actually cross at that point → always INVERTED → can be CAUGHT on a screen. VIRTUAL means your eye/brain extrapolates backward to an imaginary meeting point → always ERECT → can NEVER be caught on a screen. Every hidden phrase below is just a disguised way of stating one of these two facts.

| Phrase in question | What it secretly means | Why (the trick) |
|---|---|---|
| erect / upright / same orientation | Virtual image | Real images are ALWAYS inverted — no exceptions — so 'erect' auto-confirms virtual |
| inverted | Real image | Virtual images are NEVER inverted — this is the one fact with zero exceptions |
| can be obtained/caught on a screen | Real image | Only actual crossing light rays can be projected onto paper |
| cannot be obtained on a screen | Virtual image | Extrapolated rays don't physically exist there — nothing to catch |
| diminished / smaller / reduced | Magnification m < 1 | Object sits farther from the converging point than needed to magnify |
| magnified / enlarged | Magnification m > 1 | Object sits inside the 'magnifying zone' (between F and 2F for lens, C and F for mirror) |
| point-sized / highly diminished | Object is at infinity | Classic clue for telescope/parallel-ray problems |

| same size as object | Object at C (mirror) or 2F (lens) | This is exactly where magnification = −1 |
| formed behind the mirror | Virtual (mirror-specific) | Real images only form in FRONT of a mirror, where light actually travels |
| formed on same side as object | Virtual (lens-specific) | Real images in a lens always form on the OPPOSITE side, since light passes through |
| 'diverging mirror/lens' named directly | Skip the whole table | Convex mirror & concave lens = guaranteed virtual, erect, diminished |
═══════════ SECTION F: SIGN CONVENTION QUICK ANCHOR (yours, restated for feel) ═══════════
📐 CARTESIAN SIGN CONVENTION: Measured from the pole/optical center. Right and Up = positive. Left and Down = negative.

📐 REAL-IS-POSITIVE (R.I.P) CONVENTION: For a REAL image — up, down, and left (i.e., away from the mirror, where light actually goes) are positive. For a VIRTUAL image — right, up, down (i.e., behind the mirror, where light doesn't actually go) are negative.

🔑 FEEL IT: Both conventions are just bookkeeping — the physics (which case gives which image) never changes. What changes is only the +/- sign you write for f, u, v, and h when you plug into formulas. Get the physical picture right FIRST using Sections A–D, then attach signs LAST using this convention — don't try to do both at once.

notes: MIRROR SIGN CONVENTIONS - TWO SYSTEMS EXIST

STANDARD CARTESIAN SIGN CONVENTION: Based on treating the pole of the mirror as the origin of an X-Y graph. Left of mirror = negative, Right of mirror = positive. Up = positive, Down = negative. Real images are always formed on the left (in front of mirror) and are upside down, so image distance (v) is negative and magnification (m) is negative. Virtual images are always on the right (behind mirror) and upright, so v is positive and m is positive.

REAL-IS-POSITIVE (RIP) SIGN CONVENTION: A non-Cartesian alternative system. Distance rule: distances to real things (real object, real focus, real image) are given a plus (+) sign. Virtual rule: distances to virtual things (virtual focus, virtual image) are given a minus (-) sign. Important catch: this rule applies strictly to distances (u, v, f), NOT to the magnification's orientation meaning - even under RIP, a real image is still physically upside down.
MAGNIFICATION FORMULA - DIFFERS BETWEEN SYSTEMS: Standard Convention: m = -v/u. Real-is-Positive (RIP) System: m = v/u (the minus sign is dropped from the formula).

HOW SIGN OF m IS DETERMINED - Standard Convention: When m is Positive (m > 0): image is Virtual, Erect (upright), meaning image points same direction as object. When m is Negative (m < 0): image is Real, Inverted (upside down), meaning image points opposite to object.

HOW SIGN OF m IS DETERMINED - RIP System (opposite meaning of same values): Real Image: object distance u is real (+), image distance v is real (+), so m = +v/+u = Positive (+m). Rule: in RIP, +m means a Real, Inverted image. Virtual Image: object distance u is real (+), image distance v is virtual (-), so m = -v/+u = Negative (-m). Rule: in RIP, -m means a Virtual, Erect image.

SUMMARY COMPARISON TABLE (Image Nature vs Convention):
| Image Nature | Standard Convention | RIP System |
|---|---|---|
| Real & Inverted | -m (Negative) | +m (Positive) |
| Virtual & Erect | +m (Positive) | -m (Negative) |

FULL FEATURE COMPARISON TABLE (Standard Cartesian vs RIP):
| Feature | Standard Cartesian | Real-is-Positive (RIP) |
|---|---|---|
| Why it's named | Based on an X-Y graph axis | Based on whether light is real or fake |
| Object Distance (u) | Negative (left side of graph) | Positive (object is real) |
| Image Distance (v) | Negative (left side of graph) | Positive (image is real) |
| Focal Length (f) | Negative (left side of graph) | Positive (focus is real) |
| Magnification formula | m = -v/u | m = v/u |
| Magnification sign | Negative (because it points down) | Positive (because both v and u are positive) |

CORE POINT OF CONFUSION: The same physical image is described with completely opposite math signs depending on which system is chosen. Example - a Real, Inverted image formed by a concave mirror: physically the image is upside down and in front of the mirror in both systems, but Standard Cartesian labels it negative (u, v, f, m all negative) while RIP labels it positive (u, v, f, m all positive) for real quantities.

TWO-STEP RULE TO AVOID SIGN CONFUSION:
1. If school uses Standard System: Think of mirror as center of a math graph. Left = negative, Right = positive. Up = positive, Down = negative. Real images are always on the left and upside down → v is negative, m is negative. Virtual images are always on the right and upright → v is positive, m is positive.
2. If school uses Real-is-Positive System: Forget about the graph completely. Just ask 'Is this real or virtual?' Real images can be caught on a sheet of paper → v is positive, m is positive. Virtual images only look like they are inside the mirror → v is negative, m is negative.
PART 1: QUESTION TYPES & SOLVING APPROACHES - Every mirror problem falls into one of three categories.

TYPE 1: THE 'DIRECT FINDER' - What it is: the question gives two variables (like u and f) and asks you to find the third (v), or asks for the final magnification. Solving Approach: (1) Write down the givens with correct signs. (2) Use the mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u to find the missing distance. (3) Use the magnification formula (m = -v/u or m = v/u depending on convention) to find the image characteristics.

TYPE 2: THE 'MAGNIFICATION PIVOT' - What it is: the question gives the focal length (or radius) and says the image is 'n times magnified,' but does not give you v directly. Solving Approach: (1) Express v in terms of u using the magnification formula (e.g., v = 3u or v = -3u). (2) Substitute this expression into the mirror formula so that u is the only unknown variable. (3) Crucial: if the question does not specify if the image is real or virtual, you must solve for both cases separately.

TYPE 3: THE 'TWO-POSITION SHIFT' - What it is: the object is placed at one position, then moved to a second position. Solving Approach: Step 1 (First Position) - use the first set of data to find the focal length (f) of the mirror (the mirror doesn't change, so f stays constant). Step 2 (Second Position) - use the newly found f along with the new position data to solve for the final target.
PART 2: THE HINT DECODER (What Indicates What) - Specific words in physics problems act as hidden codes.

HINTS ABOUT THE MIRROR TYPE:
- 'Shaving mirror' or 'Makeup mirror' → it is a Concave mirror used to create an enlarged, virtual image.
- 'Rear-view mirror' or 'Driver's mirror' → it is a Convex mirror used to see a wide view of smaller, virtual images.
- 'Reflecting surface is curved inwards' → Concave mirror.
- 'Reflecting surface is curved outwards' → Convex mirror.

HINTS ABOUT IMAGE NATURE & SIGN RULES (phrase → meaning in each convention):
| Phrase in Question | Standard Cartesian | RIP |
|---|---|---|
| 'Brought to a focus on a screen' | Real Image → v negative, m negative | Real Image → v positive, m positive |
| 'Inverted image' | Real Image → v negative, m negative | Real Image → v positive, m positive |
| 'Erect image' or 'Upright' | Virtual Image → v positive, m positive | Virtual Image → v negative, m negative |
| 'Formed behind the mirror' | Virtual Image → v positive, m positive | Virtual Image → v negative, m negative |
| 'Formed in front of the mirror' | Real Image → v negative, m negative | Real Image → v positive, m positive |

STEP 1: FIND THE IMAGE NATURE FROM KEYWORDS:
| Question says... | Nature of the Image |
|---|---|
| 'Erect', 'Upright', or 'Behind the mirror' | Virtual |
| 'Inverted', 'On a screen', or 'In front of a concave mirror' | Real |
| 'Convex mirror' (for any real object) | Always Virtual (and smaller) |
| 'Magnified image by a convex mirror' | Trick question! Convex mirrors cannot magnify |
| 'Diminished image by a concave mirror' | Always Real |

STEP 2: CHOOSE THE SIGN BASED ON YOUR CONVENTION
Option A - Standard Cartesian Convention (most common):
- Real Image: image is upside down (inverted) → take magnification as negative (-m); image is in front of mirror → take image distance as negative (-v).
- Virtual Image: image is upright (erect) → take magnification as positive (+m); image is behind the mirror → take image distance as positive (+v).
Option B - Real-is-Positive (RIP) System:
- Real Image: real things get a plus sign → take magnification as positive (+m); image is real → take image distance as positive (+v).
- Virtual Image: virtual things get a minus sign → take magnification as negative (-m); image is virtual → take image distance as negative (-v).

QUICK EXAMPLE TO CLARIFY: Question: 'A concave mirror forms an image magnified 3 times on a screen.' Step 1 - Find Nature: the keyword 'on a screen' means the image must be Real. Step 2 - Apply Sign: In Standard Cartesian, take m = -3. In Real-is-Positive, take m = +3.

SOLVED NUMERICAL PROBLEM (Question 1 from practice sheet): Problem: The radius of curvature of a convex mirror is 20 cm and it forms the image of an object kept on its principal axis, at a distance of 5 cm from the pole of the mirror. Find the distance of the object from the pole.
Solution:
- Given data: Convex mirror radius of curvature (R) = +20 cm.
- Focal length (f) = R/2 = +20/2 = +10 cm.
- Convex mirrors always form virtual images behind the mirror, so image distance (v) = +5 cm.
- Using the Mirror Formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u
  1/10 = 1/5 + 1/u
  1/u = 1/10 - 1/5
  1/u = (1-2)/10 = -1/10
  u = -10 cm.
- Answer: The object is at a distance of 10 cm from the pole (on the standard convention, u = -10 cm indicates it is a real object in front of the mirror).

TRICKY PHRASINGS ABOUT 'DISTANCE BETWEEN...':
- "The distance between the object and its image is [X] cm": Meaning: |v - u| = X. How to solve: determine from context whether the image is closer to or farther from the mirror than the object, then set up the equation (e.g., v - u = X or u - v = X) to solve for one in terms of the other.
- "The distance between the object and the principal focus is...": Meaning: this gives you the value of u - f (or f - u), NOT the absolute value of u. You must add or subtract the focal length to find the actual value of u.

3. MISSING MAGNIFICATION CLUES (SIGNLESS QUANTITIES): "The size of the image is half the size of the object" → Meaning: the numerical value of magnification is |m| = 0.5. How to decide the sign: If the mirror is convex, it must be a virtual image (Cartesian: m = +0.5, RIP: m = -0.5). If the mirror is concave, it must be a real image (Cartesian: m = -0.5, RIP: m = +0.5) because concave mirrors only produce diminished images when the object is beyond the center of curvature, which always results in a real image.

3. HINTS ABOUT MAGNIFICATION SIZES:
- "Magnified"/"Enlarged" → |m| > 1 (can only be produced by a Concave mirror).
- "Diminished"/"Smaller" → |m| < 1 (can be produced by both, but if it's virtual, it must be a Convex mirror).
- "Same size as the object" → |m| = 1 (object is sitting exactly at the Center of Curvature, C, of a Concave mirror; u = 2f).
- "An image of the same size is obtained" → |m| = 1. This can only happen with a concave mirror (at the center of curvature) or a plane mirror. A convex mirror can never form an image of the same size for a real object.

4. HIDDEN MATH VALUES:
- "An object is kept..." → gives you u (in Standard system, u is always negative; in RIP, u is always positive).
- "Radius of curvature is 20 cm" → gives you f. Divide by 2 (f = R/2 = 10 cm).
- "A distant object / Object at infinity" → u = ∞, which means the image will form exactly at the focus (v = f).

1. EXCEPTIONAL GEOMETRIC PHRASES & SPECIAL POSITIONS:
- "Object placed at the Center of Curvature": Meaning: object distance u is exactly equal to the radius of curvature (u = R = 2f). Hidden Hint: the image will form exactly at the center of curvature as well (v = u), and it will be real, inverted, and exactly the same size (m = -1 in Cartesian, or m = +1 in RIP).
- "Image forms at infinity": Meaning: image distance v = ∞. Hidden Hint: the object is placed exactly at the principal focus (u = f). The image is highly magnified, real, and inverted.
- "Object placed at Focus": Meaning: u = f. Hidden Hint: the image distance v = ∞.
- "The mirror forms a real image at the same position as the object": Meaning: v = u. This only happens when the object is at the center of curvature (C) of a concave mirror.

4. HINTS EMBEDDED IN PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS:
- "A dentist holds a small mirror...": Meaning: it is a concave mirror. Hidden Hint: dentists use these to see an enlarged, upright view of teeth. This means the object (tooth) is placed between the focus and the pole (u < f), creating a virtual, magnified image.
- "Used as a solar furnace / solar cooker mirror": Meaning: it is a concave mirror. Hidden Hint: sunlight represents light coming from an infinite distance (u = ∞). The mirror converges these parallel rays to a single point, meaning the heat/cooker must be placed exactly at the focus (v = f).

How to solve: you must find the initial focal length or initial object distance using the first scenario before you can mathematically alter the distance for the second scenario.

COMPLETE CHECKLIST: PHYSICAL CONDITIONS, CONSTRAINTS & BOUNDARY RULES - These rules act as a 'sanity check' to help immediately identify if a calculated answer is physically possible or wrong.

1. OBJECT POSITION vs. IMAGE BEHAVIOR (CONCAVE MIRROR) - For a Concave Mirror (focal length f is negative in Standard / positive in RIP), where the object is placed determines exactly what happens to the image. Full table:
| If Object Position (u) is... | Then Image Nature is... | Image Location (v) is... | Magnification (m) is... |
|---|---|---|---|
| At Infinity (u = ∞) | Real & Inverted | Exactly at Focus (v = f) | Highly diminished (m ≈ 0) |
| Beyond Center (u > 2f) | Real & Inverted | Between f and 2f | Diminished (\|m\| < 1) |
| At Center (u = 2f) | Real & Inverted | Exactly at Center (v = 2f) | Same size (\|m\| = 1) |
| Between C and F (f < u < 2f) | Real & Inverted | Beyond Center (v > 2f) | Magnified (\|m\| > 1) |
| At Focus (u = f) | Real & Inverted | At Infinity (v = ∞) | Highly magnified (m → ∞) |
| Between F and Pole (u < f) | Virtual & Erect | Behind Mirror | Magnified (\|m\| > 1) |

4. ZERO AND INFINITE EDGE CONDITIONS:
- Condition for Zero Size: an image has zero size (m = 0) only when the object is infinitely far away (u = ∞).
- Condition for Infinite Size: an image becomes infinitely large (m = ∞) only when the object is placed exactly on the focus (u = f).
- Condition for Equal Distance: the image distance equals the object distance (|v| = |u|) only when the object is at the Center of Curvature (u = 2f).

3. ABSOLUTE MATHEMATICAL CONDITIONS (SANITY CHECKS) - Use these to catch sign errors when solving equations:
- The Real Object Condition: in real-world physics problems, the object is always real and placed in front of the mirror. Standard System: u must always be negative. RIP System: u must always be positive.
- The Concave Mirror Virtual Exception: a concave mirror can only form a virtual image if the object is placed closer than the focal length (u < |f|). If a problem states the image is virtual and you're using a concave mirror, the calculated u must come out smaller than f.
- The Focal Length Consistency: the focal length (f) is a physical property of the glass. It cannot change within the same problem unless the mirror is physically swapped for a different one. In two-step problems, calculate f in part 1, and plug that exact same value into part 2.

2. THE STRICT CONSTRAINTS OF CONVEX MIRRORS - Convex mirrors are simple because they have only ONE behavioral mode for any real object placed anywhere in front of them:
- Condition: u can be anywhere from the pole to infinity.
- Resulting Image Location: the image must always form behind the mirror, specifically between the Pole and the Focus (v < f).
- Resulting Magnification: the image is always virtual, erect, and diminished (|m| < 1).
- Rule: if you calculate an image for a convex mirror that is real, inverted, or magnified, the math is incorrect.

OBJECT POSITION vs IMAGE BEHAVIOR (CONCAVE MIRROR) - ADDITIONAL ROWS:
| If Object Position (u) is... | Then Image Nature is... | Image Location (v) is... | Magnification (m) is... |
|---|---|---|---|
| Between C and F (f < u < 2f) | Real & Inverted | Beyond Center (v > 2f) | Magnified (\|m\| > 1) |
| At Focus (u = f) | Real & Inverted | At Infinity (v = ∞) | Highly magnified (m → ∞) |
| Between F and Pole (u < f) | Virtual & Erect | Behind Mirror | Magnified (\|m\| > 1) |

1. ALTERNATIVE VARIABLE NAMES (used in some textbooks):
- do, p, or s → alternative symbols for Object Distance (u).
- di, q, or s' → alternative symbols for Image Distance (v).
- ho or h → Height of the Object.
- hi or h' → Height of the Image.

2. TRICKY PHYSICAL CONDITIONS:
- "The mirror is partially covered / blacked out": Meaning: if half of a concave mirror is covered with black paper, the full image is still formed. Hidden Hint: the position, size, and nature of the image remain completely unchanged, but the brightness/intensity decreases because less light is reflected.
- "Object size is negligible / point object": Meaning: the object is treated mathematically as a single point lying directly on the principal axis. Only u and v matter; linear magnification heights (hi) are ignored.
- "A plane mirror is placed next to the spherical mirror...": Meaning: a two-surface problem. The plane mirror forms a virtual image exactly as far behind it as the object is in front. Hidden Hint: questions will say 'the two images coincide' — this means finding where the plane mirror creates its image, then using that exact spatial location as the target value for the spherical mirror's image distance (v).

3. ABSOLUTE MATHEMATICAL FORMULAS SUMMARY TABLE:
| System | Mirror Formula | Magnification Formula |
|---|---|---|
| Standard Cartesian | 1/f = 1/v + 1/u | m = -v/u = hi/ho |
| Real-is-Positive (RIP) | 1/f = 1/v + 1/u | m = v/u = -hi/ho |
(Note: in the RIP system, m = v/u yields a positive sign for real/inverted images, which means a negative sign must be applied if relating it to the physical downward height ratio hi/ho.)

1. THE 'APERTURE' HINT - Phrase: 'A mirror of small aperture...'. Meaning: this is a physical constraint meaning the mirror's opening is very narrow compared to its curvature. Hidden Hint: this justifies using the standard mirror formulas. It guarantees that paraxial rays (rays close to the principal axis) are being used, meaning the relationship f = R/2 is mathematically valid for calculations.

2. MAGNIFICATION RATIO HINTS - Phrase: 'The ratio of the size of the object to the size of the image is...'. Meaning: this gives the inverse of magnification: ho/hi. Hidden Hint: if the ratio of object-to-image is 3:1, then ho/hi = 3, which means the actual magnification value is the reciprocal (m = 1/3), used to find the sign and category (magnified/diminished) accordingly.

3. SHIFT AND MOTION HINTS - Phrase: 'The object is shifted by a distance...'. Meaning: this indicates a change in position, creating a Case 1 and Case 2 scenario. Hidden Hint: the focal length (f) must be calculated from Case 1 first, because the mirror's physical shape remains constant. Then use that exact same value of f to solve for the unknown variable in Case 2.

4. MEDIUM HINTS (liquid immersion concept) - Phrase: 'The entire setup is immersed in water...'. Meaning: this is a conceptual trap often found in competitive exams. Hidden Hint: reflection depends purely on the geometry of the mirror's curved surface. Unlike lenses, the focal length of a mirror does not change when placed in water or any other liquid.
COMMON EXAM QUESTION TRICKS - The most common tricks exam writers use to cause mistakes, and how to spot and defeat them:

1. THE 'DOUBLE MAGNIFICATION' TRICK - The Trick: the question states 'A concave mirror forms an image 3 times the size of the object' without specifying if it is real or virtual. The Trap: students only calculate one position. The Defeat: concave mirrors can form both a real-magnified image (inverted) and a virtual-magnified image (erect); the problem must be solved twice: Case 1 - take m as real (e.g., m = -3 in Cartesian). Case 2 - take m as virtual (e.g., m = +3 in Cartesian).

2. THE 'CONVEX MIRROR MAGNIFICATION' TRAP - The Trick: the question states 'A convex mirror forms an image magnified 2 times...'. The Trap: students start calculating using m = 2. The Defeat: this is a conceptual trick question. Convex mirrors can never magnify a real object; they only form smaller (diminished) images. The answer is immediately 'Not physically possible' or 'No such position exists.'

3. THE 'DISTANCE BETWEEN OBJECT AND IMAGE' TRICK - The Trick: the question says 'The distance between the object and its image is 10 cm.' The Trap: students write down v - u = 10 or v = 10. The Defeat: this means the absolute gap |v - u| = 10. The mirror type must be used to figure out which one is further away: For a convex mirror, the image is always closer to the mirror than the object, so (-u) - v = 10. For a concave mirror forming a real image, if the object is beyond C, the object is further away (u > v), so (-u) - (-v) = 10.

4. THE 'LIQUID IMMERSION' TRICK - The Trick: 'A concave mirror of focal length 20 cm is completely immersed in a tank of water. Find its new focal length.' The Trap: students use the refractive index of water (μ = 4/3) to change the focal length. The Defeat: mirrors do not change focal length in liquids. The focal length depends purely on the radius of curvature (f = R/2). This only applies to lenses. The focal length remains exactly 20 cm.

5. THE 'OBJECT SHIFT' TRICK - The Trick: an object is at 30 cm, then it is 'shifted by 10 cm towards the mirror.' The Trap: students miscalculate the new object distance. The Defeat: Old distance: u1 = -30 cm. New distance: shifted towards means it is closer, so u2 = -(30-10) = -20 cm. Tip: always find the focal length (f) from the first scenario first, as it stays constant for the second scenario.

subject: physics
title: Reflection at Curved Surface
notes: 14.1 INTRODUCTION — Light shows many phenomena such as reflection, refraction, and diffraction. To observe reflection of light, a reflecting surface is needed, which may be of any shape — flat or curved. The curved surface may be concave or convex. A special type of flat and curved surface made from glass is called a plane mirror and a curved mirror respectively.

14.2 REFLECTING SURFACE — A reflecting surface is a surface that reflects a beam of light. There are two types of reflecting surfaces: (1) Smooth reflecting surface — Example: plane mirror. (2) Rough reflecting surface — Examples: wall, cloth, surface of soap, floor. A mirror is the best smooth reflecting surface.

RAY OF LIGHT — It is a straight-line path along which light travels. It is represented by a straight line with an arrow: →(ray of light). A single ray of light is not possible/practically realizable on its own; light always travels as a bundle of rays.

BEAM OF LIGHT — It is a collection of rays of light, or a bundle of light rays, which is emitted by a source of light. There are 3 types of beam of light: (a) Parallel beam — all the rays of light are parallel to each other. Figure: several arrows drawn parallel to one another pointing in the same direction (⇉⇉⇉⇉). (b) Converging/Convergent beam of light — a collection of light rays where all light rays are converged to a single point. Figure: several rays drawn from different directions meeting at a single point 'O' (rays shown converging into O). (c) Divergent beam of light — light rays diverged from a single point. Figure: several rays drawn spreading outward from a single point.

REFLECTION OF LIGHT (Definition) — Incident ray of light: A light ray striking/falling at a reflecting surface, or the light ray emitted toward a surface. Reflected ray of light: The ray of light obtained/bounced off from a reflecting surface. Normal: It is a perpendicular drawn to the surface at the point of incidence. Figure: Diagram showing normal line 'N' drawn perpendicular to a horizontal reflecting surface at the point of incidence; incident ray 'I ray' approaches from upper-left making angle 'i' with the normal; reflected ray 'R ray' leaves toward upper-right making angle 'r' with the normal; the point where incident ray meets the surface is labeled 'point of incidence', with dotted line shown as the produced/extended incident ray beyond the surface. Reflection of light is defined as: 'It is a phenomenon of light in which light rays bounce off a reflecting surface such that they return into the same medium by changing its direction.'

TYPES OF REFLECTION OF LIGHT — There are two types: (a) Regular reflection of light, and (b) Irregular reflection of light. Figure: Two small diagrams at top of page — left diagram shows an incident ray and reflected ray meeting a normal line drawn on a rough/hatched horizontal surface; right diagram shows a single vertical normal line on another hatched horizontal surface (illustrating surface roughness at microscopic level).

REGULAR REFLECTION OF LIGHT — It is such a reflection of light in which the reflected beam of light remains parallel to that of the incident beam. It takes place at smooth reflecting surfaces such as a mirror. Figure: Several parallel incident rays striking a smooth horizontal surface (marked with hatching) and reflecting as parallel rays at equal angles, drawn converging toward and diverging from the same points on the surface, labeled 'Regular reflection of light'.

IRREGULAR (DIFFUSED) REFLECTION OF LIGHT — It is such a reflection of light in which the reflected beam of light gets diffused. It is also called diffused reflection of light. It takes place at rough reflecting surfaces. Figure: Several parallel incident rays striking a rough/wavy horizontal surface and reflecting off in many different scattered directions, labeled 'Diffused reflection of light'.
OPTICAL IMAGE — It is a representation of a physical object formed by an optical system or an optical device. There are two types of optical image: (a) Real image, and (b) Virtual image.

REAL IMAGE — It is an optical image which can be obtained on a screen. It forms when two or more actual reflected or refracted rays of light meet at a point. In case of a mirror, real image is formed in front of the mirror; in case of a lens, real image is formed on the opposite side of the lens. Real image is always inverted.

VIRTUAL IMAGE — It is an optical image which cannot be obtained on a screen. It forms at the point of intersection of two or more produced (backward-extended) reflected or refracted rays of light. Figure: Diagram showing several rays diverging from a point on the left, striking a vertical mirror line, reflecting outward to the right; the reflected rays are extended backward (dashed/produced) behind the mirror line to meet at a single point on the right labeled 'Image formed' — illustrating that the virtual image is formed where the produced rays appear to meet, not where actual rays meet. In case of a mirror, virtual image forms behind it. In case of a lens, virtual image forms in front of it, i.e., on the same side as the object.

REAL OBJECT vs VIRTUAL OBJECT — An object that emits light is called a real object; it may be luminous (e.g., sun, glowing bulb) or non-luminous (e.g., book, table). A point where converging rays appear to meet is called a virtual object — for example, the image of a real object in a plane mirror is a virtual image but acts as a virtual object for our eye. For a real object O, the virtual image is I: in the absence of the mirror the rays would converge to point O, but due to the mirror's presence the rays reach point I instead. Figure 14.6(a): Real Object — rays diverging from a point O above a mirror surface, reflecting off the mirror, with the reflected rays extended backward (dotted) to meet below the mirror at point I labeled 'Virtual Image'. Figure 14.6(b): Real Image — rays converging toward a point I below a mirror surface (shown as dotted lines to a virtual object O), reflecting off the mirror surface and actually meeting above it at a point labeled 'Real Image', with O labeled 'Virtual Object' below the mirror.

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN REAL AND VIRTUAL IMAGES — Real Image: (1) Can be obtained on a screen, e.g., image formed in our eye. (2) Formed by actual intersection of reflected or refracted rays. (3) It is inverted. Virtual Image: (1) Cannot be obtained on a screen, e.g., image of a real object formed in a plane mirror. (2) Formed by producing (extending backward) reflected or refracted rays. (3) It is erect.

14.5 MIRROR — A smooth reflector of light whose one side is silvered is called a mirror. A commonly used mirror (looking glass) is made by depositing a thin layer of silver metal on one side of a plane glass sheet; the silver layer is then protected by a coating of red lead oxide (PbO) paint. In all kinds of mirrors, the silver layer acts as the reflecting surface. Figure: Classification tree — 'Mirror' branches into 'Plane' and 'Curved'; 'Curved' branches into 'Spherical' and 'Cylindrical Mirror'; 'Spherical' branches into 'Concave' and 'Convex'.

LAWS OF REFLECTION OF LIGHT (detailed) — (1) The angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence, i.e., r = i. (2) The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal all lie at the same point of incidence, in the same plane. Figure: Diagram of a concave mirror — object AB (an arrow, A at base on principal axis, B at top) placed in front of a concave mirror; two/three incident rays drawn from point B striking the concave mirror surface at different points, each reflecting according to i = r, and converging to form an inverted real image A'B' below the principal axis, labeled 'Inverted nature' and 'Real image'. A second figure below shows a plane mirror: rays diverging from a point above, striking a flat horizontal mirror line, and reflecting outward; the reflected rays are extended backward (dashed) to meet at a point below the mirror labeled 'Virtual image'.

SUMMARY FIGURE — Virtual Image (detailed diagram): It is an optical image which cannot be obtained on a screen. It forms at the point of intersection of two or more produced reflected or refracted rays of light. Figure: A point source on the left emits several diverging rays; these rays strike a vertical mirror surface and reflect outward to the right; each reflected ray is extended backward through the mirror line (shown with arrows crossing behind the mirror) to converge at a single point on the right, labeled 'Image formed'. Notes accompanying the figure: In case of a mirror, the virtual image forms behind it. In case of a lens, the virtual image forms in front of it, i.e., on the same side as the object. This is contrasted with Real object vs Virtual object as a labeled comparison at the bottom of the page.

14.4 OPTICAL IMAGE (textbook) — A representation of a physical object formed by an optical system is called an optical image, or simply image. It is formed when reflected rays or refracted rays meet or appear to meet. There are two types of image: (i) Real image — An image which can be obtained on a screen is called a real image. It is formed when the light rays after reflection or refraction actually intersect. The real image is inverted with respect to the object. Example: an image formed in our eyes. (ii) Virtual image — An image which cannot be obtained on a screen is called a virtual image. It is formed when the light rays after reflection (or refraction) do not actually intersect but intersect when produced backward. The light rays seem coming from an image. The virtual image is erect or upright with respect to the object.

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN REAL AND VIRTUAL IMAGES (table) — Real Image: (1) The image that can be obtained on a screen is called real image, e.g., the image formed in our eye is real image. (2) It is formed by the actual intersecting of reflected or refracted rays. (3) It is inverted. Virtual Image: (1) The image that can't be obtained on a screen is called virtual image, e.g., the image formed in plane mirror is virtual. (2) It is formed by producing in backward direction of reflected or refracted rays. (3) It is erect. Figure 14.6(a): Virtual Image for real object — Real Object O in front of a vertical mirror line; several rays from O strike the mirror and reflect outward; the reflected rays are extended backward (dotted) behind the mirror to converge at point I, labeled 'Virtual Image'. Figure 14.6(b): Real Image for virtual object — Virtual Object O behind a vertical mirror line (shown with dotted converging lines toward O); rays converging toward O are intercepted by the mirror and actually reflected to meet in front at point I, labeled 'Real Image'.

REAL AND VIRTUAL OBJECT (textbook) — An object that emits light is called a real object. The real object may be either luminous (e.g., sun, glowing bulb etc.) or non-luminous (e.g., book, table etc.). A point where the converging rays appear to meet is called a virtual object. For example, image of a real object in a plane mirror is virtual image but it is virtual object for our eye. For real object O, the virtual image is I as in Fig. 14.6(a). In absence of the mirror, the rays converge to point O, but due to the presence of the mirror the rays reach the point I rather than O. So, O is the virtual object whose real image I is formed as in Fig. 14.6(b).

14.5 MIRROR (textbook) — A smooth reflector of light whose one side is silvered is called a mirror. Commonly used mirror (looking glass) is made by depositing a thin layer of silver metal on one side of a plane glass sheet. The silver metal layer is then protected by a coating of red lead oxide (PbO) paint. In all kinds of mirrors, silver layer acts as the reflecting surface. Figure: Classification tree — 'Mirror' branches into 'Plane' and 'Curved'; 'Curved' branches into 'Spherical' and 'Cylindrical Mirror'; 'Spherical' branches further into 'Concave' and 'Convex'.

REFLECTION OF LIGHT AT A PLANE SURFACE (textbook, intro) — Let us see how light is reflected from a plane surface (i.e., plane mirror) and then an image is formed. Properties of image of a real object formed by a plane mirror: (i) It is virtual. (ii) It is of the same size as the object. (iii) It is erect. (iv) Object distance and image distance are equal. (v) It is laterally inverted. Point object and extended object: An object having no physical extent is called a point object. An object having length, width and height as shown in figure 14.7(a) and an object having length, width and height as shown in figure 14.7(b) is called an extended object. Figure 14.7(a): Image for point object — Real Object O in front of a mirror; several rays from O strike the mirror; reflected rays extended backward converge at virtual image point I. Figure 14.7(b): Image for extended object — Extended object AB in front of a mirror; rays from A and B strike the mirror at points such as N and are reflected; the reflected/extended rays converge to form virtual image, with points C, P labeled on the mirror line.

14.6 REFLECTION OF LIGHT AT A CURVED MIRROR (textbook) — A mirror whose reflecting surface is curved is called a curved mirror, and the curved surface may be concave, convex or cylindrical mirror, but we concentrate our study only on concave and convex mirrors. Spherical mirror: If the reflecting surface of a mirror is curved as a portion of a hollow spherical glass, then the mirror is called a spherical mirror. There are two types of spherical mirrors: (i) Convex mirror: A spherical mirror in which the silvering is done on the inner side and reflection takes place from the outer side is called convex mirror (Fig 14.8). Obviously, the reflection takes place from the bulging side. (ii) Concave mirror: A spherical mirror in which the silvering is done on the outer side and reflection takes place from the inner side is called concave mirror. Obviously, the reflection takes place from the hollow side i.e., from the inner side of this mirror. Concave mirror is also called converging mirror because it converges the light rays in different directions (Fig 14.9). Figure 14.8: Reflection from convex mirror — several parallel horizontal rays approaching a curved mirror surface (curved toward the viewer/bulging outward) and reflecting divergently outward. Figure 14.9: Reflection from concave mirror — several parallel horizontal rays approaching a curved mirror surface (curved away, hollow side facing rays) and reflecting to converge toward a point.
STOP TO THINK 14.1 (textbook box) — If angle of incidence is 0°, then what will be the glancing angle and angle of deviation?

14.7 TERMINOLOGY FOR SPHERICAL MIRRORS (textbook) — Centre of Curvature: The centre of the sphere of which the spherical mirror is a part is called the centre of curvature of the mirror. It is denoted by C. The normal at any point of the mirror passes through this centre. For a concave mirror it is in front of the mirror; for a convex mirror it is behind the mirror. Radius of curvature: The radius of the sphere of which the mirror is a part is called radius of curvature. It is denoted by R. Figure 14.10(a): Concave mirror — a curved mirror arc with centre of curvature C marked at a point on the left connected to point B on the mirror surface by radius R, with pole P marked at the vertex of the arc. Figure 14.10(b): Convex mirror — a curved mirror arc bulging toward the left with centre of curvature C marked behind the mirror on the right, connected to point B on the mirror surface by radius R, with pole P marked at the vertex.

HANDWRITTEN IMPORTANT TERMS — Pole: The point which lies in the centre of the mirror surface. Principal axis: The straight line passing through the centre of curvature and the pole. Centre of curvature: The centre of sphere of which the spherical mirror is a part is the centre of curvature. Focus: The point where incident rays meet (concave) or appear to meet (convex) after striking a reflecting surface (i.e., mirror). Radius of curvature: The normal from centre of curvature to a point on surface (i.e., distance). Focal point or focus: The point through which light rays pass (in concave mirror) or appear to pass behind the mirror, is called the focus. Aperture: The space through which light rays are reflected effectively is called the aperture. Focal length: The length between the pole and principal focus of mirror is called focal length. Secondary axis: The non-special line joining the centre of curvature and any point of surface.

14.8 RELATION BETWEEN FOCAL LENGTH AND RADIUS OF CURVATURE (textbook) — Aperture: The effective width (breadth) of a spherical mirror from which reflection can take place is called its aperture. It is the breadth of a mirror. In the Fig. 14.11 (a) and (b), the distance AB is the aperture of spherical mirror. Focal length: The distance between the pole and principal focus of the mirror is called focal length. It is denoted by f. Gateway of Knowledge (box): Reflection from spherical surface follows the same laws as for plane surface. The spherical mirror can be assumed to be made of a number of small plane mirrors. The focal length of a mirror is always equal to half of its radius and its value does not depend on a medium in which the mirror is placed and hence if a mirror is placed in water or oil, its focal length still remains the same.

CONCAVE MIRROR (textbook derivation for R = 2f) — Let a ray of light AB parallel and close to the principal axis PC be incident on the mirror. From the definition the ray AB passes through the focus F after reflection as shown in Fig. 14.12. Since the radius CB is the normal at point B of reflection, we can have: ∠ABC = ∠CBF (alternate angles). But ∠CBF = ∠BCF (⋅ AB is parallel to CD). So ∠ABC = ∠BCF. Therefore, ΔBCF is therefore isosceles, hence side BF = FC. Now if the aperture of the mirror is so small that point B is very close to the point P of the mirror surface, we may write BF = PF. ∴ PF = FC = PC/2. So, F = R/2. Figure 14.12: Relation between f and R for concave mirror — a concave mirror arc; a ray drawn parallel to the principal axis labeled A striking the mirror at point B, reflecting through F to converge with the axis, with C marked as centre of curvature and P as the pole, angles labeled i and r at point B.

CONVEX MIRROR (textbook derivation for R = 2f) — For a spherical mirror both concave and convex, the focal length is half of its radius of curvature i.e., R = 2f or f = R/2. Where PC = R is the radius of curvature. Let a ray of light AB parallel and close to the principal axis be incident on the mirror at point M. From the geometry of the Fig. 14.13 (a) and (b), the distance AB is real while that of convex mirror is virtual. Figure 14.13: Relation between f and R for convex mirror — a convex mirror arc bulging left; incident ray AB approaching parallel to the principal axis and striking the mirror at point B; normal line ND drawn from centre of curvature C through point B; reflected ray BD diverging away, extended backward (dashed) to meet the axis behind the mirror at focus F; angles i and r marked at point B; pole P and centre of curvature C marked on the principal axis.

HANDWRITTEN DERIVATION — RELATION BETWEEN f AND R USING A CONCAVE MIRROR — To derive relation between focal length and radius of curvature, a ray diagram is plotted. Using a concave mirror: a ray of light parallel to the principal axis strikes the mirror at point M near the pole P, and after reflection passes through the focus F, then continues to the centre of curvature C along the axis. Figure: horizontal principal axis with points C, F, P marked left to right; a ray drawn from far left parallel to the axis, striking the curved concave mirror surface at point M (above the axis), then reflecting down through F back onto the axis; angle i and angle r marked at point M between the incident/reflected rays and the normal (which passes through C). Here, CP = R. ∠FCM = ∠AML (alternate angles, since AM is parallel to the principal axis). ∴ r = i. ∴ ∠FCM = ∠CMF. It shows that ΔCFM is an isosceles triangle, and hence CF = FM. Since the mirror is of very very small aperture, so point of incidence M coincides with the pole P and hence, FM = FP. And from the above, CF = FP = f. ∴ Radius of curvature = CP. ∴ R = CF + FP, or, R = f + f, or, R = 2f, or, f = R/2.

HANDWRITTEN DERIVATION — RELATION BETWEEN R AND f USING A CONVEX MIRROR — To derive a relation between R and f, a ray diagram is plotted using a convex mirror. Figure: horizontal principal axis with points D, A, N, P, C marked; a ray AB drawn parallel to the principal axis approaching from the left and striking the convex mirror surface at point M; the normal (dotted line through N) drawn from the centre of curvature through M; the ray reflects as BC, diverging away from the axis, and is extended backward (dashed) through the mirror to meet the axis at F; angles i and r marked at M on either side of the normal. Here, a light ray AB strikes at point M on the convex mirror and gets reflected as BC. In the figure we see: ∠ABN = ∠FBC (corresponding angles, since AB is parallel to FC produced), and ∠NBC = ∠FMC (vertically opposite angles). But ∠NBC = ∠ABN. So, ΔFCM is an isosceles triangle, hence FM = FC. Since the mirror is of very very small aperture, so FP = FM = F (i.e., the length of FP, since FP = FM, is the focal length f). ∴ R = FP + FC, [since FM = FP = FC], ∴ R = f + f, ∴ R = 2f. ∴ F = R/2. Proved.

14.9 SIGN CONVENTION (SIGN RULE) (textbook) — To specify the position and nature of an object and an image, we need a reference point and sign convention. There are two types of sign convention discussed below. (i) New Cartesian (N.C.) sign convention: All distances are measured from the pole of the mirror taken as origin. All distances measured in the direction of light are taken as positive while distances measured against the direction of incident light are taken as negative. All distances above the principal axis are taken as positive and below the principal axis are taken as negative. Figure 14.14: New Cartesian sign convention — a standard x-y axis diagram with the pole at the origin; horizontal axis labeled X (with – on the left side and + on the right side, in the direction of incident light being taken as positive); vertical axis labeled Y (with + upward and – downward). (ii) Real is Positive (R.P.) sign convention: According to this convention, focal length, radius of curvature in case of concave mirror are taken as positive and that of convex mirror are taken as negative. All distances above and that of coordinate system of sign (graphical convention of sign) are taken as negative. The distances measured in the direction of incident light are taken as positive while the distances against the incident light are taken as negative. All real distances (of real object, real image) are positive while the virtual distances (of virtual object, virtual image) are negative. Both the conventions are being used but N.C. sign convention has found a wide application as it corresponding to the Cartesian System of coordinates. In this book R.P. sign convention is used.

MIRROR FORMULA (handwritten, definition) — It is the relation between the focal length of a mirror, object distance and the image distance. It is mathematically given by: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v (applicable for any mirror; small letters), where f = focal length, u = object distance, v = image distance.

DERIVATION OF MIRROR FORMULA USING A CONCAVE MIRROR (completed derivation, based on ray diagram) — Figure: A concave mirror with pole P and principal axis; object AB stands vertically on the axis with A on the axis and B at the top; centre of curvature C and focus F marked on the axis between A and P; a ray from B drawn parallel to the principal axis strikes the mirror at point M and reflects through F; another ray from B is drawn through the centre of curvature C, striking the mirror at N/P and reflecting back along the same path (since it hits the mirror normally); these two reflected rays intersect below the axis at point B', forming the inverted real image A'B', with A' on the axis directly below the point of intersection.

Let AB = object (perpendicular to the axis at distance u = PA from the pole), A'B' = real image (perpendicular to the axis at distance v = PA' from the pole), and PF = f = focal length, PC = R = radius of curvature.

Step 1: Triangles ABC and A'B'C are similar, because ∠BAC = ∠B'A'C = 90° and ∠ACB = ∠A'CB' (vertically opposite angles at C). 
Therefore, A'B'/AB = A'C/AC ... (i)

Step 2: Triangles MPF and A'B'F are similar, because MP is parallel to AB (both perpendicular to the axis) and ∠MPF = ∠A'B'F... wait, more precisely: ∠PFM = ∠A'FB' (vertically opposite angles at F), and ∠MPF = ∠B'A'F = 90°. 
Therefore, A'B'/MP = A'F/PF ... (ii)

Step 3: Since the aperture of the mirror is very small, point M lies very close to the pole P, so MP ≈ AB (the height of the ray at M equals the height of the object AB, since M and P nearly coincide). 
Substituting MP = AB in (ii): A'B'/AB = A'F/PF ... (iii)

Step 4: From (i) and (iii): A'C/AC = A'F/PF

Step 5: Express each segment in terms of u, v, f, R (using the R.P. sign convention, all distances measured from P): 
PA = u, PA' = v, PF = f, PC = R = 2f. 
AC = PA − PC = u − 2f 
A'C = PC − PA' = 2f − v 
A'F = PA' − PF = v − f 
PF = f

Step 6: Substitute into the equation from Step 4: 
(2f − v)/(u − 2f) = (v − f)/f

Step 7: Cross-multiply: 
f(2f − v) = (u − 2f)(v − f) 
2f² − fv = uv − uf − 2fv + 2f² 
2f² − fv = uv − uf − 2fv + 2f²

Step 8: Cancel 2f² from both sides: 
− fv = uv − uf − 2fv

Step 9: Add 2fv to both sides: 
fv = uv − uf

Step 10: Add uf to both sides: 
fv + uf = uv

Step 11: Divide both sides by uvf: 
(fv)/(uvf) + (uf)/(uvf) = (uv)/(uvf) 
1/u + 1/v = 1/f

Therefore, the mirror formula is: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v (Proved). This relation holds for both concave and convex mirrors, provided the R.P. sign convention is used consistently for u, v, and f.

HANDWRITTEN — LINEAR MAGNIFICATION (m) — It is equal to the ratio of image height (hi) or image size (hi) to the object height (ho) or object size (ho). i.e., m = hi/ho, or, it is also defined as ratio of image distance (v) to the object distance (u). i.e., m = v/u. It is unitless and dimensionless. It may either be positive or negative. Note: Linear magnification produced by a convex mirror is always negative — always virtual, so always negative. A concave mirror forms both types of image: (I) Real image (II) Virtual image. The linear magnification produced by a mirror may either be (I) smaller than 1, or (II) greater than 1.

TEXTBOOK 14.10 RAY DIAGRAM — A diagram showing the relation between an object and its image is called a ray diagram. The size, location and nature of the image formed by a spherical mirror depend on position of the object.

Rules for Tracing an Image of an Object: (i) We consider two rays from the same point of the object. (ii) An incident ray at pole is reflected making the same angle as the angle of incidence with the principal axis. (iii) A ray incident on the mirror parallel to the principal axis after reflection will either pass (concave) or will appear to come (convex) through focus. Conversely, the ray passing through the focus (concave) or appearing to converge at focus (convex) is reflected parallel to the principal axis. (iv) A line joining the centre of curvature to any point on the surface of mirror is always normal to it, therefore a ray passing from the centre of curvature (or appear to be passing from centre of curvature) gets reflected back along its own path (∵ i = 0 so r = 0).

SUMMARY TABLE — IMAGE FORMATION IN A CONCAVE MIRROR — (1) At infinity → image at focus; highly diminished; real and inverted. (2) Beyond centre of curvature → image between centre of curvature and focus; diminished; real and inverted. (3) At the centre of curvature → image at the centre of curvature; same size; real and inverted. (4) Between centre of curvature and focus → image beyond centre of curvature; magnified; real and inverted. (5) At focus → image at infinity; highly magnified; real or virtual (inverted or erect). (6) Between focus and pole → image behind the mirror; magnified; virtual and erect.

SUMMARY TABLE — IMAGE FORMATION IN A CONVEX MIRROR — (1) At infinity → image at focus; highly diminished; virtual and erect. (2) At any other point → image between focus and pole; diminished; virtual and erect.

14.11 SPHERICAL ABERRATION AND PARABOLIC MIRROR (textbook) — The inability of an optical device to converge or to diverge the rays of light from a single point after reflection (in case of a mirror) or refraction (in case of a lens) is called spherical aberration. It occurs in both a mirror as well as in a lens. This is due to large aperture of a mirror or a lens. Due to large aperture the paraxial rays and marginal rays do not meet at a point which causes the spherical aberration. It can be minimized by reducing aperture of the mirror and the lens.

The rays close to the principal axis are called paraxial rays while the rays far from the principle axis and near periphery of the mirror are called marginal rays. In Fig. 14.18(a) the paraxial rays 1 and 2 are focused at a point F, but the marginal rays 3, 4 are not focused at F — they strike their neighbouring points and hence a curve FC is formed. Similarly, the rays below the principal axis form a curve FC″. In this way, the image is formed in the form of a cusp C′FC″ (called caustic curve) with apex at C and this caustic curve is the image of an object. Obviously, due to spherical aberration in a mirror, a fuzzy image is formed.

A mirror whose reflecting surface is that of a paraboloid is called a parabolic mirror. Parabolic mirror is a mirror of small aperture so all rays parallel to the principal axis of parabolic mirror meet at a point and therefore this mirror is free from spherical aberration, as in Fig. 14.18(b). 

Figure 14.18(a): Spherical aberration in a spherical mirror — a curved mirror with several parallel rays labeled 1,2,3,4 above the axis and mirrored below; paraxial rays 1,2 converge at point F while marginal rays 3,4 converge at points forming a curve toward C' (above) and C'' (below), forming a cusp-shaped caustic region. Figure 14.18(b): No aberration in a parabolic mirror — a parabola-shaped mirror with several parallel rays all converging exactly at a single focus point F.

The parabolic mirrors do not show spherical aberration and hence they are used as reflector in search light, in head light of motor vehicles and reflecting astronomical telescope in place of concave reflector. It is also used in the head light of railway engines, cars etc. and in electric torches and search light to get strong beam of light.

Conjugate foci: A pair of points is said to be conjugate foci if an object is placed at one of the two points, its image formed at the other point. The positions of object and image are interchangeable with respect to the conjugate foci which follow from the principle of reversibility of light. For example: Focus and infinity are conjugate points.

14.12 THE MIRROR FORMULA (textbook) — The formula which shows the relationship between object distance, image distance and focal length of the mirror is called mirror formula or mirror equation and it is given by 1/f = 1/v + 1/u.

MIRROR FORMULA FOR CONCAVE MIRROR (full textbook derivation) — Let us consider a concave mirror XY with pole P. An object AB is kept in front of the mirror whose real, diminished and inverted image A'B' is formed in front of the mirror between F and C as shown in Fig. 14.19. A normal MN is drawn from M to principal axis at N. From the figure it is clear that ΔABC and ΔA'B'C are similar so we have: AB/A'B' = BC/B'C ... (14.1). Also, ΔMNF and ΔA'B'F are similar, so we have: MN/A'B' = NF/B'F (∵ AM ∥ PB and N is close to P), or, AB/A'B' = PF/B'F ... (14.2). From eqs. (14.1) and (14.2), we get: BC/B'C = PF/B'F, or, (PB − PC)/(PC − PB') = PF/(PB' − PF) ... (14.3). Applying R.P. sign convention: PB = +u, PC = +R = +2f, PB' = +v, PF = +f. Putting these values in Eq. (14.3): (u − 2f)/(2f − v) = f/(v − f). Cross-multiplying: uv − 2vf − uf + 2f² = 2f² − vf, or, uv − vf − uf = 0. Dividing by uvf: 1/f − 1/u − 1/v = 0. ∴ 1/f = 1/u + 1/v ... (14.4). This is the required mirror formula for concave mirror. The single formula (1/f = 1/v + 1/u) is applicable to both types of image (real and virtual) and for both types of spherical mirror (concave & convex). Figure 14.19: Real image formed by concave mirror — mirror curve XY with pole P; object AB above axis with A on axis; centre of curvature C and focus F between A and P; a ray from B parallel to axis strikes mirror at M and reflects through F; normal MN drawn from M perpendicular to the axis at N; the reflected ray and another ray through C intersect below the axis at B', forming inverted image A'B'.

MIRROR FORMULA FOR CONVEX MIRROR (full textbook derivation) — Let us consider a convex mirror XY with pole P. An object AB is kept in front of the mirror whose virtual, diminished and erect image A'B' is formed behind the mirror between pole and focus as shown in Fig. 14.20. A perpendicular MN is drawn on the principal axis of the mirror. From the figure it is clear that ΔABC and ΔA'B'C are similar, so we have: AB/A'B' = BC/B'C ... (14.5). Also, ΔMNF and ΔB'A'F are similar so we have: MN/A'B' = NF/FB', or, AB/A'B' = PF/FB' (∵ MN = AB and N is very close to P) ... (14.6). From eqs. (14.5) and (14.6), we get: BC/B'C = PF/FB', or, (PB + PC)/(PC − PB') = PF/(PF − PB') ... (14.7). Applying R.P. sign convention: PB = u, PC = −R = −2f, PF = −f, PB' = −v. Putting these values in Eq. (14.7): (u − 2f)/(−2f − (−v)) = −f/(−f − (−v)), or, (u − 2f)/(−2f + v) = −f/(−f + v). Cross-multiplying: −uf + uv + 2f² − 2vf = 2f² − vf, or, −uf + uv = uf. Dividing by uvf: −1/v + 1/f = 1/u. ∴ 1/f = 1/u + 1/v ... (1·3). This is the required mirror formula for convex mirror. Figure 14.20: Virtual image formed by convex mirror — mirror curve XY bulging left with pole P; object AB in front with A on axis; a ray from B parallel to axis strikes mirror at M; normal drawn from M through centre of curvature C; the reflected ray diverges and is extended backward (dashed) to meet the axis behind mirror; another ray from B directed toward C reflects back along itself; the extended (dashed) rays meet behind the mirror at B', forming erect virtual image A'B', with points B, P, N, B', F, C labeled along the axis.

DERIVATION OF MAGNIFICATION FORMULA (m = hi/ho = v/u) (textbook, general) — From the Fig. 14.22 (concave mirror case), in ΔABP: tan i = AB/BP = ho/u. Also, in ΔA'B'P: tan r = A'B'/B'P = hi/v. Since i = r (angle of incidence at pole equals angle of reflection at pole), so tan i = tan r. ∴ ho/u = hi/v, or, hi/ho = v/u. i.e., m = hi/ho = v/u.

Answer: Given, Radius of curvature (R) = −30 cm, Image distance (v) = 20 cm. 
∴ f = R/2 = −30/2 = −15 cm.

GATEWAY OF KNOWLEDGE (textbook box) — (i) The minimum distance between a real object and its image in a concave mirror is zero. (ii) The focal length of a spherical mirror (f = R/2) depends only on the radius of the mirror and is independent of the wavelength of light and nature of a medium, so the focal length of a spherical mirror in air or any other media (e.g. water) is the same for red or blue or any colour of light. (iii) In case of spherical mirror if R → ∞ (i.e. it becomes plane), f = R/2 = ∞, the mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u reduces to 1/v + 1/u = 0, i.e. v = −u, i.e. the image lies at the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front of it. This confirms that the mirror formula is also valid for a plane mirror. (iv) For a real object, convex mirror always gives virtual and diminished image; for virtual object, it gives real image if u < f and virtual image if u > f.

14.13 LINEAR MAGNIFICATION (textbook, formal) — Sometimes the image is bigger than the object and in some cases it is smaller than object or equal, so to have an idea of the size of an image relative to the size of the object, we define the linear magnification as follows: The ratio of size of the image to the size of the object is known as linear magnification or lateral magnification or transverse magnification or simply magnification. Thus, Linear magnification = Size of image / Size of object. The magnification is denoted by m. It is a ratio of same quantities so it has no unit. The object is usually placed vertically above the principal axis of the mirror and the image is formed either vertically above the axis or below the axis. So, by the size of the image and object, we mean height of the image and the height of the object. So the ratio of height of image to the height of the object is called magnification. Magnification = Height of image/Height of object, or, m = hi/ho ... (14.9). The magnification can also be defined as the ratio of the image distance to the object distance. Magnification = Image distance/Object distance, or, m = v/u ... (14.10). From Eqs. (14.9) and (14.10), we get m = hi/ho = v/u ... (14.11). This relation can be derived as follows.

MAGNIFICATION FOR CONCAVE MIRROR — DERIVATION (textbook) — Let AB be an object whose real image A'B' is formed in a concave mirror as shown in Fig. 14.21. Two rays are shown coming from A. One of these passes through the centre of curvature and since this ray is perpendicular to the mirror's surface, it is reflected back on itself. The incident ray strikes the mirror at angle i above the optical axis and is therefore reflected at the same angle i = r below the axis. The intersection of these two rays locates the image point A'. 
From the Fig. 14.22, in ΔABP: tan i = AB/BP = ho/u. Also, in ΔA'B'P: tan r = A'B'/B'P = hi/v. Since i = r so tan i = tan r. or, ho/u = hi/v, or, hi/ho = v/u. i.e., m = hi/ho = v/u. 
Figure 14.21: Real image formation in concave mirror — object AB standing vertically with B at top and A on axis, positioned beyond C; concave mirror curve with pole P; a ray from B directed through C reflects back along the same line; another ray from B strikes the mirror near P at angle i and reflects at angle r below the axis; both rays converge below the axis at B', forming the inverted real image A'B', with C and F marked on the axis between object and mirror.
