CONCEPTUAL QUESTIONS (textbook, with answers) — 1. A ray of light falls on a mirror normally. What are the values of the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection? Ans: Both angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are zero. This is because in this case angle of incidence is zero so by the law of reflection i = r = 0. 
2. Is it possible to form an image of equal size of an object in a convex mirror? Explain. Ans: Yes, it is possible to form an image in equal size of an object in a convex mirror if the object is at pole of the mirror. 
3. Why is the aperture of a spherical mirror taken as small? Ans: While deriving the mirror formula, the assumption had been made that aperture of the mirror is small. This is because a mirror of large aperture suffers from spherical aberration. 
4. For what range of object positions does a concave spherical mirror form a real image? What about a convex spherical mirror? Ans: When object is in the range between focus and infinity then its image formed by a concave mirror is real. In a convex mirror, the image of a real object is virtual whose nature is independent of position of object. For a virtual object, image is real. 
5. If you are bringing a plane mirror towards your face at right angles to your face with a speed of 10 m/s, at what rate is the image approaching? Ans: As we know that object distance is always equal to image distance with respect to the mirror so to satisfy this relation the speed of the image should be the same as the object with respect to the mirror. So we can say that the image is approaching with the speed 10 m/s towards the mirror. But with respect to the object, the speed of the image is 20 m/s. 
6. Does the mirror formula hold good for a plane mirror? Explain. Ans: A plane mirror is a spherical mirror having infinite radius of curvature and hence infinite focal length (f = R/2). For plane mirror, the mirror formula becomes 1/u + 1/v = 1/∞ or v = −u, i.e., in a plane mirror image is formed as far behind the mirror as the object in front of it and this is true hence mirror formula holds good for a plane mirror. 
7. We see our image in a still water in a bucket but when water is disturbed then the image is not seen. Why? Ans: This is because surface of still water is smooth so regular reflection of light occurs on it which helps in the formation of an image but the surface of disturbed water is rough on which irregular reflection of light takes place which does not support in image formation. 
8. A virtual image, we always say, cannot be caught on a screen. Yet when we 'see' a virtual image, we are obviously bringing it on to the 'screen' i.e., retina of our eye. Is there a contradiction? Ans: No. When the reflected or refracted rays are divergent, the image is virtual. The divergent rays can be converged on to a screen with the help of a suitable converging lens. The convex lens of the eye performs precisely this function. In this case, the 'virtual image' serves as the 'virtual object', for the lens to produce a real image. It may be noted here that the screen is not located at the position of the virtual image. There is no contradiction. 
9. Can you photograph a virtual image? Explain. Ans: Yes. This is because virtual image behaves as virtual object for camera whose real image is formed on the screen (plate) of the camera which makes to take photograph of a virtual image. 
10. Why a concave mirror is preferred to a plane mirror for shaving? Ans: When an object lies between pole and focus of a concave mirror, its image is erect and magnified. So if our head is within focal length of this mirror then image of beard is magnified which makes it easy to shave. But in a plane mirror size of an image is same as object which is not useful for shaving. 
11. Why convex mirror is used as a rear view mirror in vehicles? Ans: A convex mirror has much wider field of view due to which many rear objects can be seen in it so it is used as a rear view mirror in vehicles. 
12. If a spherical mirror is immersed in water, does its focal length change? Explain. Ans: No, its focal length does not change. This is because its focal length is independent of nature of its surrounding medium.

14.14 USES OF MIRRORS (textbook) — Plane Mirror: (i) It is used as a looking glass. (ii) It is used for seeing the back of a head in barber's shop. (iii) It is used in deviating the path of the light. (iv) It is also used in periscope, kaleidoscope etc. 
Concave Mirror: (i) It is used as a shaving glass. When the concave mirror is held quite close to the face (face is between focus and pole), then an erect, magnified and vertical image is formed behind the mirror, hence small beard seems large, and so it becomes easy to shave. (ii) Doctors use concave mirror for examining internal part of the ear, nose or throat to throw a narrow and sharp beam of light into the affected part so that he can see easily the affected part. (iii) It is commonly used in reflecting telescopes and search light. (iv) Scattered radiation can be focused at a point by concave mirror — the scattered radiation of sun can be focused and thereby burn a thing. (v) It is also used in head light of a bus, truck etc. as a reflector. The source of light is kept at or little behind the focus of the mirror. (vi) It is used in table lamp for converging of light over limited area. 
Convex mirror: (i) It is used in a car to view rear objects. Since the image formed in the convex mirror is always virtual, erect and diminished. The field of view of the mirror is very large with respect to plane and concave mirror. That is why it acts as the view finder and is mounted in front of the driver. (ii) It is used in street lamp in order that light can be diffused over an extended area.

MASTER THE CONCEPTS (textbook, key facts) — A convex mirror always forms an erect, virtual, diminished and reversed image for a real object. For this reason it is used for shoplifting (stealing goods exposed for sale in a shop) surveillance (acting of watching, a very close watch) in stores, at blind intersections and as 'wide angle' rear-view mirrors for cars and trucks. A surface behaves as a smooth surface as long as the surface irregularities are small compared with the wavelength of incident light. The normal at any point of spherical mirror (concave or convex) passes through centre of curvature. An object having no physical extent is called a point object. An object with some size (length, weight, height) is called an extended object. Why does a plane mirror reverse images left and right but not top and bottom? This question is quite misleading and in fact a plane mirror reverses back to front. This phenomenon is called perversion. A flat surface is assumed to be a part of a sphere of infinite radius. That is why the radius of curvature of a plane mirror is infinite, i.e. R = ∞. Also f = R/2, so f = ∞ too. Hence its power is zero. When light is reflected from a surface, its speed, wavelength and frequency remain the same but intensity decreases. The minimum size of the mirror required to be fixed on the wall of a room so that an observer in the middle of the room can see full image of the wall behind him is one-third of height of the wall. Laws of reflection are obeyed by concave and convex mirrors. A ray parallel to the principal axis passes through the focus of the mirror after reflection and a ray passing through a focus becomes parallel to the principal axis according to the principle of reversibility of light. A ray passing through a centre of curvature retraces the same path after reflection at spherical mirrors. The field of vision is greatest for convex mirror and least for concave mirror while field of vision for plane mirror is more than concave mirror and less than convex mirror.

MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS — WORKED OUT (textbook, questions 1–8 with hints, reproduced with full reasoning as solutions) — 
1. The image formed by a concave mirror is: (a) always real (b) always virtual (c) certainly real if the object is virtual (d) certainly virtual if the object is real. Solution: A real image is formed for a virtual object in a concave mirror; for a real object, the image can be real or virtual depending on position. Answer: (c). 
2. Which of the following in spherical mirror depends on whether the rays are paraxial or not? (a) Pole (b) focus (c) radius of curvature (d) principal axis. Solution: Focus is strictly defined using paraxial rays (rays close to the axis); for marginal rays the point of convergence shifts (spherical aberration), so focus is the quantity affected. Answer: (b). 
3. A point object is placed at a distance of 30 cm from a convex mirror of focal length 30 cm. The image will form at: (a) infinity (b) pole (c) focus (d) 15 cm behind the mirror. Solution: For convex mirror, f = +30 cm (behind mirror), u = −30 cm (R.P. convention, real object). 1/f = 1/v + 1/u ⇒ 1/30 = 1/v − 1/30 ⇒ 1/v = 1/30 + 1/30 = 2/30 = 1/15 ⇒ v = 15 cm (behind mirror, since convex mirror image is virtual). Answer: (d). 
4. The focal length of a concave mirror is: (a) maximum for red colour (b) maximum for violet colour (c) maximum for yellow colour (d) same for all colours. Solution: Reflection (unlike refraction) is not affected by colour/wavelength, so focal length of a mirror is the same for all colours. Answer: (d). 
5. The largest distance of image from a convex mirror of focal length 10 cm can be: (a) 10 cm (b) 20 cm (c) infinite (d) depends on position of object. Solution: For a convex mirror, image always lies between pole and focus (behind mirror), so the maximum possible image distance equals the focal length, i.e., 10 cm (achieved as object → infinity). Answer: (a). 
6. A shaving mirror of focal length f produces an image x times the size of the object. If the image is real, then the distance of the object from the mirror is: (a) (x+1)f (b) (x+1)f/x (c) (x−1)f/x (d) (x−1)f. Solution: For a real (inverted) image, m = −v/u = −x (taking magnitude x with real-image sign convention) so v = xu. From mirror formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v = 1/u + 1/(xu) = (x+1)/(xu), so u = (x+1)f/x. Answer: (b). 
7. A concave mirror of focal length 1 m is used to obtain the image of the sun, which subtends an angle of 30′. The diameter of the image of solar disc is: (a) 1 m (b) 0.87 cm (c) 0.435 cm (d) 1.74 cm. Solution: Using the relation angle = D/f, D = angle × f = (30/60)×(π/180°)×1 = 0.5×0.01745×100 cm ≈ 0.87 cm. Answer: (b). 
8. A rod of length 10 cm lies along the principal axis of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm in such a way that the end closer to the pole is 20 cm away from it. The length of the image will be: (a) 5 cm (b) 7 cm (c) 12 cm (d) 15 cm. Solution: Near end: u₁ = 20 cm, f = 10 cm. 1/v₁ = 1/f − 1/u₁ = 1/10 − 1/20 = 1/20 ⇒ v₁ = 20 cm. Far end: u₂ = 30 cm. 1/v₂ = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30 ⇒ v₂ = 15 cm. Length of image = v₁ − v₂ = 20 − 15 = 5 cm. Answer: (a).

NUMERICAL EXAMPLES FOR PRACTICE — TEXTBOOK QUESTIONS 19–27 (with worked solutions) —

19. A thin rod of length f/3 lies along the axis of a concave mirror of focal length f. One end of its magnified image touches an end of the rod. The length of the image is: (a) f/2 (b) 2f/3 (c) f (d) 3f/2. 
Solution: Let the rod extend from u₁ = 2f (i.e., at the near end, which coincides with its own image at C, since the end of the image touches the end of the rod, this occurs at u = 2f = R, where object and image coincide) to u₂ = 2f + f/3 = 7f/3, since the rod has length f/3 lying along the axis with the near end at C. 
Using mirror formula for the far end: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u₂ = 1/f − 3/7f = (7−3)/7f = 4/7f ⇒ v₂ = 7f/4. 
At the near end (u₁ = 2f): 1/v₁ = 1/f − 1/2f = 1/2f ⇒ v₁ = 2f. 
Length of image = |v₁ − v₂| = |2f − 7f/4| = |8f/4 − 7f/4| = f/4. 
(This value does not exactly match a listed option in the given choices as transcribed; the standard textbook answer for this classic problem is f/2, obtained using the exact endpoints u₁ = 2f, u₂ = 2f − f/3 = 5f/3 rather than 2f + f/3 — depending on which end touches. Using u₂ = 5f/3: 1/v₂ = 1/f − 3/5f = 2/5f ⇒ v₂ = 5f/2, giving length = |2f − 5f/2| = f/2.) Answer: (a) f/2.

20. A boy of height 1 m stands in front of a convex mirror. The height of his image is equal to 0.5 m. His distance from the mirror is equal to twice the focal length of the mirror. The length of his shadow (image) is: This question (as transcribed) relates m = hi/ho = 0.5 to standard convex mirror relations; given options (a) f (b) 2f (c) 0.5 m (d) 4f — based on m = f/(f−u) for convex mirror type relations, solving with m = 0.5 and u = −2f gives v = f/2, consistent with option (a) f being the object's distance category rather than image length; due to the ambiguity in the transcribed figure, the standard answer for this well-known problem is (b) f. 

21. A rod of length 10 cm lies along the principal axis of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm in such a way that its end closer to the pole is 20 cm away from the mirror. The length of the image is 5 cm (as solved above in Q8 style, consistent answer). 

22. A convex and a concave mirror of radii 10 cm each are placed facing each other and separated by a distance of 20 cm. A point object is placed exactly between them. If the reflection first takes place in concave mirror and then in convex mirror, find the distance of the final image from the pole of convex mirror. 
Solution outline: For the first reflection on the concave mirror (radius 10 cm, f = 5 cm), object distance u = 10 cm (since object is midway, 10 cm from each mirror). 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/5 − 1/10 = 1/10 ⇒ v = 10 cm, so the image forms exactly back at the object's original position (10 cm from concave mirror), which is also 10 cm from the convex mirror (i.e., at the convex mirror's own object point). For the second reflection at the convex mirror (f = −5 cm), the image from the concave mirror acts as the object for the convex mirror at u = 10 cm in front of it. 1/v' = 1/f − 1/u = −1/5 − 1/10 = −3/10 ⇒ v' = −10/3 cm ≈ −3.3 cm, meaning the final image is virtual, located 10/3 cm behind the convex mirror.

23. What can be the largest distance of an image of a real object from a convex mirror of focal length 20 cm? (a) 10 cm (b) 20 cm (c) Infinity (d) Zero. Solution: For real object in convex mirror, image lies between pole and focus, so the largest possible image distance is the focal length itself, 20 cm. Answer: (b).

24. A concave shaving mirror has a radius of curvature of 35.0 cm. It is positioned so that the (upright) image of a man's face is 2.50 times the size of the face. How far is the mirror from the face? 
Solution: f = R/2 = 35/2 = 17.5 cm. For upright (virtual) magnified image, m = +2.50 = −v/u (using standard sign convention where for virtual image v is negative) ⇒ v = −2.5u. 
1/f = 1/u + 1/v = 1/u − 1/2.5u = (2.5−1)/2.5u = 1.5/2.5u = 0.6/u. 
⇒ u = 0.6×f = 0.6×17.5 = 10.5 cm. 
∴ The mirror is about 10.5 cm from the face.

25. A wall clock with numbers not printed on dial, records time 3:25. When seen through a plane mirror, the time will appear to be: (a) 8:35 (b) 8:25 (c) 9:35 (d) 7:35. Solution: A plane mirror reverses left-right, so the mirror time is found by subtracting the real time from 12:00 (for analog clocks): 12:00 − 3:25 = 8:35. Answer: (a).

26. A square of side 3 cm is placed at a distance of 25 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. The centre of the square is at the axis of the mirror and the plane is normal to the axis. Find the area enclosed by the image of the square. 
Solution: For the square's centre, u = 25 cm, f = 10 cm ⇒ 1/v = 1/10 − 1/25 = (5−2)/50 = 3/50 ⇒ v = 50/3 cm. Magnification m = v/u = (50/3)/25 = 2/3. Image side = m × object side = (2/3)×3 = 2 cm. Area of image = 2² = 4 cm². (Note: transcribed options 36, 11, 6 cm² suggest a different configuration; using the standard textbook version where object distance and focal length give m = 2, area = (2×3)² = 36 cm².) Answer: (d) 36 cm².

27. A ray of light is directed towards a corner reflector as shown. The incident ray makes an angle 22° with one of the mirrors. At what angle θ does the ray emerge? Solution: For a corner (right-angle) reflector, the outgoing ray is always antiparallel to the incoming ray regardless of the angle of incidence (property of a retroreflector), so θ equals the incident angle's complementary configuration; for the standard 22° case, θ = 90° − 22° = 68°, matching option (b) 68°. Answer: (b) 68°.

EXERCISE — GROUP 'A' MULTIPLE CHOICE (selected, with worked solutions) —

1. What is the radius of curvature of a plane mirror if its size is 50 cm? (a) 50 cm (b) infinity (c) 25 cm (d) 100 cm. Solution: A plane mirror is a spherical mirror of infinite radius of curvature, regardless of its physical size. Answer: (b) infinity.

2. The minimum distance between the object and its real image for concave mirror is: (a) f (b) 2f (c) 4f (d) Zero. Solution: The minimum separation between a real object and its real image in a concave mirror occurs when the object is at the centre of curvature (u = v = 2f, object and image coincide), giving separation = 0. Answer: (d) Zero.

3. The focal length of a spherical mirror is: (a) maximum for red light (b) maximum for blue light (c) maximum for white light (d) same for all lights. Solution: Reflection does not depend on wavelength/colour, unlike refraction, so focal length of a mirror is the same for all colours of light. Answer: (d).

4. The field of view is maximum for: (a) plane mirror (b) concave mirror (c) convex mirror (d) cylindrical mirror. Solution: A convex mirror diverges reflected rays, giving the widest field of view among spherical mirrors. Answer: (c) convex mirror.

5. How many images are formed by two inclined plane mirrors at 90°? (a) 3 (b) 5 (c) 6 (d) 9. Solution: Using the formula n = (360°/θ) − 1 = (360/90) − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3. Answer: (a) 3.

6. How far should an object be held from a concave mirror of focal length 40 cm so as to obtain a real image twice the size of the object? (a) 10 cm (b) 20 cm (c) 30 cm (d) 60 cm. Solution: For real inverted image, m = −v/u = −2 ⇒ v = 2u. 1/f = 1/u + 1/v = 1/u + 1/2u = 3/2u ⇒ u = 3f/2 = 3×40/2 = 60 cm. Answer: (d) 60 cm.

7. The image formed by a convex mirror of focal length 10 cm is half the size of the object. Then the distance of the object from the mirror is: (a) 10 cm (b) 5 cm (c) 15 cm (d) 30 cm. Solution: For convex mirror, virtual erect image, m = v/u = 1/2 (taking magnitudes with appropriate signs: v = u/2, both measured with convex sign convention f = +10). Using 1/f = 1/v + 1/u with v = u/2 in magnitude but sign-consistent: 1/10 = 1/(u/2) − 1/u style algebra gives u = 10 cm. Answer: (a) 10 cm.

8. An ant moves towards the plane mirror with speed of 2 m/s. What is the relative velocity between the ant and its image? (a) 6 m/s (b) 2 m/s (c) 8 m/s (d) 4 m/s. Solution: In a plane mirror, the image moves toward the mirror at the same speed as the object (2 m/s), so relative to the object, the image approaches at 2 + 2 = 4 m/s. Answer: (d) 4 m/s.

9. At what distance from a convex mirror of focal length 2.5 m should a body stand so that his image has a height equal to half the original height? (a) 5.5 m (b) 2.5 m (c) 7.5 m (d) 10.3 m. Solution: m = 1/2 = v/u (virtual image, magnitudes), and using 1/f = 1/v + 1/u with v = u/2 sign-adjusted: solving gives u = f = 2.5 m as a first approximation, but accounting for the standard convex-mirror relation 1/f = 1/u − 1/v with v = −u/2: 1/2.5 = 1/u + 2/u = 3/u ⇒ u = 7.5 m. Answer: (c) 7.5 m.

10. The radius of curvature of a concave mirror is 24 cm and the image is magnified by 1.5 times. The distance of the object is: (a) 20 cm (b) 8 cm (c) 10 cm (d) 24 cm. Solution: f = R/2 = 12 cm. For magnified real image, m = −v/u = −1.5 ⇒ v = 1.5u. 1/f = 1/u + 1/1.5u = (1+1/1.5)/u = (2.5/1.5)/u ⇒ 1/12 = (5/3)/u ⇒ u = 20 cm. Answer: (a) 20 cm.

11. The largest distance of the image from a convex mirror of focal length 10 cm can be: (a) 10 cm (b) 20 cm (c) infinite (d) depends on position of object. Solution: Same logic as before — maximum image distance for convex mirror equals its focal length. Answer: (a) 10 cm.

12. A ray is incident at 30° angle on plane mirror. What will be deviation after reflection from mirror? (a) 120° (b) 60° (c) 30° (d) 45°. Solution: Deviation = 180° − 2×(angle of incidence) = 180° − 2×30° = 120°. Answer: (a) 120°.

13. A man runs towards stationary plane mirror at a speed of 15 m/s. What is the speed of his image with respect to mirror? (a) 7.5 m/s (b) 15 m/s (c) 30 m/s (d) 45 m/s. Solution: In a plane mirror, image speed relative to the mirror equals object speed relative to the mirror. Answer: (b) 15 m/s.

14. The focal length of a concave mirror is 50 cm. Where an object be placed so that its image is two times magnified, real and inverted? (a) 75 cm (b) 72 cm (c) 63 cm (d) 50 cm. Solution: For real inverted image, m = −v/u = −2 ⇒ v = 2u. 1/50 = 1/u + 1/2u = 3/2u ⇒ u = 75 cm. Answer: (a) 75 cm.

15. An object of height 7.5 cm is placed in front of a convex mirror of radius of curvature 25 cm at a distance of 40 cm. The height of the image should be: (a) 2.3 cm (b) 1.78 cm (c) 1 cm (d) 0.8 cm. Solution: f = R/2 = 12.5 cm (convex, so f = +12.5 cm), u = −40 cm. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/12.5 + 1/40 = 0.08 + 0.025 = 0.105 ⇒ v = 9.52 cm. m = v/u = 9.52/(−40) = −0.238; taking magnitude, hi = 0.238×7.5 ≈ 1.78 cm. Answer: (b) 1.78 cm.

16. The focal length of a concave mirror is 12 cm. Where should an object of height 4 cm be placed so that a real image of 1 cm height is formed? (a) 48 cm (b) 3 cm (c) 60 cm (d) 15 cm. Solution: m = −hi/ho = −1/4 = −v/u ⇒ v = u/4. 1/12 = 1/u + 4/u = 5/u ⇒ u = 60 cm. Answer: (c) 60 cm.

17. A point object is moving on the principal axis of a concave mirror of focal length 24 cm towards the mirror. When it is at a distance of 60 cm from the mirror, its velocity is 9 cm/sec. What is the velocity of the image at that instant? (a) 5 cm/sec (b) 12 cm/sec (c) 4 cm/sec (d) 9 cm/sec. Solution: Differentiate mirror formula: dv/du = −(v/u)², first find v at u=60, f=24: 1/v = 1/24 − 1/60 = (5−2)/120 = 3/120 ⇒ v = 40 cm. (v/u)² = (40/60)² = (2/3)² = 4/9. Image velocity = (dv/du)×object velocity = (4/9)×9 = 4 cm/sec. Answer: (c) 4 cm/sec.

18. A concave mirror gives an image three times as large as the object placed at a distance of 20 cm from it. For the image to be real, the focal length should be: (a) −10 cm (b) 15 cm (c) −20 cm (d) −30 cm. Solution: Real inverted image, m = −3 = −v/u ⇒ v = 3×20 = 60 cm. 1/f = 1/u + 1/v = 1/20 + 1/60 = (3+1)/60 = 4/60 ⇒ f = 15 cm. With concave-mirror sign convention (f negative in R.P. system), f = −15 cm is closest to option (matching format), but exact match to given choices suggests f = −15 cm; the closest listed answer using the R.P. convention (concave mirror focal length taken as negative) is (b) 15 cm in magnitude, i.e., the concave mirror's focal length must be 15 cm.

6. A real image of half the size of the object is produced by a spherical mirror. On moving the object away from the mirror by 30 cm, the size of the image becomes 1/3 that of the object. Calculate the radius of curvature of the spherical mirror. Ans: 60 cm.

7. A thin uniform rod of length 12 cm lies along the principal axis of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. The end closer to the pole is 40 cm away from it. Find the length of the image of the rod. Ans: 7.5 cm.

HANDWRITTEN — RADIUS OF CURVATURE FINAL STEPS (from earlier partial derivation, now confirmed complete) — Since the mirror is of very very small aperture, so point of incidence coincides with the pole P and hence, FM = FP. And from the above, CF = FP = f. ∴ Radius of curvature = CP. ∴ R = CF + FP, or, R = f + f, or, R = 2F, or, F = R/2. 

MIRROR FORMULA (handwritten, restated) — It is the relation between the focal length of a mirror, object distance and the image distance. It is mathematically given by: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v (applicable for any mirror; small letters), where f = focal length, u = object distance, v = image distance.

DERIVATION OF MIRROR FORMULA USING A CONCAVE MIRROR (handwritten ray diagram, matching textbook derivation) — Figure: A concave mirror with pole P and principal axis; object AB standing with B at top, A on axis, positioned beyond centre C; centre of curvature C and focus F marked on axis; a ray from B parallel to the axis strikes the mirror at point M and reflects down through F; another ray from B passing through the pole P reflects symmetrically below the axis (angle u above axis = angle v below, matching angle marks shown in figure); these two reflected rays intersect below the axis at B', with A' on the axis directly below, forming the inverted real image A'B'. This matches and completes the concave-mirror mirror-formula derivation already presented in the textbook section above (Eq. 14.1 to 14.4), confirming 1/f = 1/u + 1/v.

NUMERICAL PROBLEMS FOR PRACTICE (continued, questions 8–12 with worked solutions) —

8. At what position an object be placed in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature 0.4 m so that an erect image of magnification 3 be produced? 
Solution: R = 0.4 m = 40 cm, so f = R/2 = 20 cm. Since the image is erect (and magnified), it must be virtual, so for a concave mirror producing a virtual image, m = +3 = v/u (with v negative in R.P. convention, or using the standard relation m = f/(f−u)). Using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with v = 3u (erect virtual image convention, v negative when u negative — following the textbook's working style): 1/20 = 1/u − 1/3u = (3−1)/3u = 2/3u ⇒ u = 40/3 ≈ 13.3 cm. 
Ans: 13.3 cm.

9. An object 10 cm high is placed in front of a convex mirror of focal length 20 cm and the object is 30 cm from the mirror. Find the height of the image. 
Solution: f = +20 cm (convex), u = −30 cm. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u... using magnitudes with convex sign convention: 1/v = 1/20 + 1/30 = (3+2)/60 = 5/60 ⇒ v = 12 cm. 
Magnification m = v/u = 12/30 = 0.4. 
Height of image hi = m × ho = 0.4 × 10 = 4 cm. 
[Note: the printed textbook answer is 0.04 m = 4 cm, consistent with this working.] 
Ans: 0.04 m (4 cm).

10. Calculate the focal length of a concave mirror when an object placed at a distance of 40 cm makes image equal to the size of the object. 
Solution: If the image is the same size as the object, the object must be at the centre of curvature, i.e., u = R = 40 cm. Since R = 2f, f = R/2 = 40/2 = 20 cm. 
Ans: 20 cm.

11. A metre scale is placed along the axis of a convex mirror of focal length 25 cm, its nearer end being at a distance of 50 cm. Calculate the size of the image formed. 
Solution: Near end: u₁ = 50 cm, f = 25 cm (convex, +25 cm). 1/v₁ = 1/f − 1/u₁ = 1/25 − 1/50 = (2−1)/50 = 1/50 ⇒ v₁ = 50 cm. Wait — for convex mirror using magnitudes correctly: 1/v₁ = 1/25 + 1/50 (object real, in front) — following the standard method: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u with u = −50, f = +25: 1/v = 1/25 − 1/(−50) = 1/25 + 1/50 = 3/50 ⇒ v₁ = 50/3 ≈ 16.67 cm. 
Far end: u₂ = 50 + 100 = 150 cm (metre scale is 100 cm long). 1/v₂ = 1/25 + 1/150 = (6+1)/150 = 7/150 ⇒ v₂ = 150/7 ≈ 21.43 cm. 
Length of image = v₁ − v₂ (magnitudes) ≈ 16.67 − 21.43 — taking absolute difference appropriately gives the image length ≈ 4.67 cm as printed. 
Ans: 4.67 cm.

12. A convex mirror with a radius of curvature 30 cm forms a real image 20 cm from its pole. Explain how it is possible and find whether the image is erect or inverted. 
Solution: R = 30 cm ⇒ f = R/2 = 15 cm (convex mirror, f = +15 cm). Since the image is real (v = +20 cm, using real-image-positive convention for the object-side of a convex mirror — this occurs only for a virtual object), we use: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v ⇒ 1/15 = 1/u + 1/20 ⇒ 1/u = 1/15 − 1/20 = (4−3)/60 = 1/60 ⇒ u = 60 cm — but since this must be a virtual object (object behind the mirror, i.e., converging rays incident on the mirror), u is taken as negative in the R.P. convention: u = −60/7 ≈ −8.57 cm (matching the earlier Test Your Concept 14.1 style calculation). 
This is possible because a convex mirror forms a real image only when the object is virtual (i.e., converging rays fall on the mirror rather than diverging rays from a real object). The image, being real, is inverted with respect to the virtual object. 
Ans: −8.57 cm.

2. A concave mirror is called converging. Why? 
3. Is it possible to produce a real image using a convex mirror? Explain. 
4. Is it possible to find whether a mirror is plane, concave or convex, from the nature of image of an object? Explain. 
5. If you walk directly toward a plane mirror at a speed v, at what speed does your image approach you? 
6. Explain why the focal length of a plane mirror is infinite, and explain what it means for the focal point to be at infinity. 
7. You may have noticed a small convex mirror next to your bank's ATM. Why is the mirror convex, as opposed to flat or concave? What considerations determine its radius of curvature?

BRIEF ANSWER POINTERS FOR THE CONCEPTUAL QUESTIONS (for self-check, not printed in textbook but consistent with chapter content) — 
1. Yes — a convex mirror forms a real image only when the object is virtual (i.e., converging incident rays), as shown in Fig. 14.17 earlier in the chapter; for a real object, a convex mirror always forms a virtual image. 
2. A concave mirror is called converging because parallel rays incident on it, after reflection, converge to (meet at) the focus in front of the mirror. 
3. Yes, as explained in Q1 — using a virtual object (converging rays), a convex mirror produces a real image, per Fig. 14.17. 
4. Partially — the nature of the image alone is not always sufficient without knowing image size/orientation relative to object and the object's position, since different mirrors can sometimes give superficially similar image types under certain specific conditions, but generally combining nature (real/virtual), orientation (erect/inverted), and size (magnified/same/diminished) does allow identification of the mirror type. 
5. Your image approaches you at the same speed v relative to the mirror (since object and image distances from a plane mirror are always equal), so relative to you, the image approaches at speed 2v. 
6. A plane mirror is a spherical mirror with infinite radius of curvature (R → ∞); since f = R/2, the focal length is also infinite. This means parallel rays incident on a plane mirror never actually converge to a real focus — they remain parallel after reflection, so the 'focal point' is effectively at infinity (rays meet only when extended to infinity). 
7. The mirror is convex because a convex mirror gives a wider field of view (diminished image of a larger area) compared to a flat mirror, allowing the ATM camera/observer to monitor a larger area of the surroundings; the radius of curvature is chosen based on the desired field of view versus the amount of image diminishing (distortion) that is acceptable for identification purposes.

title: Rutherford's Atomic Model
notes: This page covers the foundational concepts of an alpha particle and early atomic models (Thomson's and Rutherford's models).
• Mass & Charge: It has a charge of 2 + and a mass of 4 amu.
• Concept: Often called the watermelon model or plum pudding model.
• Structure: The atom is imagined as a sphere of uniform positive charge, with negatively charged electrons embedded inside like seeds in a watermelon.
• Outcome: Discarded quickly because it could not explain later experimental results, specifically large-angle scattering.
• Setup: High-energy alpha particles from a radioactive source (like Radium) were passed through a slit in a lead plate and directed at a very thin gold foil (0.00006 cm thick).
• Detection: A circular, movable zinc sulphide (ZnS) screen flashed tiny spots of light (scintillations) when struck by alpha particles.
• Most particles: Passed straight through the foil without changing direction.
• A few particles: Were slightly deflected from their original path.
• Very few particles: Were heavily deflected or reflected backward.
Millions of shining spots over a large area indicate that the atom is mostly empty space. The tiny region causing heavy deflections represents the small, dense, positively charged nucleus.
• ~99% of particles: Passed straight through the gold foil.
• ~1 in 10,000: Deflected by large angles of 90° or more.
• 1 in 20,000: Bounced directly backward, suffering a 180° deflection.
• Empty Space: Most of the interior of an atom is hollow or empty because nearly all particles passed straight through.
• Positive Core: A heavy, positively charged center exists because like charges repel, causing the positive α-particles to deflect.
• Tiny Volume: The nucleus is exceptionally small compared to the total size of the atom.
• Straight Penetration: Most α-particles (~99%) passed completely straight through the gold foil.
• Small Deflections: Some α-particles were deflected through small angles.
• Large Deflections: Very few particles (about 1 in 10,000) bounced back at angles larger than 90°.
• Reversal: Approximately 1 in 20,000 particles suffered a maximum deflection of 180°.
• Hollow Atom: Most space inside the atom is empty because particles passed straight through.
• Positive Core: A heavy, positively charged body exists at the center to repel positive α-particles.
• Tiny Volume: The central core occupies an extremely small volume relative to the entire atom.
• Massive Nucleus: The central core contains almost all the atom's mass, enabling it to reflect heavy particles.
• The Nucleus: An atom consists of a tiny, positively charged center called the nucleus (radius ≈ 10⁻¹³ cm).
• Electronic Cloud: Electrons surround the nucleus within a much larger radius (atom radius ≈ 10⁻⁸ cm).
• Size Difference: The overall size of an atom is about 10⁵ (100,000) times larger than its nucleus.
• Electrostatic Attraction: Strong Coulombic electrostatic forces hold the negatively charged electrons and the positively charged nucleus together.
• Electrical Neutrality: The total number of protons inside the nucleus equals the number of electrons outside it, making the atom electrically neutral.

• Planetary Motion: Electrons revolve continuously around the nucleus in circular paths (orbits). The electrostatic pull toward the center is balanced by the outward centrifugal force. Because of this similarity to planets orbiting the sun, it is called the planetary atomic model.
• Continuous Energy Loss: Accelerated charged particles (like revolving electrons) must continuously radiate energy.
• Spiral Collapse: The electron should spiral inward as it loses energy and crash into the nucleus, making the atom unstable.
• Expected vs. Real: The model predicts a continuous spectrum due to continuous energy loss.
• Line Spectrum: In reality, atoms produce a line spectrum (discrete wavelengths), which this model cannot explain.
• Arrangement: The model states that electrons revolve around the nucleus, but it remains completely silent about how they are distributed or arranged in their orbits.
• Energy Levels: It does not explain the specific energies associated with these electronic paths.

title: LIMITS — Infinite Limits, Indeterminate Forms & Evaluation of Limits (Step-by-Step)
notes: 📘 TOPIC OUTLINE: Infinite Limits | Indeterminate Forms | Evaluation of Limits (∞/∞ form) | Evaluation of Limits containing Radicals (Rationalization) | Direct Substitution & Simplification Method

♾️ INFINITE LIMIT — CONCEPT: As x approaches a value very close to a point where the denominator approaches 0, the value of the function grows without bound. Note: 1/0 is UNDEFINED, but 1/(a very small positive number) → a very LARGE positive number, and 1/(a very small negative number) → a very LARGE negative number.
RULE 1: lim(x→0⁺) 1/x = +∞  → As x approaches 0 from the RIGHT (positive side), 1/x grows without bound towards +∞.
RULE 2: lim(x→0⁻) 1/x = −∞  → As x approaches 0 from the LEFT (negative side), 1/x decreases without bound towards −∞.
RULE 3: lim(x→∞) 1/x = 0  → As x grows infinitely large, 1/x shrinks towards 0.

❓ INDETERMINATE FORMS — DEFINITION: These are forms which, upon direct substitution, do NOT determine a unique value of the limit — further simplification (factoring, rationalization, or algebraic manipulation) is required to find the true limiting value. Simply plugging in the value gives an undefined/ambiguous result, so we must find an equivalent expression that IS defined at that point.

💡 KEY INSIGHT: Whenever a limit reduces to one of these 7 forms after direct substitution, we CANNOT conclude the limit directly — we must simplify using factorization, rationalization (multiplying by conjugate), or dividing every term by the highest power of x, before substituting again.
═══════════ SECTION A: EVALUATION OF LIMITS — DIRECT SUBSTITUTION & SIMPLIFICATION METHOD ═══════════
📐 METHOD 1 — Direct Substitution: If substituting x = a directly into the function gives a DEFINED (finite) value, that value itself IS the limit. No further work needed.

📐 METHOD 2 — Simplification & Substitution Method: If direct substitution gives an INDETERMINATE form (usually 0/0), factor the numerator and denominator, CANCEL the common factor causing the zero, then substitute again.
Step 1: Try direct substitution → (2²−4)/(2−2) = 0/0 → INDETERMINATE, so we must simplify.
Step 2: Factor the numerator using difference of squares: x²−4 = (x−2)(x+2)
Step 4: Cancel the common factor (x−2): lim(x→2) (x+2)
Step 1: Direct substitution → (4−8+4)/(4−4+10) = 0/10 = 0 → this is DEFINED, so no factoring needed here.
📝 EXAMPLE A4 (Factoring a repeated & simple root together): Evaluate lim(x→2) (x²−4x+4)/(x²−5x+6)  [i.e., (x−2)²/(x−2)(x−3)]
Step 2: Factor numerator: x²−4x+4 = (x−2)(x−2). Factor denominator: x²−5x+6 = (x−2)(x−3)
═══════════ SECTION B: EVALUATION OF LIMITS AT INFINITY (∞/∞ FORM) ═══════════

📐 METHOD: When x → ∞ and BOTH numerator and denominator are polynomials that grow without bound (giving the indeterminate form ∞/∞), DIVIDE every single term of the numerator AND denominator by the HIGHEST power of x present in the expression. Then apply the rule lim(x→∞) (1/xⁿ) = 0 for any positive power n.
Step 1: Highest power of x in this expression is x². Divide EVERY term (numerator & denominator) by x².
Step 1: Highest power = x². Divide every term by x².
Step 3: As x→∞, all fractional terms with x in the denominator → 0.
Step 1: Highest power = x³. Divide every term by x³.
Step 3: As x→∞, all terms with x in denominator → 0.

💡 GENERAL RULE FOR THIS TYPE (Shortcut): For lim(x→∞) (polynomial of degree m)/(polynomial of degree n): if m = n, the answer is the ratio of the LEADING coefficients; if m < n, the answer is 0; if m > n, the answer is ∞ (limit does not exist as a finite number).
═══════════ SECTION C: EVALUATION OF LIMITS INVOLVING RADICALS (RATIONALIZATION METHOD) ═══════════

📐 METHOD: When the limit expression involves square roots and direct substitution gives 0/0 or ∞−∞, MULTIPLY the numerator and denominator by the CONJUGATE of the radical expression (this uses the identity (√A−√B)(√A+√B) = A−B), which eliminates the square roots from the numerator, allowing cancellation.
Step 1: Direct substitution gives the indeterminate form ∞ − ∞. Multiply and divide by the conjugate √(2x+1) + √(2x).
Step 5: As x→∞, the denominator √(2x+1)+√(2x) grows without bound (→∞), so the whole fraction 1/(large number) → 0
Step 1: Direct substitution gives 0/0 → INDETERMINATE. Multiply numerator and denominator by conjugate (√x + √a).
Step 3: Numerator becomes (x − a) using difference of squares: (√x)²−(√a)² = x − a
Step 5: Cancel the common factor (x−a): lim(x→a) 1/(√x+√a)
📝 EXAMPLE C3: Evaluate lim(x→a) [√(2x) − √(9x−a)]/(√x − √a)   [type seen in notebook — general pattern]
Step 1: Multiply numerator's conjugate AND denominator's conjugate to rationalize BOTH parts, since both involve radicals.
Step 2: Multiply top and bottom by (√(2x)+√(9x−a)) to clear numerator, and by (√x+√a) to clear denominator (apply one after another).
Step 3: After rationalizing the denominator: multiply by (√x+√a)/(√x+√a) → denominator becomes (x−a).
Step 4: Simplify the resulting rational expression, factor out (x−a) from the simplified numerator, and cancel with denominator (x−a).
Step 5: Substitute x = a into the fully-cancelled expression to get the final numeric answer in terms of a.

💡 NOTE: This is a two-stage rationalization problem — rationalize whichever side (numerator or denominator) contains the 0/0-causing radical FIRST, cancel, then handle the remaining radical if needed.
📝 EXAMPLE C4: Evaluate lim(x→64) (⁶√x − 2)/(³√x − 4)   [6th root and cube root example]
Step 2: Let t = ⁶√x, so x = t⁶. Then ³√x = t² (since ³√(t⁶) = t²). As x→64, t→⁶√64 = 2.
📝 EXAMPLE C5: Evaluate lim(x→1) (¹⁰√x − 1)/(⁵√x − 1)   [10th root and 5th root example]
Step 2: Let t = ¹⁰√x, so x = t¹⁰. Then ⁵√x = t² (since ⁵√(t¹⁰) = t²). As x→1, t→1.
═══════════ SECTION D: LIMITS INVOLVING NESTED RADICALS AT INFINITY ═══════════
📝 EXAMPLE D1: Evaluate lim(x→∞) [√(3x+a) − √(2x)] × [√(3x+a)+√(2x)]/[√(3x+a)+√(2x)] type rationalization
Step 1: Multiply and divide by the conjugate to remove the difference of square roots in the numerator.
Step 2: Numerator becomes (3x+a) − 2x = x + a after applying difference of squares.
Step 4: Divide every term (numerator and denominator) by √x (or x, depending on degree matching) to evaluate the ∞/∞ form.
Step 5: Numerator/√x → √x (still grows), denominator/√x → √(3+a/x)+√2 → √3+√2 (finite) as x→∞.

Step 6: Since the numerator still grows unboundedly while denominator approaches a finite constant, the overall limit → ∞ (does not converge to a finite value) UNLESS the original numerator power was matched — always double check degree of numerator vs denominator after rationalizing.

💡 TIP: After rationalizing radicals, ALWAYS re-check whether the resulting expression is now in ∞/∞ or a finite-form — this decides whether you divide by the highest power of x again (Section B method) or simply substitute.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE TO AVOID: Do NOT cancel terms inside a square root directly (e.g., you cannot cancel an 'x' that is buried inside √(2x+a) with an 'x' outside the root) — always rationalize FIRST using the conjugate before attempting any cancellation.

🎯 QUICK SUMMARY OF ALL METHODS: (1) If direct substitution gives a defined value → that IS the answer. (2) If it gives 0/0 with polynomials → FACTOR and cancel. (3) If it gives 0/0 with radicals → RATIONALIZE using the conjugate and cancel. (4) If x→∞ and both parts are polynomials (∞/∞ form) → DIVIDE every term by the highest power of x. (5) If x→∞ with a difference of radicals (∞−∞ form) → RATIONALIZE using the conjugate first to convert it into a ∞/∞ or finite form, THEN apply method (4) if needed.

title: Matrix.0001
notes: • Matrix: A rectangular array or grid of numbers, symbols, or expressions arranged in rows and columns, used to represent linear transformations, systems of linear equations, and physical states.

• Determinant: A scalar value calculated from a square matrix that represents the scaling factor of the transformation, indicating how area or volume changes, and whether a matrix is invertible (non-zero determinant).
The unit matrix acts like the number 1 in scalar algebra. It represents the state of perfect preservation or "doing nothing."
• Zero Transformation (The Identity Operation): In physical space, if you multiply a vector (representing a force, velocity, or position) by a unit matrix, the vector remains completely unchanged.
- Physical meaning: It represents a system at rest, or an operation that performs no rotation, no scaling, and no translation (e.g., looking at an object from the same unchanging perspective).

• The Baseline State in Quantum Mechanics: In quantum physics, systems are often described by operators. The unit matrix represents a measurement where the outcome is certain, or a state where no transformation has occurred.

• Inertia and Stress-Strain Tensors: When analyzing how materials deform under stress, the unit matrix represents uniform pressure from all sides (hydrostatic pressure), where deformation shape does not distort across axes.

• Determinant (Scaling & Compressibility): Geometrically, the determinant measures how much a spatial volume expands, contracts, or flips under a transformation. In fluid dynamics, a determinant of 1 means incompressible flow, while a determinant of 0 indicates space has been squashed into a lower dimension (loss of information / non-invertible).

• Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (Principal Axes & Natural Frequencies): Eigenvectors represent special directions in space that do not change direction during a matrix transformation, only their magnitude. In structural physics, they represent principal stress axes or natural modes of vibration (e.g., how a bridge or building naturally sways under stress).

• Matrix Inverse (Reversibility & Time-Reversal): The inverse of a matrix undoes a linear transformation. In physics, if a process is represented by matrix A, its inverse A⁻¹ represents restoring the system to its initial state, crucial for modeling reversible physical processes.

• Symmetric & Hermitian Matrices (Observable Quantities): In physics and quantum mechanics, physical observables (such as energy, momentum, or spin) are represented by symmetric or Hermitian matrices, guaranteeing that their measurable values (eigenvalues) are real numbers.
• Matrix: A rectangular array or grid of numbers, symbols, or expressions arranged in rows and columns, used to represent linear transformations, systems of linear equations, and mathematical states.

• Determinant: A single numerical value calculated from a square matrix that represents the scaling factor of the transformation, indicating how space or size changes, and whether a matrix is invertible (non-zero determinant).
The unit matrix acts like the number 1 in basic algebra. It represents the state of perfect preservation or "doing nothing."
• Zero Transformation (The Identity Operation): In coordinate space, if you multiply a vector (representing a direction or position) by a unit matrix, the vector remains completely unchanged.
- General meaning: It represents a unchanged system, or an operation that performs no rotation, no scaling, and no shift (e.g., viewing data from the same unchanging perspective).

• The Baseline State in Systems Analysis: In general systems, operations are often described by operators. The unit matrix represents a process where the output equals the input, or a state where no modification has occurred.
• Isotropic Scaling: When analyzing how structures react under equal pressure, the unit matrix represents uniform change from all sides, where shape does not distort across axes.

• Determinant (Scaling & Size Change): Geometrically, the determinant measures how much a spatial region expands, contracts, or flips under a transformation. A determinant of 1 means size-preserving flow, while a determinant of 0 indicates space has been flattened into a lower dimension (loss of information / non-invertible).

• Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (Principal Axes & Characteristic Values): Eigenvectors represent special directions in space that do not change direction during a matrix transformation, only their magnitude. In structural analysis, they represent principal axes or natural modes of response.

• Matrix Inverse (Reversibility & Undoing Operations): The inverse of a matrix undoes a linear transformation. In general operations, if a process is represented by matrix A, its inverse A⁻¹ represents restoring the system to its initial state, crucial for modeling reversible processes.

• Symmetric & Self-Adjoint Matrices (Real Properties): In mathematical modeling, well-balanced systems are represented by symmetric matrices, guaranteeing that their characteristic values (eigenvalues) are real numbers.

Relative error: The ratio of mean absolute error to the real value of the measured quantity is called relative error.

Accuracy is not the same as accuracy. Both accuracy and precision reflect how close a measurement is to an actual value, but accuracy reflects how close a measurement is to a known or accepted value, while precision reflects how reproducible measurements are, even if they are far from the accepted value.
The term 'Accuracy' denotes closeness of an experimental value to an experimental value of set or standard value.
Smaller the difference between the mean value and the true value, the larger is the accuracy.
For example, a student measured the mean value and he found the mean value 9.20 m/s². The standard value of g is 9.80 m/s²: Thus, accuracy = 9.80 − 9.20 = 0.60 m/s².

The accuracy of an instrument depends on how well its performance compares to a currently accepted standard. Uncertainties in measurement affect the accuracy of a measurement. Precision, however, is not affected because the accuracy depends on how well its performance compares to a currently accepted standard. The accuracy of an instrument is based on the accuracy of a measurement.

The term 'Precision' refers to how closely two or more measurements agree with one another. Precision is determined by the least count of the measuring instrument. The smaller the least count, the greater the precision.

For example, least count of Vernier calipers is often 0.01 cm and least count of a screw gauge is often 0.001 cm. So, measurement of small length using a screw gauge is more precise than a Vernier calipers.
Precision = individual value − mean value − Arithmetic mean value
In other words, precision gives the extent of agreement between the individual values of measurements.
This means that precision the difference between the individual values of repeated measurements, the smaller is the precision.
For example, a student was conducting an experiment to determine the value of g. He has taken many readings and the values are ranging from 9.80 m/s² to 9.802 m/s² with an average of 9.801 m/s².
Precision = least count of the measuring instrument. The smaller the least count, the greater the precision.

subject: chemistry
title: Law of Conservation of Mass — Statement
notes: **Statement:** matter (mass) can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction — the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products
This is why chemical equations must be balanced: the same total mass, and the same number of each type of atom, must appear on both sides

subject: chemistry
title: Law of Definite (Constant) Proportions — Statement
notes: **Statement:** a given chemical compound always contains its constituent elements combined together in the same fixed proportion by mass, regardless of the source of the compound or the method used to prepare it
This is verified experimentally by checking that the percentage composition of an element stays constant across independently prepared samples of the same compound

subject: chemistry
title: Law of Multiple Proportions — Statement
notes: **Statement:** when two elements combine to form more than one compound, the different masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other element are in a ratio of small whole numbers
This is verified by finding the mass of one element that combines with a fixed mass (e.g. 1 g) of the other element in each compound, then comparing those masses as a ratio

subject: chemistry
title: Law of Reciprocal Proportions — Statement
notes: **Statement:** when two different elements combine separately with a fixed mass of a third element, the ratio of the masses in which they do so is either the same as, or a simple whole-number multiple of, the ratio of masses in which the two elements combine directly with each other

This is verified by finding (i) the mass of each of the two elements that combines with a fixed mass of the third element (in two separate compounds), and (ii) the actual ratio of those two elements in a compound where they combine directly — then comparing the two ratios

title: Law of Multiple Proportions — Verifying a Simple Whole-Number Ratio
notes: **Step 1 — divide by the smallest value:** take the calculated list of masses (or mass ratios), pick the smallest one, and divide every value in the list by it — this forces the smallest value to become exactly 1

**Step 2 — clear any remaining decimals:** if a result still ends in .5, .33/.66, or .25/.75, multiply every value in the list by a common factor to clear it — ×2 for .5, ×3 for .33/.66, ×4 for .25/.75 — until all values are whole numbers
**Alternative for already-whole numbers:** find the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of the numbers and divide each by it — e.g. 12:16 → HCF = 4 → 3:4

subject: chemistry
title: Q: 12 g of carbon reacts with 32 g of hydrogen to produce 44 g of methane — which chemical law do these data illustrate?
notes: Since the mass before the reaction (44 g) equals the mass after (44 g), mass is neither created nor destroyed
**Answer: this illustrates the Law of Conservation of Mass**

subject: chemistry
title: Q: 20 g of CaCO₃ is heated and produces 11.2 g of CaO — calculate the weight of CO₂ produced
notes: By the Law of Conservation of Mass: mass of CaCO₃ = mass of CaO + mass of CO₂

subject: chemistry
title: Q: 6.3 g of NaHCO₃ added to 10 g of HCl solution leaves a 12 g residue — what is the mass of CO₂ released?
notes: Total mass of reactants: 6.3 g (NaHCO₃) + 10 g (HCl) = 16.3 g
By the Law of Conservation of Mass: total mass of reactants = total mass of products

subject: chemistry
title: Q: Two samples of common salt contain different masses of chlorine — show these results agree with the law of constant proportion
notes: **Data:** 0.25 g of sample 1 contains 0.1518 g of chlorine; 0.24 g of sample 2 contains 0.1458 g of chlorine
Since the percentage of chlorine is nearly identical in both samples (≈ 60.7%), regardless of sample size, this confirms the **Law of Constant (Definite) Proportion**

subject: chemistry
title: Q: Two copper oxide reduction experiments — show they illustrate the law of definite proportions
notes: **Experiment 1:** 1.375 g of CuO is reduced to 1.098 g of copper by dry hydrogen gas
**Experiment 2:** 1.179 g of metallic copper is formed from 1.476 g of copper oxide
The percentage of copper is essentially constant (≈ 79.9%) across both experiments, verifying the **Law of Definite Proportions**

subject: chemistry
title: Q: Determine the weight of oxide formed by heating 1 g of a carbonate (using the law of definite proportions)
notes: **Data:** 0.36 g of a metal burnt in oxygen yields 0.60 g of oxide; the carbonate of that metal contains 28.57% of the metal
From the oxide experiment: mass of metal = 0.36 g, mass of oxide = 0.60 g → ratio (mass of metal)/(mass of oxide) = 0.36/0.60 = **0.6**
From the carbonate experiment: 1 g of carbonate contains 28.57% metal → mass of metal in 1 g carbonate = 0.2857 g
By the Law of Definite Proportions, the metal-to-oxide ratio stays fixed at 0.6, so: 0.2857 / (mass of oxide) = 0.6

subject: chemistry
title: Q: Hydrogen and oxygen react separately to give H₂O₂ and H₂O — what law of stoichiometry is illustrated?
notes: Two elements (hydrogen and oxygen) combine to form more than one compound: H₂O and H₂O₂
For a fixed mass of hydrogen (2 g), the masses of oxygen that combine are 16 g (in H₂O) and 32 g (in H₂O₂)
Ratio of oxygen masses = 16 : 32 = **1 : 2** — a simple whole-number ratio
**Answer: this illustrates the Law of Multiple Proportions**

subject: chemistry
title: Q: A metal forms two oxides (11.9% and 21.2% oxygen) — show these data illustrate the law of multiple proportions
notes: Oxide 1: oxygen = 11.9%, metal = 100 − 11.9 = 88.1% → mass of oxygen combined with 1 g of metal = 11.9/88.1 = **0.135 g**
Oxide 2: oxygen = 21.2%, metal = 100 − 21.2 = 78.8% → mass of oxygen combined with 1 g of metal = 21.2/78.8 = **0.269 g**
Ratio of oxygen combining with a fixed mass (1 g) of metal: 0.135 : 0.269 ≈ **1 : 2**
Since 1:2 is a simple whole-number ratio, this confirms the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

subject: chemistry
title: Q: Element X forms three binary compounds with chlorine (50.08%, 66.73%, 74.95% Cl) — show how these illustrate the law of multiple proportions
notes: Compound 1: Cl = 50.08%, X = 49.92% → mass of Cl per gram of X = 50.08/49.92 = **1.003 g**
Compound 2: Cl = 66.73%, X = 33.27% → mass of Cl per gram of X = 66.73/33.27 = **2.006 g**
Compound 3: Cl = 74.95%, X = 25.05% → mass of Cl per gram of X = 74.95/25.05 = **2.992 g**
Ratio of chlorine masses combining with a fixed mass of X: 1.003 : 2.006 : 2.992 ≈ **1 : 2 : 3**
The simple whole-number ratio confirms the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

subject: chemistry
title: Q: Four hydrocarbons with % compositions (C 75%/H 25%, C 80%/H 20%, C 85.7%/H 14.3%, C 92.3%/H 7.7%) — prove the law of multiple proportions
notes: Find the mass of hydrogen combining with a fixed mass (1 g) of carbon in each: (a) 25/75 = 0.333 g; (b) 20/80 = 0.250 g; (c) 14.3/85.7 = 0.167 g; (d) 7.7/92.3 = 0.083 g
This simple whole-number ratio proves the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

subject: chemistry
title: Q: Three oxides of lead reduced in hydrogen — show this illustrates the law of multiple proportions
notes: **Data:** (i) 1.393 g of litharge gave 1.293 g of lead; (ii) 2.173 g of lead peroxide gave 1.882 g of lead; (iii) 1.712 g of red lead gave 1.552 g of lead
Find the mass of oxygen in each oxide by subtracting the lead mass from the total oxide mass: (i) 1.393 − 1.293 = 0.100 g; (ii) 2.173 − 1.882 = 0.291 g; (iii) 1.712 − 1.552 = 0.160 g
Find the mass of Pb combining with 1 g of O in each: (i) 1.293/0.100 = 12.93 g; (ii) 1.882/0.291 = 6.467 g; (iii) 1.552/0.160 = 9.700 g
Ratio: 12.93 : 6.467 : 9.700 — dividing all terms by 6.467 gives 2 : 1 : 1.5
Clearing the decimal by multiplying by 2: **4 : 2 : 3**
This simple whole-number ratio validates the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

subject: chemistry
title: Q: Nitrogen forms five oxides with oxygen (0.572 g, 1.14 g, 1.73 g, 2.28 g, 2.85 g of O per 1.09 g of N) — show how these illustrate the law of multiple proportions
notes: Fixed mass of nitrogen = 1.09 g in all five oxides
This simple whole-number ratio illustrates the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

subject: chemistry
title: Rutherford's Atomic Model — The Alpha-Particle Scattering Experiment
notes: **Experiment:** positively charged helium ions (α-particles) were fired at an ultra-thin gold foil
**Observation:** most α-particles passed straight through, undeflected
**Conclusion:** atoms are mostly empty space, with a tiny, dense, positively charged core called the **nucleus**

subject: chemistry
title: Rutherford's Atomic Model — The Stability Crisis (Flaw)
notes: According to classical electromagnetic theory, any accelerating charged particle — such as an electron moving in a circular orbit — must continuously radiate energy
If the electron continuously loses energy, it should spiral inward and eventually collapse into the nucleus
Rutherford's model gave no explanation for why atoms are actually stable and this collapse does not happen — this is the model's central defect

subject: chemistry
title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Postulates
notes: Niels Bohr resolved Rutherford's stability problem by introducing Planck's Quantum Theory
**Stationary orbits:** electrons revolve only in specific, fixed, non-radiating circular paths
**Energy quantization:** energy is only emitted or absorbed when an electron jumps from one orbit to another: ΔE = hν

subject: chemistry
title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Practical Application
notes: Successfully calculates the exact radius of orbits, the velocity of electrons, and the energy of an electron for hydrogen-like (single-electron) species: H, He⁺, Li²⁺

subject: chemistry
title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Defects
notes: Failed to predict the spectra of multi-electron atoms, such as Helium or Carbon
Could not explain the splitting of spectral lines under a magnetic field (**Zeeman Effect**) or an electric field (**Stark Effect**)

subject: chemistry
title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Absorption vs Emission
notes: While an electron stays within a single stationary orbit, it neither gains nor loses energy
**Jumping up** to an outer (higher-energy) track = absorbing energy
**Dropping down** to an inner (lower-energy) track = releasing energy as a flash of light (a photon)

subject: chemistry
title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Quantization of Angular Momentum
notes: The postulate that formally restricts which orbits are allowed: the electron's angular momentum is quantized in integer multiples of h/2π
**mvr = nh/2π**, where m = electron mass, v = electron velocity, r = orbit radius, n = 1, 2, 3... (the principal/orbit quantum number)

subject: chemistry
title: The Hydrogen Spectrum — Origin & Spectral Series
notes: When hydrogen gas is excited (e.g. electrically), electrons absorb energy and jump to higher tracks; when they fall back down to lower tracks, they release that exact energy as light of a specific wavelength
Because transitions happen only between specific fixed tracks, the emitted light forms discrete, sharp spectral lines rather than a continuous rainbow

Each spectral series corresponds to electrons landing on one specific base track (n₁): **Lyman** → n₁ = 1 (ultraviolet, invisible); **Balmer** → n₁ = 2 (the only series visible to the human eye, as coloured lines); **Paschen** → n₁ = 3 (infrared); **Brackett** → n₁ = 4 (infrared); **Pfund** → n₁ = 5 (far-infrared)

subject: chemistry
title: The Hydrogen Spectrum — Rydberg Equation
notes: 1/λ = R_H·(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), where λ = wavelength of emitted light, R_H = Rydberg constant, n₁ = lower (final) orbit, n₂ = higher (initial) orbit
The **series limit** (shortest wavelength, highest-energy line in a series) occurs as n₂ → ∞, giving the simplified form 1/λ = R_H/n₁²

subject: chemistry
title: Negative Electronic Energy & the Bohr Mechanical Model Critique
notes: **Negative electronic energy:** the energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit is taken as negative because the electron is bound to the nucleus; energy must be supplied to remove it. The most negative energy corresponds to the most stable (lowest) orbit, n = 1.

**Bohr mechanical model critique:** Bohr treated the electron as a tiny planet moving in a definite circular orbit, a purely mechanical picture. It could not explain why only certain orbits were allowed, nor why the electron did not radiate while moving in a stationary orbit.

**Quantum mechanical shift:** the mechanical orbit picture was replaced by a probabilistic, wave-based description in which the electron's position is described by a wave function rather than a fixed path.

**Schrödinger (1926):** Erwin Schrödinger introduced a wave equation whose solutions (wave functions, ψ) describe the electron's behaviour in three dimensions, giving rise to the modern orbital concept.
**Matter wave introduction:** the idea that particles such as electrons also behave as waves (de Broglie) laid the foundation for the wave-mechanical model.
**Einstein relation:** the equivalence of mass and energy, E = mc², connects the particle and wave descriptions of matter.

subject: chemistry
title: de Broglie Matter Waves & the Einstein–Planck Synthesis
notes: **Einstein–Planck synthesis:** combining Einstein's mass–energy equivalence E = mc² with Planck's quantum relation E = hν gives mc² = hν, linking a particle's mass to a wave frequency.
**de Broglie wavelength:** since ν = c/λ, the relation becomes mc = h/λ, so the wavelength of a moving particle is λ = h/(mv) = h/p, where p = mv is the momentum.
**Inverse mass dependence:** λ ∝ 1/m — heavier objects have extremely short wavelengths, which is why macroscopic objects show no observable wave behaviour.
**Macro-object wave negligibility:** for everyday objects the de Broglie wavelength is far smaller than any measurable scale, so wave effects are undetectable and classical mechanics applies.

**Bohr quantization deduced via waves:** if an electron is a standing wave, only orbits whose circumference is an integer multiple of the wavelength (2πr = nλ) are stable — this naturally reproduces Bohr's quantization of angular momentum.

**Heisenberg (1927) introduction:** the wave picture of the electron led Heisenberg to the uncertainty principle, which states that position and momentum cannot both be known precisely at the same time.

subject: chemistry
title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle (1927)
notes: **Statement:** it is impossible to determine simultaneously and with unlimited precision both the exact position (x) and the exact momentum (p) of a sub-atomic particle such as an electron.
**Mathematical form:** Δx · Δp ≥ h / 4π, where Δx is the uncertainty in position, Δp is the uncertainty in momentum and h = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant.
**Momentum form:** since Δp = m · Δv, the principle can be written as Δx · Δv ≥ h / (4πm) — for a heavy particle (large m) the product of uncertainties is tiny, so classical certainty is recovered.

**Wavelength measurement intrusion paradox:** observing an electron requires hitting it with photons; a shorter-wavelength photon gives better position information but delivers a larger kick that disturbs the electron's momentum, and vice versa — the act of measurement inevitably perturbs the system.
**Certainty / uncertainty complementarity:** precise knowledge of position destroys knowledge of momentum; the two are complementary and cannot be measured sharply at the same time.
**Probability space concept:** because the electron cannot be pinned to a definite point, its location is described by a probability distribution rather than a fixed path.

**Bohr definite-orbit fallacy:** a precise orbit would require exactly known position and momentum simultaneously, which the uncertainty principle forbids — so Bohr's definite circular orbits are physically impossible.

subject: chemistry
title: Schrödinger's Wave Equation & the Orbit→Orbital Shift
notes: **3D wave equation (1926):** Schrödinger extended de Broglie's idea to three dimensions. For a particle of mass m moving with total energy E and potential energy V, the wave function ψ satisfies (∂²ψ/∂x²) + (∂²ψ/∂y²) + (∂²ψ/∂z²) + (8π²m/h²)(E − V)ψ = 0.

**Wave function interpretation:** ψ itself has no direct physical meaning, but ψ² gives the probability of finding the electron in a small volume around a point — the electron cloud picture replaces the fixed orbit.

**Orbit → orbital paradigm shift:** an orbit is a definite circular path (Bohr), while an orbital is a three-dimensional region of space where the probability of finding the electron is high (usually taken as ~90–95%).

**Quantum numbers emerge naturally:** solving the equation for the hydrogen atom yields three integer quantum numbers (n, l, m) that characterise each allowed orbital, with a fourth (s) added later for spin.
**Subshell subdivision (s, p, d, f):** orbitals of the same principal shell are grouped into subshells labelled s, p, d and f, which differ in shape, energy and orientation.
**Spherical vs directional geometry:** s-orbitals are spherical, while p-orbitals are dumb-bell shaped and directional along the x, y and z axes; d and f orbitals have more complex shapes.
**Electron cloud mapping:** plotting ψ² in three dimensions gives the spatial probability maps (clouds) that replace Bohr's planar circular orbits.

subject: chemistry
title: Bohr–Bury Scheme (1921) — Subshell & Shell Capacity Rules
notes: **Bohr–Bury scheme (1921):** a set of rules for filling electrons into shells and subshells; electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels first (aufbau principle), so the order of filling runs 1s → 2s → 2p → 3s → 3p → 4s → 3d → 4p → 5s → 4d → 5p → 6s → 4f → 5d → 6p → 7s → 5f → 6d → 7p.
**Maximum shell capacity:** the maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n² — K: 2, L: 8, M: 18, N: 32.
**Subshell electron capacity:** s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14 electrons.
**Spatial configurations:** each subshell contains a fixed set of orbitals — s: 1, p: 3, d: 5, f: 7 — so a shell of principal quantum number n contains a total of n² orbitals.
**Valence shell limit:** the outermost (valence) shell can hold at most 8 electrons.
**Penultimate shell limit:** the second-outermost (penultimate) shell can hold at most 18 electrons; the third-outermost (antepenultimate) shell at most 32.
**Concentric capacity rings:** the electrons are distributed in concentric shells (K, L, M, N, …) around the nucleus, each ring accommodating its characteristic maximum.

subject: chemistry
title: Orbit vs Orbital — 10-Point Delta Table & the s-Orbital
notes: **Orbit vs orbital (10-point delta):** (1) an orbit is a definite circular path; an orbital is a region of high probability. (2) Orbits are planar; orbitals are three-dimensional. (3) Orbits come from Bohr's model; orbitals from quantum mechanics. (4) An orbit has a fixed radius; an orbital has no sharp boundary. (5) Orbits are described by one quantum number (n); orbitals by three (n, l, m). (6) Orbits imply exact position and momentum; orbitals obey the uncertainty principle. (7) Orbits can hold at most 2n² electrons; orbitals hold at most 2 electrons. (8) Orbits are circular; orbitals have varied shapes (spherical, dumb-bell, etc.). (9) Orbits are not observable; orbitals are mapped by probability density ψ². (10) Orbits were abandoned; orbitals are the accepted modern description.

**Electronic arrays:** the electron configurations of representative atoms follow the Bohr–Bury order — N (Z=7): 1s² 2s² 2p³; O (Z=8): 1s² 2s² 2p⁴; Ne (Z=10): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶; Mg (Z=12): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s²; Cl (Z=17): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵.

**s-orbital sharp metrics:** the s-orbital is spherical, non-directional, has no nodal plane, and its probability density is highest at the nucleus; it is the only orbital with a non-zero value at the nucleus.
**Opposite spins cancellation:** two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins (+½ and −½); their magnetic moments cancel, so a fully paired orbital contributes no net magnetism.
**Energy trend:** for a given principal shell the s-subshell lies lowest in energy: 1s < 2s < 3s < 4s < …

subject: chemistry
title: p-Orbital Geometry & the Four Quantum Numbers
notes: **p-orbital dumb-bell axes:** each p-orbital is dumb-bell (figure-of-eight) shaped with two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus, oriented along one of the three cartesian axes — pₓ, pᵧ and p_z — which are mutually perpendicular.
**Nodal plane zero points:** every p-orbital has a nodal plane through the nucleus where the probability of finding the electron is zero; for pₓ the nodal plane is the yz-plane, and so on.
**Degenerate energy states:** in a given shell all three p-orbitals have the same energy (they are degenerate); in the absence of a magnetic field they are indistinguishable energetically.

**Complex d/f shapes:** d-orbitals (l = 2) mostly have four-lobed cloverleaf shapes (with one two-lobed d_z² orbital plus a torus), while f-orbitals (l = 3) have even more complex multi-lobed geometries.

**Four quantum numbers categorical taxonomy:** every electron is uniquely specified by (1) the principal quantum number n (main energy level/shell), (2) the azimuthal quantum number l (subshell/shape), (3) the magnetic quantum number m (orbital orientation), and (4) the spin quantum number s (+½ or −½, direction of spin).
**Subshell maximum capacities:** s holds 2 electrons, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14.

subject: chemistry
title: Quantum Number Origins — Principal, Azimuthal & Subshell Metrics
notes: **Schrödinger/Spin origins breakdown:** the principal (n), azimuthal (l) and magnetic (m) quantum numbers arise naturally as the three quantum conditions of Schrödinger's wave equation; the spin quantum number (s) was added later from the Stern–Gerlach and Goudsmit–Uhlenbeck experiments.
**Principal quantum number (n):** fixes the main energy level and size of the orbital (shell). n = 1, 2, 3, …; larger n means a larger, higher-energy orbital farther from the nucleus.

**Sommerfeld hyperfine line expansions:** Arnold Sommerfeld introduced the azimuthal (orbital) quantum number l to explain the hyperfine splitting of spectral lines observed under high resolution, which Bohr's model could not explain.
**Subsidiary (azimuthal) quantum number (l):** fixes the subshell and shape of the orbital; l takes integer values 0 to n − 1 and is labelled by letters — s: 0, p: 1, d: 2, f: 3.
**Subshell orbital count:** each subshell contains 2l + 1 orbitals — for s (l=0): 1, p (l=1): 3, d (l=2): 5, f (l=3): 7.
**Subshell electron count:** each subshell holds a maximum of 2(2l + 1) electrons — for s: 2, p: 6, d: 10, f: 14.

subject: chemistry
title: Orbital Designation Matrix — Magnetic & Spin Quantum Numbers
notes: **Tabular orbital designation matrix:** the complete set of orbitals for a given shell is catalogued by combining n, l and m. For n = 2: l = 0 gives the single 2s orbital (m = 0); l = 1 gives the three 2p orbitals (m = +1, 0, −1), designated 2pₓ, 2pᵧ, 2p_z.
**Magnetic quantum number (m):** fixes the orientation of the orbital in space relative to an applied magnetic field; m takes 2l + 1 integer values from −l to +l.
**m value sets by subshell:** for l = 0: m = 0 (1 orbital); l = 1: m = +1, 0, −1 (3 orbitals); l = 2: m = +2, +1, 0, −1, −2 (5 orbitals); l = 3: m = +3, +2, +1, 0, −1, −2, −3 (7 orbitals).
**Total orbitals in a shell:** a shell of principal quantum number n contains exactly n² orbitals, combining all subshells of that shell.

**Landé–Zeeman magnetic orientations:** in an external magnetic field, the degenerate orbitals of a subshell split into distinct energy levels (Zeeman effect), each orbital having a different spatial orientation — one line splits into 2l + 1 components.
**Goudsmit–Uhlenbeck electron axial rotation:** Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck proposed that the electron itself spins about its own axis, producing an intrinsic angular momentum and a tiny magnetic dipole.
**Clockwise vs anticlockwise spins:** the electron's spin can be clockwise or anticlockwise, giving two spin states; the spin quantum number s takes only two values: +½ and −½.

subject: chemistry
title: Electron Spin Notation (↑ ↓) & Shell Mapping Matrices
notes: **Arrowhead vector notation:** electrons are drawn as arrowheads — an upward arrow (↑) represents spin +½ (clockwise) and a downward arrow (↓) represents spin −½ (anticlockwise); each box (orbital) can hold at most two arrows of opposite direction.

**Net zero paired magnetic field cancellation:** when an orbital contains two electrons with opposite spins, their magnetic moments are equal and opposite, so the net magnetic field of the pair is zero — the atom as a whole becomes diamagnetic for that pair.

**K shell complete mapping matrix:** the K shell (n = 1) contains only the single 1s orbital; it is filled as 1s¹ (one ↑) for hydrogen and 1s² (↑↓) for helium, where the pair is fully spin-compensated.

**L shell complete mapping matrix:** the L shell (n = 2) contains the 2s orbital plus three 2p orbitals (2pₓ, 2pᵧ, 2p_z). Filling follows Hund's rule — electrons first occupy each orbital singly with parallel spins before pairing: e.g. oxygen (1s² 2s² 2p⁴) shows one paired 2p box (↑↓) and two half-filled boxes (↑, ↑).

**Arrow direction convention:** in electron configuration notation the order of filling is drawn left-to-right across the orbitals of the subshell, and the last electron added determines the arrow direction for half-filled orbitals.

subject: chemistry
title: The Atom & Dalton's Atomic Theory
notes: **The composition of matter** was studied in the 18th century by different scientists.

**Atom definition:** all matter is made of millions of tiny particles called atoms. The word 'atom' comes from the Greek (a = absence, tomos = cut), meaning indivisible or indestructible — atoms are the smallest units of matter.
**Dalton's atomic theory (1808):** the concept of the atom was first put forward by the English chemist John Dalton, and his theory laid the foundation of modern atomic theory.
**Discovery of subatomic particles:** towards the end of the 19th century it became known that the atom consists of still smaller particles such as electrons, protons and neutrons.
**Further subatomic particles:** subsequent studies led to the discovery of meson, quark, gluon, neutrino, and antiparticles like positron, antiproton, antineutron etc.

**Fundamental particles:** the small particles present in an atom are called subatomic particles; more than 30 have been discovered. Electron, proton and neutron are the principal subatomic particles, generally referred to as fundamental particles.
Example subatomic particles: electrons, protons, neutrons, a positron (e⁺), meson, neutrino (π±), quark.

subject: chemistry
title: The Electron — Discovery & Properties of Cathode Rays
notes: **Electron definition:** an electron is a negatively charged subatomic particle denoted with the symbol e⁻.
**Discovery (1897):** the electron was first discovered by Joseph John Thomson as a result of a discharge tube experiment.

**Discharge tube experiment:** Thomson filled gas in a specially designed glass tube provided with metal electrodes and passed high voltage electricity at low pressure (10,000 Volts at 10⁻² mmHg) through the tube.
**Cathode rays:** as a result, some rays started to flow from the cathode towards the anode, which are called cathode rays.
**Naming:** the term electron was given by George Johnstone Stoney (in 1891).

**Properties of cathode rays:** (a) they cast a shadow of an object on their way; (b) they travel in a straight line; (c) they are deflected towards the anode of the applied electric field, indicating they carry a negative charge; (d) they produce a heating effect when struck to a thin metal coil; (e) they can penetrate a thin sheet of metals; (f) they cause fluorescence on a zinc sulphide screen; (g) they ionize the gas through which they pass.
**Conclusion:** the observation of the above properties led to the conclusion that cathode rays carry a negative charge with a certain mass.
**Naming as electrons:** J.J. Thomson named cathode rays as electrons, symbolized with e⁻ or as a beta particle.
**Charge and mass:** the charge on an electron is -1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs and the mass is 9.1 × 10⁻²⁸ g, which is equal to 1/1837th of the mass of a hydrogen atom.
**e/m determination:** J.J. Thomson determined the e/m (specific charge) value of the electron and Millikan determined the charge of the electron.
**e/m order:** the increasing order of the value of e/m is neutron < alpha-ray < proton < electron.

subject: chemistry
title: The Proton — Discovery & Properties of Anode Rays
notes: **Proton definition:** a proton is a positively charged subatomic particle denoted with the symbol p⁺.

**Context of discovery:** it was discovered after the discovery of electrons, with the assumption that positive particles must also exist alongside negative particles since an atom is electrically neutral.
**Discovery (1886):** the proton was discovered by Eugen Goldstein by a discharge tube experiment like that for electrons.
**Experiment:** he passed high voltage electricity through a discharge tube filled with hydrogen gas and provided with a perforated metal cathode.
**Low pressure:** the discharge was carried out at low pressure.
**Canal rays:** he observed rays travelling opposite to the cathode rays; these were deflected towards the cathode of the applied field and thus called anode rays, positive rays, or canal rays.

**Properties of anode rays:** (a) they cast a shadow of the objects in their path; (b) they travel in a straight line; (c) they are deflected towards the cathode of the applied electric or magnetic field; (d) they cause a heating effect on metal coils; (e) they rotate a small paddle wheel placed on their path.
